stages.prompt: MSPC, Calculation: play the plan out. Black's replies come automatically.

12.Rxe4.note: Take with the rook. This is the whole point of Re1: the rook lands on an active square and the bishop keeps the diagonal for the attack.

alt.Bxe4: Also playable, but it gives a normal, dull position with far fewer attacking chances.

bad.Qe2: Does not recapture, and Black keeps the extra piece activity.

12...Nf6.note: Black develops the knight to the natural square.

13.Rh4.note: The rook lift. It attacks h7 together with the bishop on d3.

13...Be7.note: Black develops. Note how natural Black's moves have been and he is already in danger.

14.Bf4.note: The bishop develops with tempo against the queen on c7.

debrief.t: 11...Nxe4 left a knight on e4 that could be recaptured in two ways. The decision is which piece.
Specific feature: the rook on e4 can swing to h4 and attack h7 with the bishop on d3. The bishop on e4 would have no such future.
Priority: keep the attacking pieces active. The rook recapture is the reason Re1 was played.
Calculate the alternatives: 12.Bxe4 is playable but dull, and 12.Qe2? does not recapture at all.

The plan: recapture with the rook, lift it to h4, bring the bishop to f4 with tempo and aim everything at the black king. Black's natural developing moves never solve the problem, because h7 is attacked twice and the pieces that could help are far from the kingside. The honest assessment: the engine gives White a pleasant edge, about seven tenths of a pawn, and the practical chances are much bigger than the number suggests.

think.title: Build the wedge: e5 supported by f4
think.brief: You are White in the Colle against 5...Nbd7 when the e4 break does not work. You have traded on e5 and recaptured with the d-pawn, and Black has just attacked it with ...Nd7. The pawn on e5 now has to be defended in the right way.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Move: what did 9...Nd7 do?

options.text: It attacks the e5-pawn, and nothing of mine defends it yet.
options.why: Correct. The knight attacks the pawn and no White piece guards it. Count the defenders first.

options.text: It attacks my bishop on d3.
options.why: The knight on d7 attacks b6, b8, c5, e5, f6 and f8, not d3.

options.text: It threatens ...Nxe5 only after ...f6.
options.why: The threat is already there. e5 is attacked by the d7-knight and undefended.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Specifics: tap the square the f-pawn goes to, so that e5 is supported by a pawn.
stages.hint: The pawn on f2 supports e5 from the neighbouring file.
stages.explain: f4. It supports e5 with a pawn, so the knight on d7 cannot take it, and the d4, e3 and f4 chain stands behind the wedge.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Priorities: which move carries out the plan?

options.text: 10.f4: support the pawn with the f-pawn and complete the wedge.
options.why: Correct. The wedge gives space, a permanent outpost and a clear attacking direction.

options.text: 10.Nf3: guard e5 with the knight.
options.why: It guards the pawn but blocks the f-pawn, so the wedge can never be completed. You trade the outpost for a passive set-up. Engine: about two thirds of a pawn worse than f4.

options.text: 10.Qc2: develop the queen and eye h7.
options.why: It does not defend e5. 10...Nxe5 wins the pawn with tempo.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Calculation: play the plan out. Black's replies come automatically.

10.f4.note: The wedge is built: a pawn on e5 supported by f4. The structure appears in every Colle where e4 does not work.

bad.Nf3: Blocks the f-pawn. The wedge is lost.

10...f5.note: Black's only lever against the wedge is a pawn move on the f-file.

11.exf6.note: Essential: take en passant, or Black gets a comfortable position.

12.e4.note: You take the centre. Black has a space problem on the queenside as well.

13.Be2.note: The right retreat. From e2 the bishop eyes g4 and f3, hitting e6 and d5.

bad.Bc2: Less accurate. The bishop stays passive on c2, and Be2 is simpler and better.

14.e5.note: You push on in the centre and play for the kingside break.

debrief.t: 9...Nd7 attacks the e5-pawn, and nothing of White's defends it yet.
Specific feature: the wedge pawn on e5 can be supported by the f-pawn from f4, and the squares d4, e3 and f4 form the chain behind it.
Priority: defend with a pawn, not with a piece. 10.f4 keeps all the options and keeps the outpost permanent.
Calculate the alternatives: 10.Nf3? blocks the pawn, and 10.Qc2? loses e5. After 10...f5 the en passant capture is essential.

The plan: keep the wedge on e5, answer ...f5 with exf6 en passant, take the centre with e4 and play for the kingside break. The wedge gives space, a permanent outpost and a clear attacking direction. The costs are the d5-square and a slightly loose king if you push too far. The honest assessment: the engine sees the position as about equal. The wedge plan gives a long-term initiative rather than a forced advantage.

think.title: Undermine the centre from the wing: c4 against the knight
think.brief: You are White in the Phoenix. Instead of the central break you gained queenside space with b4 and b5. Black has just attacked your bishop on d5 with ...Ne7. The queenside pawns now turn from slow moves into direct attacks on the centre.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Move: what did 15...Ne7 do?

options.text: It attacks my bishop on d5.
options.why: Correct. The knight attacks d5, so the bishop has to be defended, moved or exchanged.

options.text: It attacks my pawn on b5.
options.why: The knight on e7 attacks c6, c8, d5, f5, g6 and g8, not b5.

options.text: It threatens ...f4 trapping my bishop.
options.why: The bishop on d5 has several squares and the threat is not real.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Specifics: tap the White piece that is attacked and needs a decision.
stages.hint: The black knight on e7 attacks it.
stages.explain: d5. Your bishop is attacked by the knight. Defending it with a pawn changes the structure in your favour.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Priorities: which move carries out the plan?

options.text: 16.c4: defend the bishop with the pawn and keep undermining the centre from the wing.
options.why: Correct. The queenside pawns are direct attacks on the centre, and c4 supports the bishop on d5.

options.text: 16.Bb3: retreat the bishop.
options.why: It keeps the bishop but gives up the central grip. Engine: about two thirds of a pawn worse than c4.

options.text: 16.Ng5: attack the f7-pawn and ignore the bishop.
options.why: 16...Nxd5 17.Qxd5 and the bishop is traded, the pressure on the centre is gone and the position is equal. Engine: no edge instead of a clear one.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Calculation: play the plan out. Black's replies come automatically.

16.c4.note: More undermining. Note how your slow queenside moves are direct attacks on the centre.

bad.Bb3: A retreat that gives up the central grip.
bad.Ng5: 16...Nxd5 17.Qxd5 and the central pressure is gone.

17.Qxd5.note: You recapture with the queen and keep the centre under pressure.

17...e4.note: Black pushes the pawn, but the e4-pawn becomes a target.

18.Rfd1.note: White grabs the initiative. The e4-pawn is weak, Black's king is airy and every white piece has a job.

debrief.t: 15...Ne7 attacks the bishop on d5, so you have to decide how to defend it.
Specific feature: Black's centre pawns on e5 and f5 are overextended, and your queenside pawns on b5 and c4 attack them.
Priority: defend with a pawn that also attacks. 16.c4 supports d5 and keeps the initiative.
Calculate the alternatives: 16.Bb3 retreats and loses the grip, and 16.Ng5 allows ...Nxd5 and the pressure disappears.

The plan: the hypermodern method. Attack the centre from the wing, so that the slow queenside pawns become direct attacks. Black's overextended pawns have no stable support, so every piece trade makes the e4 and e5 pawns weaker. The honest assessment: the engine gives White an edge of about three quarters of a pawn, and the course line is a model of how the Phoenix idea works, not a forced win.

think.title: Retreat to c2: the opposite-coloured bishops favour the attacker
think.brief: You are White in a Master-level Phoenix. You have a queenside bind with c5 and b4, and Black has just played ...f5, attacking your bishop on e4. The bishop has to decide where to go. One square is more accurate than the others.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Move: what did 21...f5 do?

options.text: It attacks my bishop on e4 and loosens Black's own kingside.
options.why: Correct. The pawn attacks e4, and it also leaves weaknesses on e5 and g5 and opens his king.

options.text: It threatens ...f4 winning a piece.
options.why: The f5-pawn does not threaten anything beyond the attack on e4. The bishop has several retreat squares.

options.text: It defends the d4-pawn.
options.why: The pawn on d4 is defended by other pieces. The move f5 does not touch it.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Specifics: tap the White piece that Black's bishop will trade, leaving opposite-coloured bishops.
stages.hint: Black's light-squared bishop goes to d5 and takes it.
stages.explain: f3. After Qd3 and ...Bxf3 Qxf3, you keep a light-squared bishop against Black's dark-squared bishop with queens and rooks on the board, and that favours the attacker.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Priorities: which retreat is the most accurate?

options.text: 22.Bc2: keep the bishop on the diagonal towards h7 and prepare Qd3.
options.why: Correct. It is more accurate than 22.Bd3. Next comes Qd3 and Bxf3, leaving Black with a clearly inferior bishop.

options.text: 22.Bd3: retreat to d3.
options.why: Playable, but the course shows it as the less accurate version. Engine: clearly less than Bc2.

options.text: 22.Bxb7: grab the pawn.
options.why: 22...Qxb7 and you have given a bishop for a pawn. Engine: Black is about two pawns better.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Calculation: play the plan out. Black's replies come automatically.

22.Bc2.note: More accurate than 22.Bd3. The bishop keeps the b1-h7 diagonal.

alt.Bd3: Also playable, but the course marks it as less accurate.

bad.Bxb7: 22...Qxb7 and the bishop is lost for a pawn.

22...Bd5.note: Black offers a trade of the light-squared bishops.

23.Qd3.note: The queen supports f3 and is ready to take.

23...Bxf3.note: Black trades the bishop for the knight.

24.Qxf3.note: White holds a pleasant edge. Opposite-coloured bishops do not mean a draw when there are major pieces on the board. Here they favour the attacker.

debrief.t: 21...f5 attacks the bishop on e4 and loosens Black's own king.
Specific feature: the c5-pawn gives White a queenside bind, Black's king is airy after ...f5, and the bishop pair is about to become an opposite-coloured pair.
Priority: keep the bishop on the diagonal that points at the king. 22.Bc2 prepares Qd3.
Calculate the alternatives: 22.Bd3 is playable but weaker, and 22.Bxb7? loses material.

The plan: Bc2, Qd3, trade the knight for Black's bishop and play with opposite-coloured bishops and major pieces on the board. In that structure the side with the initiative has an extra attacker, because Black's dark-squared bishop cannot defend the squares that White's light-squared bishop attacks. The honest assessment: the engine gives White a clear edge, about two pawns. Opposite-coloured bishops are a drawish sign only when the major pieces are gone.

think.title: The Meran break: ...c5 against the big centre
think.brief: You are Black in the Meran. Everything so far has been preparation: ...dxc4, ...b5, ...Bb7 and ...a6. White has just claimed the full centre with 10.e4. Now the move you prepared must be played.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Move: what did 10.e4 change?

options.text: White claimed the centre with pawns on d4 and e4 and threatens e4-e5, hitting my f6-knight.
options.why: Correct. The pawn centre is the structure, and e5 is the threat. Read the threat first.

options.text: It wins my pawn on b5.
options.why: The b5-pawn is defended by the a6-pawn and the c6-pawn. Nothing is hanging.

options.text: It attacks my bishop on b7.
options.why: A pawn on e4 attacks d5 and f5. The bishop on b7 is not attacked.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Specifics: tap the square where your pawn breaks the centre.
stages.hint: It is the pawn on c6 that attacks the d4-pawn.
stages.explain: c5. The break hits d4 and fights for the centre at once. This is the single biggest reason to prefer the Semi-Slav over a passive set-up where Black accepts a cramped position.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Priorities: which move carries out the plan?

options.text: 10...c5: the central break, prepared by ...a6.
options.why: Correct. Everything so far was preparation for this move.

options.text: 10...b4: push the queenside pawn at once.
options.why: It loses time and leaves the centre to White. Engine: clearly worse than ...c5.

options.text: 10...Nb6: retreat the knight and keep everything protected.
options.why: A passive move that gives White the centre for free. Engine: clearly worse than ...c5.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Calculation: play the plan out. White's replies come automatically.

10...c5.note: The central break. The Semi-Slav asks for a fight in the centre at the earliest opportunity.

bad.b4: Too slow, and White keeps the centre.

11.d5.note: White pushes. This is the usual reply.

11...Qc7.note: Step off the d-file first. In every Meran line, ask where your queen stands before the centre opens.

12...fxe6.note: Recapture with the f-pawn. The f-file opens for the rook and the centre stays intact. The e6-pawn looks loose, but it is defended three times.

debrief.t: 10.e4 gave White the centre and threatens e5. Name the threat before you reply.
Specific feature: I own a queenside majority and a bishop on b7, White owns the centre, and c5 is the square where the two meet.
Priority: strike the centre at once. 10...c5 is the move the whole set-up was built for.
Calculate the alternatives: 10...b4? and 10...Nb6? both give White the centre for free. After 11.d5 Qc7 12.dxe6 fxe6 the f-file is yours.

The plan: use the queenside majority and the bishop on b7, open the f-file after the exchange on e6 and keep the king safe. White cannot easily attack the e6-pawn, so the extra space in the centre does not turn into an attack. The honest assessment: the Meran is sharp and the engine sees it as roughly equal. Remember three things: the bishop on b7 and the queenside majority are your assets, the f-file belongs to you, and you must watch your king.

think.title: Recapture with the queen: keep the bishop pair
think.brief: You are Black in the Moscow Variation. After 5...h6 White has given up the bishop pair with 6.Bxf6. You must recapture, and the choice decides your structure and your plan for the next ten moves.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Move: what did 6.Bxf6 change?

options.text: White gave up his bishop pair for a knight and extra space, and I must recapture on f6.
options.why: Correct. White settles for a small structural plus and you get the bishop pair.

options.text: It wins my knight for free.
options.why: The knight is recaptured by the queen or the g-pawn. It is an exchange, not a win.

options.text: It threatens mate on f7.
options.why: Nothing is attacking f7 with enough force. The only urgent matter is the recapture.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Specifics: tap the square where the queen finds a home after ...g6.
stages.hint: After ...g6 the queen can step back along the long diagonal.
stages.explain: g7. The pawn move gives the queen a home on g7 instead of standing loose on f6, and it prepares ...Bg7 with the dark-squared bishop that has no opponent left.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Priorities: which recapture fits the plan?

options.text: 6...Qxf6: recapture with the queen, keep a healthy structure and the bishop pair.
options.why: Correct. You own the two bishops, have no structural weakness and develop easily with ...Bd6 or ...Be7, ...O-O and ...Rd8.

options.text: 6...gxf6: recapture with the pawn.
options.why: It doubles your pawns for nothing. Engine: clearly worse than Qxf6.

options.text: 6...Qb6: ignore the recapture and attack b2.
options.why: You are a piece down. Engine: about three pawns worse.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Calculation: play the plan out. White's replies come automatically.

6...Qxf6.note: Recapture with the queen, not the pawn. You own the bishop pair and have no weakness.

bad.Qb6: Does not recapture. A piece is lost.

7.e3.note: White develops and keeps a small space advantage.

7...Nd7.note: The knight develops towards e5 and c5, your two breaks.

8...dxc4.note: Take on c4 with tempo on the bishop.

9...g6.note: The key little move. It looks slow, but it gives the queen a home on g7 and prepares ...Bg7.

10...Bg7.note: The bishop takes its diagonal. A pleasant position for Black: play ...e5 or ...c5 at the right moment.

debrief.t: 6.Bxf6 gave up the bishop pair for a small lead in space. You must recapture.
Specific feature: you own the two bishops, your pawn structure is healthy, and the dark-squared bishop has no opponent left on the board.
Priority: structure and bishops. Recapture with the queen and develop without weaknesses.
Calculate the alternatives: 6...gxf6? damages the structure, and 6...Qb6? loses a piece. The line 6...Qxf6 7.e3 Nd7 8.Bd3 dxc4 9.Bxc4 g6 gives the queen its home.

The plan: develop calmly, play ...g6 and ...Bg7, and free the position with ...e5 or ...c5 once all your pieces are ready. White has only a small space advantage and no target, so he cannot punish you for waiting. The honest assessment: this is balanced and comfortable, and it teaches patience. The bishop pair will speak when the position opens.

think.title: A typical Meran moment: ...Bxg3 against d5
think.brief: You are Black in the Meran. You have played ...c5, and White has just pushed d5 and attacks the e6-pawn. His knight on g3 is attacked by your bishop. This is a typical Meran moment where concrete calculation matters more than memory.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Move: what did 12.d5 change?

options.text: It attacks my e6-pawn and challenges the centre; I have to choose how to react.
options.why: Correct. The push attacks e6 and cramps my pieces. Name the threat before you pick a reply.

options.text: It wins my c5-pawn.
options.why: A pawn on d5 attacks c6 and e6. The c5-pawn is not attacked.

options.text: It traps my bishop on d6.
options.why: The bishop has the squares g3, e7 and b8 and is not trapped.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Specifics: tap the White piece that my bishop on d6 attacks.
stages.hint: The bishop on d6 looks down the b8-h2 diagonal.
stages.explain: g3. The knight on g3 is attacked by the bishop. Taking it changes the structure before White can follow up in the centre.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Priorities: which move carries out the plan?

options.text: 12...Bxg3: capture the knight at once.
options.why: Correct. Captures first: the bishop takes the knight on its own terms.

options.text: 12...Nb6: attack the d5-pawn with the knight.
options.why: It ignores the knight on g3 and gives White the initiative. Engine: about one pawn worse than Bxg3.

options.text: 12...Qb6: attack the pawn on b2.
options.why: It ignores the central pressure. Engine: about one pawn worse than Bxg3.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Calculation: play the plan out. White's replies come automatically.

12...Bxg3.note: A typical Meran moment. The course does not give a full sequence here: the line is too concrete to summarise safely.

alt.Bxd5: Also good: the engine rates it about equal to Bxg3.

bad.Nb6: Ignores the knight on g3 and gives White the initiative.
bad.Qb6: Ignores the pressure in the centre and loses time.

13.dxe6.note: White plays the in-between move dxe6. Material flows back and forth for several moves before the position settles.

13...Qc7.note: The queen move is the safety move, and it keeps appearing in this structure. Black is fine.

debrief.t: 12.d5 attacks the e6-pawn and cramps my pieces. The bishop on d6 attacks the knight on g3.
Specific feature: the knight on g3 is attacked, the e6-pawn is attacked, and the diagonal b8-h2 belongs to my bishop.
Priority: captures first. 12...Bxg3 removes the attacked knight and keeps the initiative.
Calculate: after 12...Bxg3 13.dxe6 Qc7 Black is fine. The alternatives 12...Nb6? and 12...Qb6? both give White the initiative.

The plan: take the knight, answer dxe6 with ...Qc7, and rely on the safety of the king and the activity of the pieces. This line is concrete and sharp, so work through the full theory later. The honest assessment: the engine sees the position as about equal. Do not try to calculate it all at the board: learn the pattern and the safety move.

think.title: Meet e4 with ...b4: counter before e5 forks
think.brief: You are Black in the Meran at Advanced depth. White has played 13.e4 and threatens to push the pawn to e5. You must counter at once with a pawn move on the queenside, otherwise a fork follows.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Move: what did 13.e4 threaten?

options.text: e4-e5, forking my bishop on d6 and my knight on f6.
options.why: Correct. A pawn on e5 attacks d6 and f6 at once. This is the threat you must meet.

options.text: e4xd5, winning a pawn.
options.why: There is no pawn on d5 for the e4-pawn to capture.

options.text: Nothing yet: it only claims space.
options.why: It is a real threat: e5 forks two pieces. Read the threat first.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Specifics: tap the White knight that the pawn on b4 will attack.
stages.hint: Your b-pawn can attack it from b4.
stages.explain: c3. The knight on c3 supports the push to e5. Attack it with ...b4 and the structure changes before e5 comes.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Priorities: which move meets the threat with a counter-threat?

options.text: 13...b4: attack the knight on c3 first.
options.why: Correct. A counter-threat that deflects the knight before e5 can be played.

options.text: 13...Be7: retreat the bishop out of the fork.
options.why: 14.e5 attacks the knight, and after 14...Nd5 15.Bxh7+ White wins material. Engine: clearly worse than ...b4.

options.text: 13...c5: strike in the centre at once.
options.why: It leaves the b5-pawn undefended: 14.Bxb5 wins a pawn. Engine: clearly worse than ...b4.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Calculation: play the plan out. White's replies come automatically.

13...b4.note: Attack the knight on c3 before White can play e5.

bad.Be7: 14.e5 attacks the knight and after 14...Nd5 15.Bxh7+ White wins material.
bad.c5: Leaves the b5-pawn undefended: 14.Bxb5 wins a pawn.

14...axb4.note: Black recaptures and keeps the pawn on b4.

15.e5.note: White pushes the pawn and forks the bishop and the knight.

15...bxc3.note: Black takes the knight on c3 first.

17...Bxf3.note: Black takes the knight on f3. The position is equal and very sharp.

debrief.t: 13.e4 threatens e5, which forks the bishop on d6 and the knight on f6.
Specific feature: the c3-knight supports the push, and my b-pawn can attack it from b4.
Priority: a counter-threat. 13...b4 meets the threat with a threat.
Calculate the main line: 14.axb4 axb4 15.e5 bxc3 16.exd6 c5 17.dxc5 Bxf3 leads to a sharp, balanced position. 13...Be7? loses material to 14.e5 and 13...c5? loses the b5-pawn.

The plan: use the tactical resource ...b4 to deflect the knight and then play ...c5. This is a sharp line, so the moves must be known. The honest assessment: the engine sees the position as equal. The point is the timing, not a long-term pawn structure.

think.title: Deflect the knight with ...b4, then strike with ...c5
think.brief: You are Black in a Master-level Meran. You have played ...Rc8 and ...b4, and White has retreated his knight to a4. The knight on a4 now eyes c5, the square of your central break.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Move: what did 13.Na4 change?

options.text: The knight retreated from c3 and now eyes c5, so my central break looks prevented.
options.why: Correct. The knight on a4 covers c5 and b6. Check what the retreat attacks before you continue.

options.text: It attacks my bishop on d6.
options.why: The knight on a4 does not attack d6. It attacks b6, c5, b2 and c3.

options.text: It forks my queen and my rook.
options.why: The knight on a4 attacks b6, c5, c3 and b2. There is no fork on my queen and rook.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Specifics: tap the square of your central break.
stages.hint: The pawn on c6 wants to advance.
stages.explain: c5. The break has been prepared by ...b4, which pulled the knight to a4. The pattern is: ...b4 first to deflect the knight, then ...c5.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Priorities: which move carries out the plan?

options.text: 13...c5: strike at once, now that the knight has been deflected.
options.why: Correct. This is the key resource of the structure: ...b4 first, then ...c5.

options.text: 13...a5: support the b4-pawn.
options.why: It is too slow and White consolidates. Engine: clearly worse than ...c5.

options.text: 13...bxa3: take the pawn.
options.why: It opens the b-file for White and gives up the pressure. Engine: clearly worse than ...c5.

stages.prompt: MSPC, Calculation: play the plan out. White's replies come automatically.

13...c5.note: The key resource. The knight was deflected by ...b4, and now ...c5 hits the centre.

bad.bxa3: Gives up the pressure and opens the b-file for White.

14...Nxc5.note: Black recaptures with the knight and is fine.

debrief.t: 13.Na4 retreated the knight and covers c5, but it is no longer on c3.
Specific feature: the knight was deflected from c3 by ...b4, and the c5-break is the key square of the structure.
Priority: strike while the knight is offside. 13...c5 uses the deflection.
Calculate the alternatives: 13...a5? is too slow and 13...bxa3? gives up the pressure. After 14.dxc5 Nxc5 Black is fine.

The plan: deflect the knight with ...b4, strike with ...c5, and use the open lines and the bishop on b7. White's knight on a4 is badly placed, so the pawn break wins time. The honest assessment: the engine rates this position as clearly good for Black, around one pawn, but it is a concrete resource, not a general rule. Know the pattern and check the position each time.

groups.name: Caro-Kann
groups.intro: 1...c6 against 1.e4. A solid centre, a light-squared bishop that gets out before ...e6, and structures that repeat, so your plans transfer from game to game.

groups.name: Colle-Koltanowski
groups.intro: d4, Nf3, e3, Bd3, c3 and Nbd2 against almost everything, then the e3-e4 break. Minimal theory and a plan you can repeat every game.

groups.name: Semi-Slav
groups.intro: 1...c6 against 1.d4 as well: the Slav triangle, the Meran and Moscow plans, and a calm answer to the London.

groups.name: Colle Model Games
groups.intro: Complete model games that reach your Colle-Koltanowski positions, grouped by the branch of the tree they follow. Play through each game once, then read the notes.

groups.name: Black Model Games
groups.intro: Complete model games that reach your Semi-Slav and Caro-Kann positions, grouped by the branch of the tree they follow. Play through each game once, then read the notes.

middlegame.title: Knight on e5: build the wedge (vs the fianchetto)
middlegame.brief: You are White in the Colle against 4...b6. The knight reached e5 on move 6 and Black has castled. Do not drift: choose the move that makes the outpost permanent.

stages.prompt: Which move forces the e5-structure, and why?

options.text: 8.f4: builds the wedge: d4, e3 and f4 stand behind the e5-knight, so it can never be kicked out cheaply.
options.why: Correct. The knight needs a pawn chain, not just a good square. f4 turns a temporary outpost into a permanent one.

options.text: 8.Qe2: develops the queen and keeps everything flexible.
options.why: The e3-pawn blocks the queen from e5, so the knight still has only d4 behind it. Flexible is not the same as forcing.

options.text: 8.Ndf3: guards e5 a second time with the other knight.
options.why: It does guard e5, but it blocks your own f-pawn, so f4 can never arrive. You trade the outpost wedge for a passive set-up.

stages.prompt: Tap the square your knight must never leave voluntarily.
stages.hint: It is the square your d4-pawn already covers and f4 will cover too.
stages.explain: e5. It is the permanent outpost. The weak dark squares f6, g6 and h6 around Black's king are what it points at.

stages.prompt: MSPC Priorities: which plan is yours at Beginner level in this structure?

options.text: Challenge e5 directly with ...Nc6 or ...Nd7-f6 pressure, or prepare ...f6.
options.why: That is the opponent's plan at this level, not yours. Know it, because it is what you will face on the other side of the board.

options.text: Trade the e5 knight voluntarily to simplify the position.
options.why: This is the typical mistake in this structure, and the companion names it as the thing to avoid.

options.text: Pile onto e5: Ne5, f4, Bd3, Qe2 or Qc2. Never trade the e5 knight voluntarily.
options.why: Correct. This is your plan at this level: it follows from the Specifics of the structure.

stages.prompt: Play it out. Black's replies come automatically.

8.f4.note: The wedge is built. Black's only lever against e5 is ...f6 or ...f5, and both cost him kingside dark squares.

8...c5.note: Black switches to the queenside, which is where his counterplay has to come from. His light-squared bishop is stuck behind d5.

9.c3.note: You hold d4 and keep the centre solid. No need to hurry on the kingside.

9...Ba6.note: Black trades off your best light-squared bishop to get play on the other wing.

10.Bxa6.note: You accept the trade: the e5 knight stays, and that is the piece that matters in this structure.

debrief.t: Move 6-8, once Black shows no intention of contesting e5. This is a deliberate plan switch away from the c3/e4 plan, not a forced continuation. It does NOT work against a fianchetto (...g6/...Bg7 covers e5), so there you keep the normal c3/e4 plan. Correction: Earlier text described only the knight form of this structure. Both forms appear in your trees, so both are taught here.

Centre: Closed. d4-e3(-f4) against Black's d5/e6 chain. The position only opens when you choose to (f4-f5 or e3-e4). Structure: The e5 square is your permanent outpost; the weak dark-square complex around f6/g6/h6 is Black's long-term problem. Black's break is ...f6 (or ...f5).

1) Keep the e5 piece and support it with f4. 2) Bring the queen to e2 or c2 and the rooks to e1/f1. 3) Watch Black's only lever, ...f6/...f5: answer ...f5 by exf6 and e3-e4 (verified in the 5...Nbd7 line: 10.f4 f5 11.exf6 Nxf6 12.e4). 4) Decide whether to storm with g4-g5 or switch to the centre.

WHY THIS PLAN WORKS: Black has to attack e5 to get counterplay and he has nothing to attack it with once ...g6/...Bg7 is missing. Every ...f5, ...g6 or ...h6 loosens the dark squares f6-g6-h6 for good, so his kingside gets weaker with each move he spends on defence. The engine does not call it winning: the position stays about equal, and the point is a durable plan with a clean fallback in minor-piece endings.

Calculate Black's ...f5 break before you play f4 (what happens to e5 and e3?) and every capture on e5. In position (b) the engine confirms 10.f4 is clearly best (0.0 versus -0.65 for the next move). In position (a) 8.f4 is within 0.05 pawns of 8.b3, so the choice is about the plan, not a tactic.

middlegame.topic: The e5 outpost: knight or pawn wedge

middlegame.title: Pawn wedge on e5 (vs ...Nbd7)
middlegame.brief: You are White in the Colle against 5...Nbd7. After 8.Ne5 Nxe5 9.dxe5 Nd7 the knight is gone but the pawn on e5 cramps Black. One move decides whether it holds.

stages.prompt: Which move supports the wedge on e5, and why?

options.text: 10.Bxh7+: cashes in the Greek gift at once.
options.why: No knight can reach g5 with tempo: your f3-knight was traded on e5. The sacrifice has only the queen behind it and Black simply takes.

options.text: 10.Qc2: keeps the queen flexible and eyes the b1-h7 diagonal.
options.why: It does not defend e5, so 10...Nxe5 wins a pawn and the knight hits your bishop on d3 at once.

options.text: 10.f4: supports the e5-pawn with the f-pawn and prepares the kingside play.
options.why: Correct. In the companion's engine check 10.f4 scores about 0.0 against about -0.65 for the next best move.

1) Answer the pin and the attack with ...g5 and ...b5. 2) Develop ...Bb7, ...Nbd7, ...Bg7. 3) Use ...g5-g4 to gain space and dislodge White's pieces. 4) Calculate every central strike (e4-e5, Ne5) before White's attack matures.

WHY THIS PLAN WORKS: ...g5 and ...b5 answer the pin and the attack, and ...Bb7, ...Nbd7 and ...Bg7 build counterplay on the long diagonal. The honest limit: the engine rates White about +0.3 throughout, so this is a practical, study-heavy advanced upgrade. The calm alternative is 6...Be7.

The engine accepts your repertoire moves as first choices (6...dxc4, 7...g5, 8...b5, 9...Bb7) but rates White about +0.3 throughout: the gambit is practical rather than objectively equal. That is why it is an Advanced upgrade: you must know the lines and calculate concrete tactics, because general principles will not hold the pawn.

bridge.title: Knight on e5: build the wedge (vs the fianchetto)
bridge.summary: Black has fianchettoed and nobody contests e5. Your knight is already there: now you back it up.
plan: Beginner: Pile onto e5: Ne5, f4, Bd3, Qe2 or Qc2. Never trade the e5 knight voluntarily.
What to expect from the opponent (Beginner): Challenge e5 directly with ...Nc6 or ...Nd7-f6 pressure, or prepare ...f6.

WHY THIS PLAN WORKS: Black has to attack e5 to get counterplay and he has nothing to attack it with once ...g6/...Bg7 is missing. Every ...f5, ...g6 or ...h6 loosens the dark squares f6-g6-h6 for good, so his kingside gets weaker with each move he spends on defence. The engine does not call it winning: the position stays about equal, and the point is a durable plan with a clean fallback in minor-piece endings.
bridge.mistake: Trade the e5 knight voluntarily to simplify the position.

drill.prompt: Which move forces the e5-structure, and why?

accept.f4: Correct. The knight needs a pawn chain, not just a good square. f4 turns a temporary outpost into a permanent one.

alt.b3: Also playable: the companion's engine puts 8.b3 within 0.05 pawns of 8.f4. The choice is about the plan, not a tactic. f4 is the repertoire move because it commits to the e5 structure.

bad.Qe2: The e3-pawn blocks the queen from e5, so the knight still has only d4 behind it. Flexible is not the same as forcing.
bad.Ndf3: It does guard e5, but it blocks your own f-pawn, so f4 can never arrive. You trade the outpost wedge for a passive set-up.

bridge.topic: The e5 outpost: knight or pawn wedge

bridge.title: Pawn wedge on e5 (vs ...Nbd7)
bridge.summary: Black has traded on e5 and recaptured so that your d-pawn stands on e5. The wedge is a pawn this time.
plan: Beginner: Pile onto e5: Ne5, f4, Bd3, Qe2 or Qc2. Never trade the e5 knight voluntarily.
Intermediate: Use g4-g5 to dislodge a defending ...Nf6, and aim rooks at the e- and f-files instead of rushing.
What to expect from the opponent (Intermediate): Avoid an early ...cxd4: it opens the long diagonal and e-file exactly when White wants them. ...f5 blunts the light-squared bishop.

drill.prompt: Which move supports the wedge on e5, and why?

accept.f4: Correct. In the companion's engine check 10.f4 scores about 0.0 against about -0.65 for the next best move.

bad.Bxh7+: No knight can reach g5 with tempo: your f3-knight was traded on e5. The sacrifice has only the queen behind it and Black simply takes.
bad.Qc2: It does not defend e5, so 10...Nxe5 wins a pawn and the knight hits your bishop on d3 at once.

bridge.title: Rook or bishop? The recapture on e4
bridge.summary: After the exchanges on e4 you decide how to recapture. The rook is the repertoire move and the reason Re1 was played.
plan: Beginner: Complete the manoeuvre Re1, e4, Rxe4, Rh4, aiming a Qd3/Qc2 + Rh4 + Ng5 battery at h7.
Intermediate: Keep Bd3 trained on h7 throughout. Avoid trades that let Black consolidate before the lift is complete.
What to expect from the opponent (Intermediate): Trade White's attacking minor pieces (the bishop on d3, the knight heading for g5) wherever offered.

WHY THIS PLAN WORKS: after 12.Rxe4 your rook, bishop and queen all point at h7 while Black's pieces are still unfinished, and each natural-looking Black move adds a defender that is too slow. The companion's engine check puts 13.Rh4 at about +1.3 against a barely-above-equal 13.Re1. The honest limit: if ...h6 and ...Nf6 are both in place the rook is offside, so keep the central Plan B ready.
bridge.mistake: Rush the rook to h4 even when ...h6 and a knight on f6 are both already in place.

drill.prompt: Which recapture forces the rook-lift structure, and why?

accept.Rxe4: Correct. The companion's engine prefers 12.Rxe4 (about +0.6) over 12.Bxe4 (about +0.2). This is why Re1 was played.

bad.Bxe4: It gives a normal, slightly dull position and the rook stays passive on e1. It is a legitimate fallback, not the plan.

bridge.title: The rook lift: Rh4
bridge.summary: The knight has just gone to f6. The rook lift lands now or never.

Intermediate: Keep Bd3 trained on h7 throughout. Avoid trades that let Black consolidate before the lift is complete.

Advanced: Decide by Specifics: if Black's knight leaves f6 or the king is short of defenders, the attack is on; if ...h6 and ...Nf6 are both in place, switch to central play (Be5, Bf4) and e-file pressure.
What to expect from the opponent (Advanced): Keep a knight on f6 as long as you can: it guards h7, h5 and g4.

bridge.title: Greek gift: the conditions are met
bridge.summary: Black's knight has left f6 and nothing covers g5. Check the three conditions, then strike.
plan: Beginner: Know the mechanics cold: Bxh7+ Kxh7 Ng5+ then Qh5 (or Qg4), with mate threats on h7/h8 depending on king placement.
Intermediate: Recognise when the sacrifice is unsound (Black keeps ...Nf6 covering g5/h5, or has an in-between ...Qxg5) and do not force it.
What to expect from the opponent (Intermediate): Know the defensive geometry after the sacrifice (...Kg8 and ...Nf8 rerouting) well enough to survive an unsound try over the board.

WHY THIS PLAN WORKS: the sacrifice is only on when three conditions meet: a knight that reaches g5 with tempo, a queen that joins at once, and no black knight on f6 to guard g5/h5/h7. When they do, Black's king is dragged into the open before his pieces can follow. In the two verified tabiyas the engine gives about +2.4 and +1.1. When any condition is missing, play Qc2/Re1 first and fall back on the slower plans.
bridge.mistake: Sacrifice on h7 whenever the bishop can, even when a knight on f6 or an in-between ...Qxg5 refutes it.

drill.prompt: Which move forces the structure, and why?

accept.Bxh7+: Correct. The companion's engine gives about +2.4 here against about +1.0 for the best alternative. The key detail is that Black's knight has left f6.

bad.Nbd4: It is a sound developing move, but it gives Black the one tempo he needs for ...h6, which is the cure for the whole sacrifice.
bad.Bf4: It spends a tempo on the wrong bishop: the attack lives on Bd3, Nf3 and the queen, not on the c1-bishop.

bad.Qh5: 16...Nxh5 simply wins the queen: the f6-knight guards h5.

bridge.title: The isolani tabiya: put a piece on e5
bridge.summary: You hold the isolated d4-pawn. The plan is activity: bishops on e5, rooks on the open files, and the attack on h7.
plan: Beginner: Keep pieces on. Centralise the rooks on the c- and e-files and put a piece on e5.
What to expect from the opponent (Beginner): Survive the middlegame without weakening your king just to dodge the initiative. It is provisional and fades naturally.

WHY THIS PLAN WORKS: the isolani is a debt you repay with activity, and the debt is only collected if the pieces stay on. Black's best answer is to trade and blockade d5, so you must keep the initiative every move. In the verified tabiya the companion's engine gives about +2.5 to +3.0, and a full-width mate search confirms that after 17.Qg5 Bd7 18.Rxh7 every Black reply loses to mate in at most four more White moves. Black's queen on a5 is out of the defence: that is the structural reason the plan cannot be parried.
bridge.mistake: Trade pieces to reach a calm ending: every trade shrinks the attack while the weakness stays.

drill.prompt: Which move forces the structure, and why?

accept.Be5: Correct. In the companion's engine check 16.Be5 and 16.Bc7 are both winning (about +2.5 to +3.0). The IQP rewards activity.

alt.Bc7: Also winning according to the companion's engine. The repertoire move is Be5 because it keeps the bishop central and the plan simple.

bad.Qe3: Every trade shrinks your attack while the isolated pawn stays. Trading queens is exactly what Black wants.

bridge.title: The isolani attack: Rxh7
bridge.summary: After 17.Qg5 Bd7 the rook sacrifice on h7 is decisive. A full-width mate search confirms it.
plan: Beginner: Keep pieces on. Centralise the rooks on the c- and e-files and put a piece on e5.
Intermediate: Fight to keep e5 and c5 as outposts before Black's pieces blockade them. Use the bishops for cross-board pressure toward f7/h7.
Advanced: Link it with the rook lift (I.2): Rh4 and Qg5 turn the IQP into a king attack. Pick the plan by the Specifics: exposed king means attack, solid king means keep tension.
What to expect from the opponent (Advanced): After simplification, target d4 with rooks and queen on the d- and c-files.

accept.Rxh7: Correct. A full-width search shows that every Black reply loses to mate in at most four more White moves.

bad.Qh5: It is not forcing: in a full-width search most Black replies, such as ...Kh8 or ...Rd8, are not mated within three moves. Rxh7 is the move that leaves no defence.

bridge.title: Hanging pawns: you hold them (Anti-Moscow ...Be7)
bridge.summary: You are Black. ...c5 and, after dxc5 bxc5, you own the pair on c5 and d5 with half-open b- and e-files.
plan: Beginner: Use the extra space and open lines the pawns give. Do not fear them because they are 'weak' on paper.
Intermediate: Keep both pawns mobile as long as possible: the moment they become permanently fixed, they turn from an asset into a target. Rooks go behind them.
What to expect from the opponent (Intermediate): Avoid unnecessary trades that reduce your control of the blockade squares.

WHY THIS PLAN WORKS: hanging pawns are strong while they are mobile and a target once they are fixed. As the owner you keep both mobile and choose the moment; as the attacker you blockade in front and provoke the advance at the wrong time. The structure decides nothing by itself: one timing judgment, calculated to the end, defines the whole game. The engine calls both reference positions about equal or slightly better for Black.
bridge.mistake: Push the pawn pair forward at once to claim space, instead of timing the advance.

drill.prompt: Which move forces the structure, and why?

accept.c5: Correct. In the companion's engine check 15...c5 is the first choice and the position is about equal: the break is right.

bad.Rfd8: A waiting move leaves White time to play Rac1 and fix the structure before your pawns are mobile. The pair must be created while it can still move.

bridge.summary: You are Black. After ...Bxc3 bxc3 White owns c3 and d4 as hanging pawns plus an isolated a-pawn. Pile on.

bridge.title: Bishop pair: Nxg6 hxg6 (vs 3...Bf5)
bridge.summary: Black has retreated the bishop to g6. Take it: you bank the bishop pair and Black gets doubled g-pawns.
plan: Beginner: Do not overpress. Bank the extra space or the bishop pair and simply finish development.
What to expect from the opponent (Beginner): Accept the trade-off calmly: conceding the bishop pair for a solid structure is a fair deal, not a mistake.

WHY THIS PLAN WORKS: the bishop pair gains value as the position opens and Black's doubled g-pawns are a fixed target for bishops, not for pawns. The engine's verdict is a small, durable edge of about +0.25 to +0.5. That is a technical game, not a forced win: bank the pair, fix the pawns, and open the game only when your bishops are ready.
bridge.mistake: Overpress: chase more than the bishop pair and a small durable edge are worth.

accept.Nxg6: Correct. The companion's engine rates this a small, durable edge of about +0.25. It is a technical game, not a forced win.

bad.Nf5: 6...Nf5 7...exf5 simply wins the knight for a pawn: the e6-pawn takes f5.

bridge.title: The Phoenix: 9.b4

bridge.title: Advance: the bishop comes out first
bridge.summary: You have played 3...c5 to keep the French-Advance chain without the bad bishop. Develop it before ...e6.

bridge.title: Tartakower: Re8 before anything else
bridge.summary: After the knights are traded you recapture with the e-pawn. The regrouping starts with ...Re8.
plan: Beginner: Standard regrouping: Bd6, O-O, Re8, Nd7-f8, Be6, Qd7.
What to expect from the opponent (Beginner): Use the open e-file (Re1) and aim pressure at the e6/e5 complex.

WHY THIS PLAN WORKS: the open e-file, active pieces and the ...f5 lever are your compensation, and the regrouping Bd6, O-O, Re8, Nd7-f8, Be6, Qd7 is textbook. Both sides keep both bishops, so you do not own the bishop pair. The honest limit: keep queens and heavy pieces on, because mass simplification turns the structure into a liability.

accept.Re8: Correct. The companion rates ...Bg4 slightly higher, so both are playable; ...Re8 is the repertoire move.

bridge.title: Tartakower: the h3 sacrifice

chapters.title: Pawn endgames: opposition and key squares

endgame.title: Rule of the square: catch the b-pawn

1.Ke3.note: Enters the square of the b-pawn, so the king catches it. With Black to move, 1...b3 would have promoted: the side to move decides this position. Draw.

3.Kc2.note: The pawn falls next move; only the two kings are left, a dead position.

endgame.brief: White to move. Black has a far-advanced passed pawn and his king is on the other side of the board.
endgame.principle: Draw the square: a king inside it, or one that steps into it with the move, catches the pawn.
endgame.topic: The rule of the square and first passed pawns
endgame.source: The Endgame Blueprint (Zero to Grandmaster), P0.2
endgame.verified: python-chess: legal position and legal line

endgame.title: King first, pawn behind: White wins

1.e3.note: A spare pawn move hands Black the move while the king keeps its place in front of the pawn.

2.Kd5.note: The king reaches a key square (d5, e5 or f5 for a pawn on e3): from here White wins whoever is to move.

5.e4.note: Only now does the pawn follow its king.

6.Kd7.note: The king owns the 7th rank, so the pawn will queen: 7.e5 and the pawn walks home. Black could not stop it with either side to move.

endgame.brief: White to move. The white king is already in front of its pawn, but the black king is in the way.
endgame.principle: In K+P vs K, lead with the king and let the pawn follow; spare pawn moves win the opposition battle.
endgame.topic: The rule of the square and first passed pawns
endgame.source: The Endgame Blueprint (Zero to Grandmaster), P0.3

endgame.title: The rook-pawn corner: Black draws
endgame.tag: Endgame Blueprint · P0.4 · The rook-pawn corner

1...Kb8.note: The only move, and it is enough: the king stays next to the corner.

2...Ka8.note: Back into the corner: the only drawing move (2...Kc8? 3.a8=Q+ wins for White).

3.Ka6.note: Stalemate: the pawn guards b8, the king guards b7 and a7. The corner is a fortress.

endgame.brief: White plays 1.a6. Black's king is already in the corner in front of the rook pawn.
endgame.principle: A rook pawn cannot win once the defending king owns the corner: draw with either side to move.
endgame.topic: The rule of the square and first passed pawns
endgame.source: The Endgame Blueprint (Zero to Grandmaster), P0.4
endgame.verified: python-chess: legal position and legal line

endgame.title: Opposition decides: Black draws with 1...Kd8

1...Kd8.note: The only drawing move: the king stays in front of the pawn. With White to move, 1.e7 Kf7 2.Kd7 and the pawn queens.

3.Ke6.note: Stalemate: the pawn on e7 guards d8 and f8, the king on e6 guards d7 and f7.

endgame.brief: Black to move. White has a pawn on e6 supported by his king on d6.
endgame.principle: Opposition and stalemate: the defender steps in front of the pawn and heads for the stalemate on e8.
endgame.source: The Endgame Blueprint (Zero to Grandmaster), P1.1
endgame.verified: python-chess: legal position and legal line

endgame.title: The outside passed pawn as a decoy
endgame.tag: Endgame Blueprint · P1.2 · Outside passer as decoy

1.a5.note: The outside passer is the decoy: Black's king must run to the queenside.

3.Kf4.note: Black's king has been dragged to a5 while the white king heads for g4.

4.Kxg4.note: White's king collected the g-pawn and wins the resulting king-and-pawn ending.

endgame.brief: White to move. A pawn on the a-file is far away from the kingside pawns.
endgame.principle: The outside passed pawn drags the enemy king away while your king collects the pawns on the other wing.
endgame.source: The Endgame Blueprint (Zero to Grandmaster), P1.2

endgame.title: The wrong bishop: a fortress in the corner
endgame.tag: Endgame Blueprint · P1.3 · The wrong bishop

1...Kb8.note: The only move, and enough: the dark-squared bishop can never control a8, so the king returns to the corner.

2...Ka8.note: Back to the corner. Whatever White does, he cannot dislodge the king without stalemating it.

3.Kc7.note: Stalemate: the dark-squared bishop can never control a8, so the corner is a fortress.

endgame.brief: Black to move. White has a bishop and an a-pawn, but the bishop does not control a8.
endgame.principle: A bishop that cannot control the promotion corner cannot win with a rook pawn.

endgame.title: Lucena: build the bridge
endgame.pgn: 1.Rf1+ Kg7 2.Rf4 Rc1 3.Ke7 Re1+ 4.Kd6 Rd1+ 5.Ke6 Re1+ 6.Kd5 Rd1+ 7.Rd4

1.Rf1.note: Check the defending king one file further away from the pawn.

2.Rf4.note: Lift the rook to the 4th rank: this prepares the bridge.

7.Rd4.note: The bridge: the rook blocks the last check and the king walks away.

endgame.brief: White to move. The pawn is on the 7th, White's king is on the promotion square and the black king is cut off.
endgame.principle: Lucena: check from the side, lift the rook to the 4th rank, walk the king out and block the last check with the rook.
endgame.source: The Endgame Blueprint (Zero to Grandmaster), P1.4
endgame.verified: python-chess: legal position and legal line

endgame.title: Philidor: the third-rank defence

1...Rh1.note: The key moment: the pawn is on the 6th, so the rook swings to the far end and checks from behind.

3...Re1.note: Checks from behind forever: the king has lost its shelter and cannot hide. Draw.

endgame.brief: White plays 1.e6. Black's rook is on the third rank and his king is on the promotion square.
endgame.principle: Philidor: wait on the third rank, and when the pawn reaches the 6th swing the rook to the far end and check from behind.
endgame.source: The Endgame Blueprint (Zero to Grandmaster), P1.5
endgame.verified: python-chess: legal position and legal line

endgame.title: The breakthrough: three pawns against three

1.b6.note: The sacrifice. After 1...cxb6 2.a6! bxa6 3.c6 the c-pawn queens.

2.c6.note: A second sacrifice clears the way for the a-pawn.

3.a6.note: The a-pawn is passed and queens: Black's king arrives too late. With Black to move, the breakthrough fails.

endgame.brief: White to move. Three pawns on the 5th face three on the 7th and the kings are far away.
endgame.principle: Breakthrough: a pawn sacrifice creates a passed pawn by force when three pawns face three.
endgame.source: The Endgame Blueprint (Zero to Grandmaster), P2.1
endgame.verified: python-chess: legal position and legal line

endgame.title: Réti: one king walk, two goals

1.Kg7.note: Heads for the h-pawn and, at the same time, the squares near the c-pawn.

3.Ke5.note: The king move that does both jobs: it is inside the square of the h-pawn and supports the c-pawn.

4.Kf4.note: One king walk supported the c-pawn and then caught the h-pawn: a draw.

endgame.brief: White to move. The black king stops the c-pawn, and the h-pawn is running.
endgame.principle: A king moving diagonally can chase two goals at once.
endgame.source: The Endgame Blueprint (Zero to Grandmaster), P2.2
endgame.verified: python-chess: legal position and legal line

endgame.title: Saavedra: underpromote to a rook
endgame.pgn: 1.c7 Rd6+ 2.Kb5 Rd5+ 3.Kb4 Rd4+ 4.Kb3 Rd3+ 5.Kc2 Rd4 6.c8=R Ra4 7.Kb3

1.c7.note: Push the pawn: the king hides on b3 and a rook promotion follows.

6.c8=R.note: The only winning move: 6.c8=Q? Rc4+ 7.Qxc4 is stalemate.

7.Kb3.note: Now Rc1 mate and Kxa4 are both threatened.

endgame.brief: White to move. The c-pawn is on the 6th and Black's rook keeps checking.
endgame.principle: Underpromotion: a rook promotion avoids a stalemate that a queen would allow.
endgame.source: The Endgame Blueprint (Zero to Grandmaster), P2.3

endgame.title: Rook versus bishop: the wrong corner
endgame.tag: Endgame Blueprint · P2.4 · Rook vs bishop: the corner decides

1.Rh8.note: Check along the edge: the only block lands on a square the rook can capture with mate.

2.Rxg8.note: Mate: same material as a draw, but the wrong corner.

endgame.brief: White to move. Rook against bishop, and the black king is in the corner of the bishop's own colour.
endgame.principle: Against a bishop the defending king must run to the corner that is not the bishop's colour.

1...Ra6.note: The rook goes behind the pawn and the king stays on g7: a draw.

endgame.brief: White plays 1.a7. Black's rook defends the pawn from the side along the 6th rank.

courses.endgame.title: The laws that decide endgames (level 1)
courses.endgame.idea: Before technique, know when a game is already over: stalemate, dead position, repetition, the 50-move rule, flag-fall and the free choice of promotion piece.
courses.endgame.takeaway: A won position is only won if you do not stalemate, repeat or run out of time.
learn: Before technique, know when a game is already over: stalemate, dead position, repetition, the 50-move rule, flag-fall and the free choice of promotion piece.
R0.1 (Law). Stalemate is a draw. The side to move has no legal move and is not in check.
R0.2 (Law). Dead position = immediate draw. When neither side can checkmate by any series of legal moves — K vs K, K+B vs K, K+N vs K, K+B vs K+B with same-coloured bishops — the game ends drawn.

R0.3 (Law). Repetition. A draw can be claimed when the same position occurs for the third time (same player to move, same castling and en passant rights). The fifth occurrence ends the game automatically.

R0.4 (Law). The 50-move rule. 50 moves by each player without a capture or a pawn move: a draw can be claimed. 75 moves: automatic draw, unless the last move is checkmate. Online platforms use their own implementations.
R0.5 (Law). Flag-fall. Run out of time and you lose — unless your opponent has no possible way to checkmate you; then it is a draw.
R0.6 (Law). Promotion. A pawn reaching the last rank must become a queen, rook, bishop or knight of its own colour. The choice is free.
R0.12 (Principle). The stalemate check. In a winning position, before every move ask: "After my move, does my opponent still have a legal move?"
C0.6 (Concept). Stalemate is the defender's friend. A lone king heads for the corner and for "no-move" positions.

debrief.t: Read their last move for a stalemate or repetition idea: did it leave a king with no legal move?
Count the material: can either side still checkmate at all (dead position)? Note the move count since the last capture or pawn move.
Checks, captures and attacks come after one safety question: after my move, does my opponent still have a legal move?
Calculate to the very last position of the line. A winning line that ends in stalemate, repetition or a dead position is a draw.

courses.endgame.title: Winconditions: the two ways endgames end (level 1)
courses.endgame.topic: Winconditions: the two ways endgames end
courses.endgame.idea: Every endgame ends with exactly one of two mechanisms: a Mate Wincondition or a Passer Wincondition. Everything else is a lever that helps you create, execute or deny one.
courses.endgame.takeaway: No Wincondition, no win: name yours before you plan.
learn: Every endgame ends with exactly one of two mechanisms: a Mate Wincondition or a Passer Wincondition. Everything else is a lever that helps you create, execute or deny one.
Wincondition framework, 0.1 Definition.
A Wincondition is a concrete mechanism that ends the game in your favour. The endgame has exactly two:
– Mate Wincondition — any checkmate attack or mating net.
– Passer Wincondition — any passed pawn: a pawn that no enemy pawn can stop on its own file or on the adjacent files. Its final form is promotion, which normally converts into a Mate Wincondition.
Wincondition framework, 0.2 Everything else is a lever.
Material, king activity, piece activity, space, weak pawns, zugzwang and the tempo count do not win by themselves. They are levers: tools to create a Wincondition, execute it, or deny the opponent's.
Wincondition framework, 0.3 The five laws of the framework.
– Law 1 — No Wincondition, no win. If neither side can create a Wincondition, the position is a draw, whatever the material count.

– Law 2 — Material is not a Wincondition. K+B vs K and K+N vs K are dead draws; K+2N vs K cannot force mate. In endings with only a minor piece against pawns, database statistics put the bishop at about 2½ pawns and the knight even lower — partly because the piece cannot win once its own last pawn disappears.

– Law 3 — Guard the last pawn. Playing for a win, keep at least one pawn: it is the raw material of your Passer Wincondition. Defending, trade pawns: every pawn trade deletes a potential Passer Wincondition.
– Law 4 — Count both sides. Your Wincondition only matters relative to your opponent's. Races are decided by tempi.
– Law 5 — Every exchange changes the Wincondition balance. Before trading, ask: does this trade speed up my Wincondition, or kill my opponent's?
R0.7 (Principle). Name the Wincondition before you plan. Every winning plan ends in a Mate Wincondition or a Passer Wincondition.
C0.1 (Concept). What is an endgame? Not a fixed move number but a change of priorities: the kings become fighters, and pawns become the main source of Winconditions.

debrief.t: What did their last move change? Did it create, speed up or stop a Wincondition?
Inventory both sides: is there a passed pawn or a mating net for either side? If neither side has one, the position is a draw.
Forcing moves that create or execute a Wincondition: checks, captures that clear the path and pawn pushes that gain time.
Count the moves to promotion or mate for both sides, including checks and captures on the way.

courses.endgame.title: The Endgame Scan and the Conversion Ladder (level 2)
courses.endgame.topic: Winconditions: the two ways endgames end
courses.endgame.idea: A five-step scan tells you what to do whenever the position changes character, and a four-rung ladder shows how every won endgame is converted.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Scan, then climb: Secure, Improve, Create, Execute.
learn: A five-step scan tells you what to do whenever the position changes character, and a four-rung ladder shows how every won endgame is converted.
Wincondition framework, 0.5 The Endgame Scan.
Run it whenever the position changes character (an exchange, a pawn break, a new passed pawn):
1. Inventory — Which Winconditions exist for both sides: active, potential, none?
2. Tempo — Who executes first? Count moves to promotion or mate, including checks, captures and queening with check.
3. Levers — Which lever speeds up mine or slows down theirs?
4. Transition test — Can I trade into a known win? Can my opponent trade into a known draw?
5. Decision — Create · Execute · Deny · or Improve ("do not hurry").
Wincondition framework, 0.6 The Conversion Ladder.
Every won endgame is won in this order:
1. Secure — kill counterplay, protect loose pieces and pawns.
2. Improve — centralise the king, activate the worst piece, fix enemy weaknesses.
3. Create — produce a Passer Wincondition or a Mate Wincondition.
4. Execute — escort the Passer Wincondition or deliver mate, without allowing stalemate or perpetual check.

debrief.t: Run the scan after every exchange: what Wincondition did their last move create or deny?
Inventory both sides' Winconditions (active, potential, none) and list the levers: king, rook, space, weak pawns.
Use levers to create or speed up your Wincondition: forcing moves first, quiet improving moves after.
Tempo count and transition test: can I trade into a known win, can they trade into a known draw? Then decide: create, execute, deny or improve.

courses.endgame.title: Wincondition denial: the defender's mirror (level 3)
courses.endgame.topic: Winconditions: the two ways endgames end
courses.endgame.idea: The defender has seven ways to deny a Wincondition: blockade, elimination, theoretical draw, fortress, stalemate, perpetual check and a counter-Wincondition.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Name the denial method before you choose a defence.
learn: The defender has seven ways to deny a Wincondition: blockade, elimination, theoretical draw, fortress, stalemate, perpetual check and a counter-Wincondition.
Wincondition framework, 0.4 The defender's mirror — Wincondition denial.
1. Blockade — stop the Passer Wincondition on the square directly in front of it (king or knight ideal).
2. Elimination — trade the last pawns; give a piece for the last pawn when the remaining material cannot mate.
3. Theoretical draw — steer into a known drawn position (Philidor, wrong bishop, rook vs bishop).
4. Fortress — a setup the attacker cannot break.
5. Stalemate.
6. Perpetual check or repetition.
7. Counter-Wincondition — create your own Passer or Mate Wincondition so the attacker must stop and defend.

debrief.t: What Wincondition is the opponent building? Name it before you choose a defence.
Which of the seven denial methods exists here: blockade, elimination, theoretical draw, fortress, stalemate, perpetual or counter-Wincondition?
Blockade or capture first; forcing counterplay (checks, a counter-passer) comes second.
Verify that the denial really holds: calculate the attacker's best breakthrough and every stalemate or repetition resource.

learn: Theory is a map of targets: steer toward winning anchors and away from drawn ones, and know the zones where the defending king must stand.

C3A.2 (Concept). Zones — many endings are decided by where the defending king stands: the queen's winning zone, the Troitzky line, the Rule of Five, g7/h7 in rook-pawn endings.

debrief.t: Which anchor position can the opponent reach with their last move?

courses.endgame.title: The Wincondition switch (level 5)
courses.endgame.topic: Winconditions: the two ways endgames end
courses.endgame.idea: The strongest technique combines both Winconditions: a passer drags defenders to passive squares, then a mating threat strikes the stripped king, or the reverse.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Alternate Passer and Mate Winconditions, and spend the passer when it is worth more as a decoy.
learn: The strongest technique combines both Winconditions: a passer drags defenders to passive squares, then a mating threat strikes the stripped king, or the reverse.
C3B.1 (Concept). Advantage transformation — material ↔ activity ↔ structure ↔ Winconditions.

R3C.9 (Principle). The switch. The strongest technique combines both Winconditions: a Passer Wincondition that drags defenders to passive squares, then a Mate Wincondition against the stripped king — or mating threats that force the defender to let a passed pawn through.

R3C.10 (Principle). Spend the Passer Wincondition at the right moment. It can be worth more as a decoy than as a queen: its sacrifice deflects a defender, opens a line, or gains the decisive king tempo.

R3C.11 (Principle). Defend with a counter-Wincondition. At the top level the best defence is often a race, not a blockade: create your own Passer or Mate Wincondition and make the attacker spend tempi.
C3C.3 (Concept). The Wincondition switch — alternating Passer and Mate Winconditions until one defence cracks.

debrief.t: Which Wincondition did their last move switch to?
Does a passer drag defenders to passive squares, or does a mating threat force a passed pawn through?
The switch: alternate Passer and Mate Winconditions until one defence cracks; spend the passer as a decoy at the right moment.
Calculate the counter-Wincondition race: the tempo count in both directions.

courses.endgame.title: Basic mates: queen, rook and the ladder (level 1)
courses.endgame.idea: The lone king is always mated on the edge. Learn to shrink the box without giving stalemate.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Shrink the box, bring your king, check last, and always ask whether the lone king still has a legal move.
learn: The lone king is always mated on the edge. Learn to shrink the box without giving stalemate.
R0.11 (Theory). In the basic mates (K+Q, K+R, K+2B, K+B+N vs K) the lone king is always mated on the edge. Drive it there.
C0.2 (Concept). The edge is a prison. Mate Wincondition technique means shrinking the enemy king's space (the "box") until it stands on the edge.
C0.3 (Concept). The basic mates — your first Mate Wincondition drills.
– K+Q vs K — shrink the box with the queen a knight's move away from the enemy king; when it reaches the edge, stop and bring your own king; mate with king support. At most 10 moves with best play.
– K+R vs K — the rook cuts the board, the king approaches; when the kings face each other, check from the side to push the enemy king back; use rook waiting moves. At most 16 moves.
– K+2R (or K+Q+R) vs K — the ladder: the heavy pieces alternate checks rank by rank. If the king attacks one of them, move it to the far end of its rank.
P0.1 (Must-know position). The stalemate trap. FEN: k7/8/1Q6/8/8/8/8/2K5 b - - 0 1.
Black to move: stalemate. The queen, a knight's move from the cornered king, takes every square but gives no check.

debrief.t: Where did the lone king step? Every king move changes the size of the box you are shrinking.
Locate the edge and the nearest corner, and where your king stands relative to theirs.
Shrink the box with the queen a knight's move away; give a check only when it takes squares away or mates.
Before every move verify stalemate, then count the moves left to mate.

courses.endgame.idea: Bishop and knight, two bishops and two knights against a pawn are theoretical results you must be able to execute.

learn: Bishop and knight, two bishops and two knights against a pawn are theoretical results you must be able to execute.
R3A.16 (Theory). K+B+N vs K is a forced mate in at most 33 moves: drive the king to a corner of the bishop's colour. Learn the knight's W-manoeuvre (or Delétang's triangle method).
R3A.17 (Theory). K+2B vs K is mate in at most 19 moves. Side-by-side bishops build a wall, the king approaches, and mate can be given in any corner.

R3A.18 (Theory). K+2N vs K cannot be forced — but K+2N vs K+P often can. The knights generally win when the pawn is securely blockaded by a knight on or behind the Troitzky line — Black pawns: a4, b6, c5, d4, e4, f5, g6, h4 (White pawns, mirrored: a5, b3, c4, d5, e5, f4, g3, h5). Some of these wins take more than 50 moves.

debrief.t: Which corner did the lone king head for? With bishop and knight the corner colour matters.
The bishop's colour, the knights' squares and the Troitzky line for the pawn.
Drive the king to the right corner and keep the pieces coordinated; check only when it restricts.

courses.endgame.title: Core principles, typical errors and vocabulary (level 1)
courses.endgame.idea: Once the queens are off the king becomes a fighting piece. These principles, the common errors and the vocabulary carry through every later level.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Activate the king, ahead trade pieces, behind trade pawns, and speak the endgame vocabulary.
learn: Once the queens are off the king becomes a fighting piece. These principles, the common errors and the vocabulary carry through every later level.
R0.8 (Principle). Activate the king. Once the queens are gone, the king is a fighting piece. March it to the centre.
R0.9 (Principle). Know the values. Pawn 1 · knight 3 · bishop 3 · rook 5 · queen 9. An active endgame king fights roughly like a minor piece.
R0.10 (Principle). Ahead → trade pieces, not pawns. Behind → trade pawns, not pieces. (Framework Law 3.)
C0.4 (Concept). Kings move diagonally as fast as straight. A diagonal path is often the shortest route — the seed of the Réti manoeuvre (Tier 2).
Typical errors at Tier 0:
– Stalemating with the queen a knight's move from the cornered king.
– Chasing the king with random checks instead of building the box.
– Leaving the king at home once the queens are off.
– Trading the last pawn while ahead in material.
– Pushing an unsupported pawn straight into the enemy king.
Upgrade triggers: move up when you can do these.
– You mate with K+Q vs K and K+R vs K against a computer from random positions, ten times in a row, without stalemate.
– You apply the rule of the square in seconds, including the double-step case.
– You can list every dead-position material combination.
– You can point out both Winconditions in your own games.
Glossary of endgame vocabulary:

Wincondition — a concrete mechanism that ends the game in your favour: the Mate Wincondition or the Passer Wincondition. · Mate Wincondition — any checkmate attack or mating net. · Passer Wincondition — any passed pawn heading for promotion. · Lever — an advantage that is not itself a Wincondition: material, activity, space, weaknesses, zugzwang. · Candidate — a pawn that can become a passed pawn. · Outside passer — a passed pawn far from the other pawns and the kings. · Protected passer — a passed pawn defended by a pawn. · Opposition — kings facing each other with an odd number of squares between them; the side not to move has it. · Key squares — squares that win for the attacking king, whoever is to move.

Corresponding squares — matching pairs of squares for the two kings. · Mined squares — mutual-zugzwang squares; whoever steps on them first loses. · Triangulation — losing a tempo with a three-square king route. · Zugzwang — having to move is a disadvantage; mutual when it applies to both sides. · Shouldering — blocking the enemy king's path with your own king. · Breakthrough — a pawn sacrifice that creates a passed pawn by force. · Blockade — a piece stopping a passed pawn on the square in front of it. · Fortress — a defensive setup the attacker cannot break. · Cut-off — a rook separating the enemy king from the action along a rank or file.

Short side / long side — the side of a pawn with fewer / more files. · Checking distance — the room a rook needs to check effectively from the flank. · Bridge — Lucena's rook block that ends the checks. · Cross-check — blocking a check with a check. · Domination — taking away every square from an enemy piece. · Dead position — a position in which no series of legal moves can produce checkmate for either side. · WDL / DTZ / DTM — tablebase metrics: win-draw-loss; distance to the next capture or pawn move; distance to mate.

debrief.t: Which piece did the opponent just activate or trade? That tells you whose king and pawns matter now.
King activity, pawn structure and material: ahead you trade pieces, behind you trade pawns.
Activate the king first; checks, captures and attacks come after your king reaches the centre.
Calculate the plan to the end: where does each king stand when the pawn moves arrive?

courses.endgame.title: The rule of the square and your first passed pawns (level 1)
courses.endgame.topic: The rule of the square and first passed pawns
courses.endgame.idea: A defending king that stands inside the pawn's square, or steps into it, catches the pawn. Rook pawns, the corner and the king in front of the pawn complete the foundation.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Draw the square before you move: inside it the king catches the pawn, outside it the pawn runs.
learn: A defending king that stands inside the pawn's square, or steps into it, catches the pawn. Rook pawns, the corner and the king in front of the pawn complete the foundation.

R0.13 (Theory). Rule of the square — stopping a Passer Wincondition with the king. Draw a square from the pawn to its promotion rank. If the defending king is inside it, or steps into it with the move, it catches the pawn (provided nothing blocks its path). A pawn on its starting square counts from one square further, because of the double step.
R0.14 (Principle). King in front, pawn behind. In K+P vs K, lead with the king; the pawn follows.
R0.15 (Theory). The rook pawn is special. K + rook pawn vs K is a draw once the defending king reaches the corner in front of the pawn.
R0.16 (Principle). Push your Passer Wincondition when it is safe. Every step forward ties down more enemy force.
R0.17 (Principle). Blockade enemy Passer Winconditions on the square directly in front of them.

C0.5 (Concept). Passer Wincondition vocabulary. Passed pawn · protected passer (defended by a pawn) · connected passers (adjacent files) · outside passer (far from the other pawns) · candidate (a pawn that can become a passer).
P0.2 (Must-know position). The square. FEN: 7k/8/8/8/1p3K2/8/8/8 w - - 0 1.
White to move: 1.Ke3 enters the square and catches the pawn — draw. Black to move: 1...b3 and the Passer Wincondition promotes.
P0.3 (Must-know position). King first. FEN: 8/8/4k3/8/4K3/8/4P3/8 w - - 0 1.
White wins with either side to move: the king is already ahead of its pawn, and the e-pawn's spare moves win the opposition battle (Tier 1).
P0.4 (Must-know position). The rook-pawn corner. FEN: k7/8/1K6/P7/8/8/8/8 w - - 0 1.
Draw with either side to move: the defending king owns the corner.

debrief.t: Which pawn just moved? A pawn push changes the square, so redraw it.
Pawn file and rank, promotion square, both kings; rook pawns are special.
Check whether the defending king is inside the square, or can step into it with the move.
Count the moves for the pawn and for the king; do not forget the double step from the starting square.

courses.endgame.title: Opposition and key squares (level 2)
courses.endgame.idea: Opposition is the tool, key squares are the goal: it decides every king-and-pawn ending.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Ask where your king must stand, not which pawn move to play.
learn: Opposition is the tool, key squares are the goal: it decides every king-and-pawn ending.

R1.1 (Theory). Opposition. Kings on the same file, rank or diagonal with one square between them: the side not to move has the opposition. With three or five squares between them it is distant opposition — same logic.
R1.2 (Theory). Key squares decide K+P vs K. If the attacking king reaches a key square and the pawn cannot be captured, it wins — no matter who is to move.
– Pawn on its 2nd–4th rank: the three squares two ranks in front of it.
– Pawn on its 5th–6th rank: the three squares one rank in front and the three squares two ranks in front.
– Rook pawn: only the two squares on the adjacent file that touch the promotion square (White a-pawn: b7 and b8).
R1.3 (Theory). Shortcut. With your pawn on the 4th or 5th rank (not a rook pawn), a king on the 6th rank — on the pawn's file or an adjacent file — always stands on a key square.
R1.4 (Principle). Opposition is the tool; key squares are the goal. Use the opposition to shoulder your way onto a key square.
R1.5 (Principle). Defender: stay in front, retreat straight back. In K vs K+P keep your king in front of the pawn; when pushed, step straight backward so you can retake the opposition.
R1.6 (Theory). Spare pawn moves win the opposition. A pawn that has not advanced far keeps tempo moves in reserve — use them to hand the move to the opponent.

R1.7 (Theory). The rook-pawn trap. Refines R0.15. K + rook pawn vs K is also drawn when the defending king controls the two key squares (b7 and b8 against a White a-pawn) — for example by locking the attacking king in front of its own pawn.
C1.1 (Concept). Zugzwang — the obligation to move becomes a disadvantage. It is the engine of every pawn ending.
C1.2 (Concept). The opposition family — direct, distant and diagonal: one parity idea at different distances.
C1.3 (Concept). Key squares — ask "where must my king stand?", not "which pawn move?"
C1.4 (Concept). Spare tempi — pawn moves held in reserve are the currency of pawn endings.
P1.1 (Must-know position). Opposition decides. FEN: 4k3/8/3KP3/8/8/8/8/8 b - - 0 1.
Black to move draws: 1...Kd8! 2.e7+ Ke8 3.Ke6 stalemate. White to move wins: 1.e7 Kf7 2.Kd7 and the pawn queens.

debrief.t: Who just moved? Opposition is about who has to move, so re-read the last move and count tempi.
Pawn rank and file, both kings and the key squares; spare pawn moves are tempo reserves.
Use the opposition to shoulder your king onto a key square; do not push the pawn before the king is ahead of it.
Test both move orders, with you to move and with them to move, and check stalemate on the edge.

courses.endgame.idea: Tempo is the currency of pawn endings: triangulate to hand over the move, shoulder the enemy king away and use diagonal king walks.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Count tempi and routes: the diagonal is as short as the straight line.
learn: Tempo is the currency of pawn endings: triangulate to hand over the move, shoulder the enemy king away and use diagonal king walks.
R2.1 (Theory). Triangulation. If the position is won with the opponent to move, and your king can use three squares while the enemy king has only two useful ones, walk the triangle to lose a tempo.
R2.2 (Theory). A knight cannot lose a tempo. It changes square colour on every move, so it can never return to the same square in an odd number of moves. Kings, bishops, rooks and queens can.
R2.3 (Theory). Distant and diagonal opposition follow the same parity logic — take them early to win the race to the key squares.
R2.4 (Principle). Shouldering. Use your king's body to block the enemy king's route. Often stronger than approaching directly.

R2.5 (Theory). The Réti manoeuvre. A king moving diagonally can chase two goals at once — hunting an enemy Passer Wincondition while supporting its own. Count diagonal routes before you give up a race.
C2.1 (Concept). Tempo economy — pawn endings are arithmetic: moves to promote, spare moves, king steps.
C2.2 (Concept). Two-goal geometry — the diagonal is as short as the straight line (Réti).
P2.2 (Must-know position). Réti. FEN: 7K/8/k1P5/7p/8/8/8/8 w - - 0 1.
Draw: 1.Kg7 h4 2.Kf6 Kb6 (2...h3 3.Ke7 h2 4.c7 — both pawns queen) 3.Ke5! Kxc6 4.Kf4 — one king walk supported the c-pawn and then caught the h-pawn.

debrief.t: Did the opponent's last move waste or keep a tempo?
Triangle squares for your king and theirs, diagonal routes, and the fact that a knight cannot lose a tempo.
Triangulate to hand over the move; use shouldering and diagonal king walks as forcing moves.
Count three-move and two-move routes: the triangle only works when you have three squares and the enemy king only two.
