courses.endgame.idea: Opposition is the simplest case of corresponding squares; some squares are mines where the side that steps on them loses.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Find the key squares first, then map the correspondence backwards.
learn: Opposition is the simplest case of corresponding squares; some squares are mines where the side that steps on them loses.

R3A.1 (Theory). Corresponding squares. Opposition is a special case of a larger system: every square of the attacking king has a matching square for the defending king. Find the key squares first, then map the correspondence backwards.
R3A.2 (Theory). Mined squares (mutual zugzwang). Some squares are mines — whoever steps on them first loses. Approach them only with the move in hand.

debrief.t: Which mined square did their move step on or avoid?
Key squares first, then correspondence backwards: every square of the attacking king has a defending twin.

courses.endgame.title: Tempo parity, routes and domination (level 5)
courses.endgame.idea: Tempo parity is global: count every spare move on the board, think in routes instead of single moves and take every square from a minor piece.
courses.endgame.takeaway: The last spare tempo wins the mutual zugzwang, and a knight cannot lose a tempo.
learn: Tempo parity is global: count every spare move on the board, think in routes instead of single moves and take every square from a minor piece.
R3C.5 (Principle). Think in routes, not moves. King routes that serve two purposes, rook switches with tempo, queen checks that also centralise.
R3C.6 (Principle). Tempo parity is global. In complex endings, count the spare tempi of the whole board — pawn moves, bishop and rook waiting moves. The last spare tempo wins the mutual zugzwang.

R3C.7 (Principle). Design zugzwangs against knights. Refines R2.2. A knight cannot lose a tempo: aim for positions where the opponent's only free piece is a knight, or where every other waiting move is gone.
R3C.8 (Principle). Domination wins minor pieces. Take away every square of a knight or bishop until it is lost or permanently tied down.
C3C.2 (Concept). Global zugzwang — zugzwang as a whole-board resource, not a king-and-pawn trick.

debrief.t: Which spare tempo did their last move spend?
Global tempo parity: pawn moves, bishop and rook waiting moves, knight tempo traps.
Route the king and rook with tempo; dominate the knight or bishop until it is lost.

courses.endgame.title: Outside, protected and separated passed pawns (level 2)
courses.endgame.idea: A passed pawn is a Passer Wincondition: used as a decoy it drags the enemy king away, and in a race the details decide.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Use the outside passer as a decoy, then count the race to the last tempo.
learn: A passed pawn is a Passer Wincondition: used as a decoy it drags the enemy king away, and in a race the details decide.
R1.8 (Principle). The outside Passer Wincondition wins pawn endings. Use it as a decoy: while the enemy king runs to stop it, your king invades on the other wing.
R1.9 (Theory). A protected Passer Wincondition cannot be captured by the king alone. As long as its protector stands, the enemy king stays tied to it.
R1.10 (Principle). Separated Passer Winconditions overload a lone king. Check each one with the rule of the square — often one of them promotes.

R1.11 (Theory). Passer Wincondition races. Count the moves to promotion for both sides. Then check the details: does a queen arrive with check, and can the first queen stop the second (by controlling its promotion square, or by skewering king and new queen)?
C1.5 (Concept). Decoy — an outside Passer Wincondition pulls the enemy king away from the real battlefield.
C1.6 (Concept). Underpromotion — a knight for a check or fork, a rook to avoid stalemate (P2.3).
P1.2 (Must-know position). The outside Passer Wincondition as decoy. FEN: 8/8/3k4/8/P2K2p1/6P1/8/8 w - - 0 1.
White wins: 1.a5 Kc6 2.Ke5 Kb5 3.Kf4 Kxa5 4.Kxg4 — Black's king was dragged to a5 while White's king collected g4.

debrief.t: Which king did their last move pull toward which wing? An outside pawn is a decoy.
Outside, protected, connected or separated passers, and the distance of both kings to each pawn.
Push the passer that drags the enemy king away, then invade on the other wing.

courses.endgame.title: Breakthroughs, majorities, tempi and rook pawns (level 3)
courses.endgame.idea: Three pawns against three can create a passer by force; majorities, reserve tempi and the rook pawn decide the rest.
courses.endgame.takeaway: The candidate moves first; count spare tempi before the kings reach zugzwang.
learn: Three pawns against three can create a passer by force; majorities, reserve tempi and the rook pawn decide the rest.
R2.6 (Theory). The breakthrough. Three pawns on the 5th facing three on the 7th, kings far away: a pawn sacrifice creates a Passer Wincondition by force.
R2.7 (Principle). The candidate moves first. In a pawn majority, advance the pawn with no enemy pawn in front of it — your future Passer Wincondition. The others support it.
R2.8 (Principle). Healthy majorities create Passer Winconditions; crippled (doubled) majorities often cannot.
R2.9 (Principle). Reserve tempi decide blocked pawn endings. Count spare pawn moves on both sides before the kings reach zugzwang. Doubled pawns can be a hidden source of tempi.
R2.10 (Principle). The more active king usually decides the pawn ending.
R2.11 (Principle). Rook pawns are the most drawish pawns in pawn, bishop and rook endings, and against a queen on the 7th. Against a knight they are the most dangerous.
P2.1 (Must-know position). The breakthrough. FEN: 6k1/ppp5/8/PPP5/8/8/8/6K1 w - - 0 1.
White to move wins: 1.b6! axb6 (1...cxb6 2.a6! bxa6 3.c6) 2.c6! bxc6 3.a6 and the a-pawn queens. With Black to move, Black's king arrives in time and the breakthrough fails — count the tempi.
P2.3 (Must-know position). Saavedra. FEN: 8/8/1KP5/3r4/8/8/8/k7 w - - 0 1.
White wins: 1.c7 Rd6+ 2.Kb5 Rd5+ 3.Kb4 Rd4+ 4.Kb3 Rd3+ 5.Kc2 Rd4! 6.c8=R! (6.c8=Q? Rc4+ 7.Qxc4 stalemate) Ra4 7.Kb3 — Rc1 mate and Kxa4 are both threatened.

debrief.t: Which pawn is a candidate now? Their last move may have created a passer for you or for them.

courses.endgame.title: Lucena and Philidor (level 2)
courses.endgame.idea: Two positions decide a huge share of rook endings: Lucena wins by building a bridge, Philidor draws with the third-rank defence.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Rooks belong behind passed pawns; Lucena builds the bridge, Philidor waits on the third rank and then checks from behind.
learn: Two positions decide a huge share of rook endings: Lucena wins by building a bridge, Philidor draws with the third-rank defence.
R1.16 (Principle). Rooks belong behind Passer Winconditions — behind your own (the rook pushes) and behind the enemy's (the rook attacks while the enemy rook stays stuck in front). Tarrasch's rule.
R1.17 (Principle). Activity first. An active rook is often worth a pawn. A rook passively guarding a pawn is a bad investment.
R1.18 (Principle). Cut off the enemy king. A king cut off from the Passer Wincondition by your rook is out of the game — the first step of almost every winning rook ending.

R1.19 (Theory). Lucena position — WIN ("building a bridge"). Pawn on the 7th (not a rook pawn), attacking king on the promotion square, defending king cut off from the pawn. Method: check the defending king one file further away, lift your rook to the 4th rank, walk your king out, and block the last check with the rook.

R1.20 (Theory). Philidor position — DRAW ("third-rank defence"). Defending king on the promotion square; defending rook on its own third rank, keeping the attacking king off the 6th. The moment the pawn advances to the 6th, swing the rook to the far end of the board and check from behind: the king has lost its shelter.
R1.21 (Principle). Two connected Passer Winconditions on the 6th rank usually beat a lone rook when both kings are far away — unless the rook can win one of them at once, with tempo.
C1.7 (Concept). Cut-off geometry — ranks and files are walls built by rooks.
C1.8 (Concept). The bridge and the shield — in Lucena the rook shields its own king from checks; in Philidor the rook guards the 6th rank, then checks from behind.
P1.4 (Must-know position). Lucena. FEN: 3K4/3P1k2/8/8/8/8/2r5/4R3 w - - 0 1.
White wins: 1.Rf1+ Kg7 2.Rf4! Rc1 3.Ke7 Re1+ 4.Kd6 Rd1+ 5.Ke6 Re1+ 6.Kd5 Rd1+ 7.Rd4 — the bridge.
P1.5 (Must-know position). Philidor. FEN: 4k3/R7/7r/3KP3/8/8/8/8 w - - 0 1.
Draw: 1.e6 Rh1! 2.Kd6 Rd1+ 3.Ke5 Re1+ — checks from behind, forever.

debrief.t: Did their rook cut your king off, or did the pawn advance to the 6th or 7th rank?
Pawn on the 7th, both kings, the cut-off file and where the rooks stand relative to the pawn.
Checks first: in Lucena check from the side and lift the rook to build the bridge, in Philidor wait on the third rank.
Verify every check from a distance and every bridge move: one skipped check ends the win.

courses.endgame.title: The practical rook ending (level 3)
courses.endgame.idea: Rook endings are the most common and the most drawish: activity first, short side and long side, and exact checking distance.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Down a pawn, activate before you defend; check from a distance of at least three files.
learn: Rook endings are the most common and the most drawish: activity first, short side and long side, and exact checking distance.
R2.12 (Principle). The rook on the 7th rank attacks pawns from the side and cages the enemy king on the back rank.
R2.13 (Principle). Down a pawn? Activate before you defend. Give a second pawn if needed to activate rook and king. Passive defence usually loses slowly.
R2.14 (Theory). Short side, long side. The defending king goes to the short side of the pawn (fewer files); the defending rook goes to the long side to check from the flank.

R2.15 (Theory). Checking distance. Flank checks normally need three empty files between the checking rook and the pawn (sometimes two with the pawn on the 7th). Any closer, and the attacking king simply walks up to the rook.

R2.16 (Theory). Passive back-rank defence holds only against knight and rook pawns. Refines R1.20. Against bishop and centre pawns it loses once the attacking king reaches the 6th rank on the short side of its pawn: the pawn shields the king from flank checks and the back rank collapses. Use Philidor's defence while you still can.
R2.17 (Principle). 3 vs 2 and 4 vs 3 on the same wing are usually drawn in rook endings. An extra pawn wins far more often when it is a distant Passer Wincondition.
R2.18 (Principle). "All rook endings are drawn." Tartakower's quip is a warning, not a law. Rook endings are the most common endgame type and among the most drawish: a pawn up is not yet a win.
C2.3 (Concept). Activity as material — an active rook or king often outweighs a pawn.
C2.7 (Concept). The Mate Wincondition in rook endings — a king cut off on the back rank, plus an active rook and king, can produce mating nets even with many pawns left.

debrief.t: Did their rook go passive? Down a pawn: activate; a pawn up: ask what they now threaten.
Rook on the 7th, short side versus long side of the pawn, checking distance, centre pawn versus rook pawn.
Checks and rook activity first: flank checks from at least three files away.
Verify the checking distance, then count whether passive defence holds against bishop and centre pawns.

courses.endgame.title: The rook canon: Rule of Five, Vančura and the g7/h7 rule (level 4)
courses.endgame.idea: The great rook-ending positions are anchors: know exactly when they draw and when they lose.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Rook behind the pawn, flank checks from distance, and the defending king on g7 or h7 against a rook pawn.
learn: The great rook-ending positions are anchors: know exactly when they draw and when they lose.

R3A.5 (Principle). The Rule of Five. Pawn protected, defending king cut off by files: add the pawn's rank to the number of files the defending king is cut off. More than five: usually a win. Five or less: normally a draw. Knight and rook pawns are exceptions.
R3A.6 (Theory). Against a pawn on the 7th, only flank checks work; against a pawn on the 6th, checks from behind work too — the Philidor mechanism.

R3A.7 (Theory). Vančura position — DRAW. Rook pawn on the 6th with the attacking rook in front of it: the defending rook attacks the pawn from the side along the 6th rank, and the defending king shuttles between g7 and h7 (against an a-pawn). Meet the approaching king with checks from the side, keeping your distance; if the pawn advances to the 7th, put the rook behind it (R3A.8).

R3A.8 (Theory). The g7/h7 rule. Rook pawn on the 7th, attacking rook in front (Ra8, Pa7), defending rook behind the pawn: a draw with the defending king on g7 or h7. Anywhere else, a rook check or skewer usually forces the pawn through (e.g., Rh8! Rxa7, Rh7+).

R3A.9 (Principle). Rook + two pawns vs rook usually wins — connected pawns most easily. The notorious exception is f- and h-pawns: often a theoretical draw with an excellent defence, yet regularly lost in practice.

R3A.10 (Principle). Rook vs connected Passer Winconditions. Refines R1.21. The rook attacks from behind and the rook side's king must come fast; the pawns win when they reach the 6th with tempo and the rook cannot pick one of them off.
P3A.1 (Must-know position). Vančura. FEN: R7/6k1/P4r2/8/2K5/8/8/8 w - - 0 1.

Draw: Black's rook stays on the 6th, hitting a6 from the side; the king shuttles g7–h7; an approaching White king is met by checks from the side. If 1.a7, then 1...Ra6 — rook behind the pawn, king on g7.
P3A.3 (Must-know position). The g7/h7 rule.
R7/P5k1/8/8/8/8/r7/6K1 w - - 0 1 — Draw: the king stands on g7.
R7/P4k2/8/8/8/8/r7/6K1 w - - 0 1 — White wins: 1.Rh8! (1...Rxa7 2.Rh7+ and 3.Rxa7).

debrief.t: Which rook position did their last move aim for: Philidor, Vančura or g7/h7?

courses.endgame.title: The grandmaster layer of rook endings (level 5)
courses.endgame.idea: Activity can outweigh two pawns: the side that completes its triangle of active rook, active king and passer first usually wins.

R3B.20 (Principle). Tarrasch's rule serves activity, not the other way round. Refines R1.16. If a rook in front of or beside a passed pawn is more active — cutting off the king, attacking pawns — activity wins the argument.
R3B.21 (Principle). In rook endings, counterplay beats passive material defence. The side that creates a Passer Wincondition first often wins even while behind in pawns.
R3C.12 (Principle). Activity can outweigh two pawns. When your rook is the most active piece on the board and your king escorts a Passer Wincondition, material counts less than tempo.

R3C.13 (Principle). The activity triangle (teaching model): active rook + active king + Passer Wincondition. The side that completes its triangle first usually wins; defend by breaking one side of the opponent's triangle.

R3C.14 (Theory). Know the drawing zones exactly — Philidor, Vančura, flank checks with enough distance, the Rule of Five, the g7/h7 rule — so you can calculate transitions into R+P vs R long before they happen.

courses.endgame.title: Queen versus a pawn on the seventh (level 2)
courses.endgame.idea: A queen usually stops a pawn on the seventh, but against bishop and rook pawns the stalemate tricks save the defender.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Check and pin until the king steps in front of its pawn, and never capture into a stalemate.
learn: A queen usually stops a pawn on the seventh, but against bishop and rook pawns the stalemate tricks save the defender.

R1.13 (Theory). Queen vs pawn on the 7th, defending king beside it. The queen wins against centre (d/e) and knight (b/g) pawns. Against bishop (c/f) and rook (a/h) pawns it is a draw by stalemate tricks — unless the attacking king is already close.
R1.14 (Theory). Queen vs pawn — the method. Check and pin until the defending king must step in front of its pawn. That buys one tempo for your king to approach. Repeat.

debrief.t: Where did the defending king step? In front of its pawn it costs a tempo.

courses.endgame.title: Queen endings: winning zone, fortresses and cross-checks (level 4)
courses.endgame.idea: The queen beats most pawns and the rook, but stalemate tricks, fortresses and perpetual check are the defender's resources.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Use cross-checks against perpetual, and never capture the pawn when it is stalemate.
learn: The queen beats most pawns and the rook, but stalemate tricks, fortresses and perpetual check are the defender's resources.

R3A.11 (Theory). The winning zone. Refines R1.13. Against bishop and rook pawns on the 7th, the queen still wins when the attacking king is close enough to create a Mate Wincondition or to support the capture.

R3A.12 (Theory). Queen vs rook is a win (barring immediate tactics). Drive the king to the edge, then separate rook and king by zugzwang — the queen can pass the move with a triangle of checks (P3A.4) — and finish with a fork or mate.
R3A.13 (Theory). Queen vs rook + pawn can be a fortress. A rook on its third rank, protected by a pawn on its second rank next to its king, often cannot be broken.
R3A.14 (Principle). In queen endings the Passer Wincondition outranks material. A far-advanced passer escorted by the queen beats one or two extra pawns elsewhere.

R3A.15 (Principle). Perpetual check is the defender's main denial tool. The attacker centralises the queen, uses pawns as shelter, and answers checks with cross-checks — blocking a check while giving check.
C3A.5 (Concept). Cross-check — blocking a check with a check; the attacker's weapon against perpetual.
P3A.2 (Must-know position). Queen vs bishop pawn. FEN: 7K/8/6Q1/8/8/8/1kp5/8 w - - 0 1.
Draw: 1.Qb6+ Ka1! 2.Qd4+ Kb1 3.Qb4+ Ka1 4.Qc3+ Kb1 5.Qb3+ Ka1! — 6.Qxc2 is stalemate, and White's king is too far away to help.
Contrast (same setup): the centre pawn 7K/8/7Q/8/8/8/2kp4/8 w - - 0 1 and the knight pawn 7K/8/6Q1/8/8/8/kp6/8 w - - 0 1 are White wins; the rook pawn 7K/8/6Q1/8/8/8/pk6/8 w - - 0 1 is a draw.
P3A.4 (Must-know position). Queen vs rook: the zugzwang triangle. FEN: 1k6/1r6/2K5/Q7/8/8/8/8 w - - 0 1.
White wins. With Black to move this is zugzwang: the rook must leave its king. With White to move, pass the move: 1.Qe5+ Ka8 2.Qa1+ Kb8 3.Qa5 — same position, Black to move.

R3B.25 (Principle). Queen vs two rooks. Rooks are strong when they protect each other; the queen wins with forks against loose rooks and with attacks on weak pawns and the king.

R3C.15 (Principle). Queen endings are races of Passer Winconditions and checks. The attacking king walks toward its passed pawn or toward the enemy king, where checks can be blocked with cross-checks.

R3C.16 (Principle). Trust the position, not the piece myth. Capablanca's claims that queen + knight beats queen + bishop, and rook + bishop beats rook + knight, hold only by small statistical margins (Kaufman). King safety, colour complexes and Passer Winconditions decide.

debrief.t: Did their queen check to centralise or to start a perpetual?

courses.endgame.title: Good bishop, bad bishop, bishop versus knight and the blockade (level 3)
courses.endgame.idea: Pawns on the bishop's colour make it bad; knights love closed positions and blockade squares; knight endings behave like pawn endings.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Put your pawns on the opposite colour of your bishop and blockade with a knight or the king.
learn: Pawns on the bishop's colour make it bad; knights love closed positions and blockade squares; knight endings behave like pawn endings.

R2.19 (Principle). Good bishop, bad bishop. A bishop is bad when its own pawns are fixed on its colour. Put your pawns on the opposite colour of your bishop; fix enemy pawns on the colour of your bishop so you can attack them.
R2.20 (Principle). Bishop vs knight. Bishops prefer open positions and pawns on both wings; knights prefer closed positions, outposts and all pawns on one wing.
R2.21 (Principle). Knight endings behave like pawn endings (Botvinnik). The outside Passer Wincondition and king activity are even more decisive than usual.
R2.25 (Principle). Blockade with the right piece. The knight is the ideal blockader of a Passer Wincondition — it stays active on the blockade square. In endings, so is the king.
C2.4 (Concept). Colour complexes — a bishop fights for one colour; pawns and the king must cover the other.
C2.5 (Concept). Blockade — the main Wincondition-denial tool in minor-piece endings.

R3A.20 (Principle). Knight vs rook pawn on the 7th. The knight holds only if it controls the promotion square or reaches it in time. Rook pawns are the knight's nightmare.

R3A.24 (Principle). Bishop + pawn vs same-coloured bishop. A draw if the defending king gets in front of the pawn on a square the attacking bishop cannot attack. Otherwise the result depends on whether the defending bishop keeps a diagonal across the pawn's path that the attacker cannot cut.

R3A.25 (Principle). Knight + pawn vs knight is usually a draw with the defending king in front — and the defending knight can often give itself up for the last pawn, since K+N vs K is a dead position.

courses.endgame.title: Pawnless endings: 2B v N, R+B v R, queen v minor pieces (level 4)
courses.endgame.topic: Rook versus minor pieces and material balance
courses.endgame.idea: Tablebases overturned old verdicts: two bishops beat a knight, queen beats two bishops, but the 50-move rule can rescue the defender.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Know the winning and drawing verdicts, and count the 50 moves yourself.
learn: Tablebases overturned old verdicts: two bishops beat a knight, queen beats two bishops, but the 50-move rule can rescue the defender.
R3A.19 (Theory). Two bishops vs knight (no pawns) is generally a win — tablebases overturned the old drawing verdict — but some wins exceed the 50-move limit.

R3A.21 (Theory). Rook + bishop vs rook is generally a theoretical draw — but hard to defend. Winning positions: Philidor's and Lolli's. Drawing methods: the Cochrane defence (pin the bishop to its king, away from the edge) and the second-rank defence.
R3A.22 (Theory). Rook + knight vs rook is a draw and much easier to hold.

R3A.23 (Theory). Queen vs two bishops: the queen wins most positions , but it can take up to 71 moves — the 50-move rule can rescue the defender. Queen vs two knights: the queen wins many positions, but the knights hold a large share of draws.

courses.endgame.idea: Winning a pawn is step one of three: win it, turn it into a passer, escort it home. Calculate every trade into a pawn ending.

R1.22 (Principle). Trade into a pawn ending only after calculating it to the end. Pawn endings are the most forcing and least forgiving endings: there, Winconditions are pure tempo arithmetic.
R1.23 (Principle). The three steps of a material advantage. Win the pawn → turn it into a Passer Wincondition → escort it home.
Typical errors at Tier 1:
– Pushing the pawn early and losing the opposition.
– Defending K vs K+P from the side instead of in front.
– Philidor: dropping the rook to the back rank before the pawn reaches the 6th, letting the attacking king in.
– Lucena: skipping the bridge and walking into endless checks.
– Queen vs c/f/a/h pawn: capturing the pawn when it gives stalemate.

learn: One weakness can be defended, two cannot. When the opponent has no counterplay, improve every piece first.
R2.26 (Principle). The principle of two weaknesses. One weakness can be defended. Create a second one on the other wing and switch between them until the defence breaks.
R2.27 (Principle). Do not hurry. If the opponent has no counterplay, improve every piece first. The decisive break comes when everything is ready.
R2.28 (Principle). The pawn-ending test. Before trading into a pawn ending, remove all pieces in your head and ask who wins. Winning → trade. Not winning → keep pieces.
C2.6 (Concept). Weakness targeting — fix the pawn, attack it with more pieces than can defend it, then add a second target.
Typical errors at Tier 2:
– Entering a rook ending a pawn up and treating it as won (R2.18).
– Waiting passively on the back rank against a centre pawn (R2.16).
– Checking from the flank with the rook too close to the pawn (R2.15).
– Fixing your own pawns on your bishop's colour.
– Trading the last rooks without the pawn-ending test (R2.28).
– Attacking one weakness forever instead of creating a second.

courses.endgame.title: Fortresses, stalemate architecture and the 50-move horizon (Tier 3A checklist) (level 4)
courses.endgame.idea: A fortress is a setup the attacker cannot break; stalemate can be a designed defence; theory and the 50-move rule can disagree.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Before simplifying, ask whether the defender can build a setup you cannot break.
learn: A fortress is a setup the attacker cannot break; stalemate can be a designed defence; theory and the 50-move rule can disagree.
C3A.3 (Concept). Fortress (introduction) — a static setup the attacker cannot break: wrong bishop, opposite-bishop blockade, queen vs rook + pawn.
C3A.4 (Concept). Stalemate architecture — stalemate as a designed defence: queen vs c/f/a/h pawns, desperado rooks, the wrong-bishop corner.
C3A.6 (Concept). The 50-move horizon — several theoretical wins (2B vs N, 2N vs P, Q vs 2B) collide with the 50-move rule. Theory and practice can give different results.
Appendix A, theoretical results at a glance:
"Generally" means exceptions exist in specific positions. Move counts assume best play.
Mate Wincondition — the basic mates:
– K+Q vs K — win, at most 10 moves
– K+R vs K — win, at most 16 moves
– K+2B vs K (opposite colours) — win, at most 19 moves
– K+B+N vs K — win, at most 33 moves
– K+2N vs K — no forced mate
– K+B vs K · K+N vs K — dead position
Pawnless endings:
– Q vs R — generally a win
– Q vs 2B — generally a win (up to 71 moves)
– Q vs 2N — many wins, but a large share of draws
– R vs B — generally a draw (defending king to the corner not of its bishop's colour)
– R vs N — generally a draw (knight next to its king, away from corners)
– R+B vs R — generally a draw (Philidor and Lolli positions win; Cochrane and second-rank defences hold)
– R+N vs R — generally a draw
– 2B vs N — generally a win (some wins exceed 50 moves)
Passer Wincondition endings:
– K+P vs K — decided by key squares
– K + rook pawn vs K — draw once the defender reaches the corner or traps the attacking king
– K+B + wrong rook pawn vs K — draw once the defending king reaches the corner
– Q vs pawn on the 7th — win vs b/d/e/g pawns; vs a/c/f/h pawns a draw unless the attacking king is close
– R+P vs R — Lucena wins; Philidor and Vančura draw; the Rule of Five as a guide
– R+2P vs R — usually a win (f+h notoriously drawish)
– 2N vs P — generally a win when blockaded on or behind the Troitzky line (sometimes beyond 50 moves)
– Q vs R+P — fortress draws exist
– Opposite-coloured bishops — +1 usually drawn; +2 depends on the distance between the passed pawns
Typical errors at Tier 3A:
– Assuming every rook-pawn ending is drawn — the defending king must reach g7/h7 (R3A.8).
– Starting flank checks too close to the pawn (R2.15).
– B+N mate: pushing the king to the wrong corner and never switching.
– Taking the bishop pawn with the queen when it is stalemate (P3A.2).
– Allowing a queen vs rook + pawn fortress when pieces could have been kept.
– Forgetting the 50-move count in 2B vs N, 2N vs P and Q vs 2B.
Upgrade triggers: move up when you can do these.
– You mate with K+B+N vs K well inside 50 moves under blitz conditions.
– You win Lucena and hold Philidor and Vančura against an engine from random starts.
– You recite the Troitzky line and the queen-vs-pawn rule without notes.
– You survive 50 moves of R vs R+B against an engine with the Cochrane defence.

debrief.t: Is the defender heading for a fortress or a stalemate setup?
Static versus dynamic fortresses: wrong bishop, opposite bishops, queen versus rook plus pawn.
Before simplifying, ask: can the defender build a setup I cannot break?
Count the 50-move horizon: theory and practice can differ.

courses.endgame.title: The art of exchanging (Tier 3B checklist) (level 5)
courses.endgame.idea: Trade the defender's best piece, keep your best attacker, convert into the endgame type that magnifies your advantage and know what each exchange does.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Name what the exchange does before you make it.
learn: Trade the defender's best piece, keep your best attacker, convert into the endgame type that magnifies your advantage and know what each exchange does.
R3B.5 (Principle). Trade the defender's best piece; keep your best attacker.

R3B.6 (Principle). Convert into the endgame type that magnifies your advantage. An extra pawn converts most reliably in pawn and minor-piece endings (except opposite-coloured bishops), least reliably in rook and opposite-bishop endings. See Appendix B.

R3B.7 (Principle). Know what each exchange does. It removes a defender against your Passer Wincondition, removes an attacker from the opponent's Mate Wincondition, or changes the endgame type. Name which one before you trade.
R3B.8 (Principle). The defender trades pawns and chooses the drawing material — rook endings, opposite-coloured bishops, the wrong bishop, the queen vs rook + pawn fortress.
Appendix B, the extra pawn: conversion ladder (principle). From easiest to hardest in typical positions; structure and activity can overturn the order:
– Pawn endings — usually winning.
– Knight endings — usually winning.
– Same-coloured bishop endings — often winning; harder if your pawns sit on your bishop's colour.
– Queen endings — real winning chances, but perpetual check is always lurking.
– Rook endings — often drawn.
– Opposite-coloured bishop endings — usually drawn.
Typical errors at Tier 3B:
– Trading pieces automatically when ahead — straight into a rook or opposite-bishop ending.
– Pushing pawns into the defender's zone before the king is ready (hurrying).
– Activating the king while enemy heavy pieces can still build a Mate Wincondition.
– Defending one weakness passively instead of creating counterplay.
– Planning without asking what the opponent wants.
Upgrade triggers: move up when you can do these.
– In your own games you can name the exchange that changed the Wincondition balance, and why.
– You convert slightly better endings with no extra material against strong opposition.
– You annotate a master endgame without an engine, and your plans match the engine's key decisions.

debrief.t: Which defender did their last move bring in, and can I trade it?
Which endgame type magnifies my advantage: pawn and minor-piece endings versus rook and opposite-bishop endings.
Trade the defender's best piece; keep your best attacker; name what the exchange does.
Test the resulting ending (pawn-ending test, fortress test) before you trade.

courses.endgame.title: Planning, prophylaxis and the king (level 5)
courses.endgame.idea: Picture the ideal setup first, ask what the opponent wants, improve your worst piece and restrict before you attack.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Prophylaxis first, then restrict, then attack, and calculate only where the opponent can interfere.
learn: Picture the ideal setup first, ask what the opponent wants, improve your worst piece and restrict before you attack.
R3B.1 (Principle). Schematic thinking. Before calculating, picture the ideal setup — where every piece and the king belong — and the route there. Calculate only where the opponent can interfere.
R3B.2 (Principle). Prophylaxis first. Ask what your opponent wants: usually an active rook, a Passer Wincondition or a known draw. Stop that before pursuing your own plan.
R3B.3 (Principle). Improve the worst piece. In slow endings, the side whose worst piece is better usually wins.
R3B.4 (Principle). Restrict before you attack. Take squares away from the enemy king and pieces first; Winconditions become unstoppable once the defender is paralysed.

R3B.18 (Principle). The king-safety paradox. With queens or two rooks each on the board, activity and safety compete: the Mate Wincondition is still alive. Activate the king only where enemy heavy pieces cannot build a mating net.
R3B.19 (Principle). Pawns are an umbrella. A king beside or in front of its pawns is shielded from checks along those lines.
R3B.26 (Principle). Clock economy. In long endings play the obvious improving moves quickly; spend your time at transitions — exchanges, pawn breaks, entering theoretical positions.
R3B.27 (Law). Count the 50 moves yourself in long defences (R+B vs R, Q vs 2B): every capture or pawn move resets the count.
C3B.2 (Concept). Domination — controlling every square an enemy piece could use.
C3B.3 (Concept). Two weaknesses, deep version — the second weakness can be a Mate Wincondition threat rather than a pawn.
C3B.4 (Concept). Harmony — pieces protecting each other and the king, so that no tactic interrupts the plan.

debrief.t: What does the opponent want: an active rook, a passer or a known draw?
The ideal setup for every piece, the worst piece, and the king-safety paradox.
Prophylaxis first, then restrict, then attack: take squares away.
Calculate only where the opponent can interfere; picture the schematic setup first.

courses.endgame.title: Transformations and structure-born endgames (level 5)
courses.endgame.idea: Turn a static advantage into a dynamic one at the right moment, and know which endgames your middlegame structures leave behind.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Return material or sacrifice a pawn to create a second Wincondition.
learn: Turn a static advantage into a dynamic one at the right moment, and know which endgames your middlegame structures leave behind.
R3B.11 (Principle). Turn static advantages into dynamic ones at the right moment — return material to activate your king or rook, or to create an unstoppable Passer Wincondition.

R3B.12 (Principle). Sacrifice a pawn to create a second Wincondition. Two threats — a Passer Wincondition on one wing, a king invasion or Mate Wincondition on the other — break defences that hold against one.
R3B.14 (Principle). Structural weaknesses grow as pieces disappear. Isolated, doubled and backward pawns are defended by pieces; every exchange removes a defender.
R3B.16 (Principle). Fix, then attack. Fix enemy pawns on squares your pieces can hit, then bring the king.
R3B.17 (Principle). Create an entry square. Kings win endings by invasion — use a pawn lever to open a door.
C3B.5 (Concept). Structure-born endgames — what middlegame structures leave behind:
– Isolated queen's pawn — its dynamism fades with every exchange; the pawn becomes a target and the square in front of it a permanent blockade post.
– Hanging pawns — dynamic with pieces on the board; targets that need constant protection without them.
– Carlsbad (minority attack) — the minority attack leaves a weak pawn (usually on c6 or c3) that becomes the main endgame target.

– …c6 structures after …dxe4 (Caro-Kann main lines) — White has a 4 vs 3 majority on the queenside (a–d vs a–c), Black on the kingside (e–h vs f–h). With both kings castled short, the queenside majority is the one that produces the outside Passer Wincondition.
– Doubled pawns — a crippled majority may never create a Passer Wincondition, but the extra pawn controls squares and supplies spare tempi.
– Space advantage — worth less as pieces come off; the cramped side usually welcomes exchanges.

debrief.t: Which static advantage does their last move allow me to transform?
Isolated, hanging, Carlsbad, ...c6 structures, doubled pawns and space.
Return material to activate; sacrifice a pawn to create a second Wincondition.
Verify the transformation: material for activity must create an unstoppable threat.

courses.endgame.title: Fortress and anti-fortress (level 5)
courses.endgame.idea: Test for fortresses before you simplify, know the warning signs and the toolkit for breaking them.
courses.endgame.takeaway: A large engine evaluation with no visible progress is a fortress alarm.
learn: Test for fortresses before you simplify, know the warning signs and the toolkit for breaking them.
R3C.1 (Principle). Test for fortresses before you simplify. At every major exchange ask: "Afterwards, can the defender build a setup I cannot break?" If yes, change the structure first — then trade.

R3C.2 (Principle). Fortress warning signs. The defender has safe waiting moves; your king has no entry square; the blockaders cannot be attacked by enough pieces; your pawns are fixed on the wrong colour.

R3C.3 (Principle). The anti-fortress toolkit. Zugzwang (remove the waiting moves) · pawn breaks and sacrifices that open entry lines · changing the colour complex of the pawns · exchanging the key defender · returning material to reach a known win · a second Wincondition on the other wing.

R3C.4 (Principle). Engines can misjudge fortresses. A large evaluation with no visible progress over long lines is a fortress alarm. Check with tablebases (up to 7 pieces) or search for a concrete break yourself.
C3C.1 (Concept). Static vs dynamic fortresses — static: the attacker has no entry at all; dynamic: the defender holds only with exact waiting moves or perpetual threats.

debrief.t: Did their last move give them a safe waiting move?
Fortress signs: waiting moves, no entry square, blockaders that cannot be attacked, pawns fixed on the wrong colour.
Anti-fortress toolkit: zugzwang, breaks and sacrifices, change the colour complex, exchange the key defender.
Check with tablebases or find a concrete break; engine numbers can mislead.

courses.endgame.title: Grandmaster technique (level 5)
courses.endgame.idea: Maximum problems for the opponent, minimum risk for you; repeat once, never three times; know tablebase metrics and build a personal anchor library.
courses.endgame.takeaway: Calculate backwards from the anchor and choose methods you can execute inside the 50-move horizon.
learn: Maximum problems for the opponent, minimum risk for you; repeat once, never three times; know tablebase metrics and build a personal anchor library.
R3C.17 (Principle). Maximum problems, minimum risk. In equal or slightly better endings, choose lines that demand accurate moves from the opponent for a long time while you keep zero losing risk.
R3C.18 (Principle). Repeat once to gain time — never three times. A single repetition banks clock time and tests whether the defender knows the right waiting moves.

R3C.19 (Law). The flag-fall nuance. Refines R0.5. You lose on time if your opponent could checkmate you by any series of legal moves — even a helpmate. So K+N or K+B against your K+P can still win on time; against your bare king they cannot.

R3C.20 (Principle). Tablebase literacy. Learn WDL (win/draw/loss), DTZ (distance to the next capture or pawn move that resets the 50-move count) and DTM (distance to mate). All positions with up to 7 pieces are solved and partial 8-piece work is ongoing — expect published "rules" to keep being refined.
R3C.21 (Principle). A win beyond 50 moves is not a practical win. Choose winning methods a human can execute inside the 50-move horizon.
R3C.22 (Principle). Know the endgames your openings produce. Every repertoire has typical structures; steer the middlegame toward endings where your structure's Winconditions are healthier.
R3C.23 (Principle). Calculate backwards from the anchor. Identify the target theoretical position first, then find the move order that reaches it with the right side to move.
R3C.24 (Principle). Build a personal anchor library — 100–150 positions you can play perfectly from both sides, grouped by material and structure, reviewed with spaced repetition.
C3C.4 (Concept). Practical probability — choosing lines by how hard they are for the opponent, not only by their evaluation.

C3C.5 (Concept). Model technique — Capablanca (simplification), Rubinstein (rook endings), Smyslov (harmony), Karpov (restriction and domination), Fischer (bishop vs knight), Carlsen (pressure in equal endings).
Typical errors at Tier 3C:
– Simplifying straight into a fortress.
– Trusting engine numbers in blocked positions.
– Winning too slowly and running into the 50-move rule.
– Applying theory without its exceptions: knight pawns in the Rule of Five, the wrong rook pawn in opposite-bishop endings, the king's square in rook-pawn endings.
Grandmaster standard:
– You explain any endgame result through its Winconditions and denial mechanisms.
– You steer ten to twenty moves ahead into anchor positions.
– You win "equal" endings against masters and hold worse ones against stronger players.

debrief.t: Which line gives the opponent the most problems while I risk nothing?
Your anchor library, practical probability and the 50-move horizon.

WELCOME TO YOUR BLACK REPERTOIRE.

THE BIG IDEA: you answer everything with 1...c6.
- Against 1.e4 you get a Caro-Kann.
- Against 1.d4 you get a Slav or Semi-Slav.
- Against 1.c4 and 1.Nf3 you transpose into one of those two.

One move, one system, every game. That is the same principle as a good White system opening: less memorising, more understanding.

IMPORTANT WARNING BEFORE YOU START:
Even if your opponent is a "1.d4 player", he can answer 1.d4 c6 with 2.e4 and you are simply in a Caro-Kann. So EVERY student needs this course, not only the ones who expect 1.e4. Do not skip it.

WHAT THIS COURSE COVERS: the Caro-Kann only. The Slav and Semi-Slav are a separate course.

HOW MUCH TO LEARN: eight short lessons. Learn Lessons 01 and 05 properly - together they cover the large majority of your games. The rest you can look up when you meet them.

THIS COURSE IS DIFFERENT FROM THE OTHER FIVE.

The opening courses tell you WHICH MOVES to play. This one tells you what to do once the opening is over - which is where your games are actually decided.

A NOTE ON WHAT THESE ARE:
These are model PLANS, shown as complete move sequences from the opening into the middlegame. They are not annotated historical games. Where a plan comes from a specific game, the source books contain it in full and I point you there rather than reproducing it here.

THE SIX STRUCTURES OF YOUR BLACK REPERTOIRE:
1. The Advance French with the good bishop (Caro, 3...c5)
2. The Tartakower doubled f-pawns
3. The isolated queen's pawn, seen from the defending side (Panov)
4. The Meran queenside majority
5. The bishop-pair structure (Moscow)
6. The doubled g-pawns after Nxg6 hxg6 (appears in FOUR different openings)

HOW TO STUDY THIS COURSE:
Play through each lesson once. Then close the file and answer two questions: what was Black's plan, and which move made it work. If you can answer both, you have what you need.

THE HABIT THIS COURSE BUILDS: at move fifteen, name the structure before you calculate anything.

AT THIS LEVEL YOUR OPPONENTS PREPARE.

Everything in the first two courses stays correct. What changes is that you now meet people who know the same lines you do, and who have chosen their move order to make life hard for you.

WHAT THIS COURSE ADDS:
1. The critical tries in each variation - the moves a prepared opponent actually plays.
2. Move-order traps in both directions: the ones you must avoid, and the ones you can set.
3. An honest assessment of where our lines stand, including the places where strong authors disagree.
4. A second weapon, for when you need to step out of your own preparation.

A WORD ON HONESTY IN OPENING STUDY:
Every repertoire has soft spots. A course that pretends otherwise is selling comfort, not chess. Where our lines are only "fine" rather than "better", this course says so - because knowing which of your positions are worse is what stops you from over-pressing and losing them.
The move that makes the whole repertoire work. We prepare ...d5 while keeping the c8-bishop free - unlike the French, where that bishop gets locked in.
Let's begin.
Let's get to work.

THE TRAPS YOU MUST AVOID.

1. In the Advance, ...e6 before the bishop is out. This is not a small inaccuracy - it is the whole variation thrown away. You reach an Advance French a tempo down, and Lakdawala calls it a clear mistake.

2. In the Advance with 4.dxc5, spending two or three moves recovering the pawn immediately. Develop first. The pawn usually comes back on its own.

3. In the Tartakower, recapturing with the g-pawn. 5...gxf6 is a completely different variation with a different character and much more risk.

4. In the Panov, ...Nc6 instead of ...Nbd7 at the wrong moment, allowing d4-d5 with tempo.

THE TRAPS YOU CAN SET:

1. The delayed pin. In the Tartakower, play ...Re8 before ...Bg4 and let White commit to h3. Most opponents play it automatically and hand you a target for the rest of the game.

2. The delayed capture. Against 6.Qc2 setups and in the Advance with 4.c3, wait until White commits a knight before taking or releasing the tension. The same move is worth much more two moves later.

3. The queen retreat. Against system players, provoking a committal pawn move and then retreating the queen is a real gain, even though it looks like you wasted time. Students hate this - teach it explicitly.

THE HABIT THAT SEPARATES 1600 FROM 2000:
Before every capture and every developing move, ask one question: does this move commit me to something? If yes, can I wait one move and make my opponent commit first?

SOURCES: Sverre Johnsen and Torbjorn Ringdal Hansen, Win with the Caro-Kann, for the Tartakower or Korchnoi Variation and the Bareev; Cyrus Lakdawala and Keaton Kiewra, Opening Repertoire: ...c6 (Everyman 2017) for the Advance and Panov; Peter Wells, Grandmaster Secrets: The Caro-Kann, for the dissenting assessment quoted in Lesson 08.

WHAT IS DIFFERENT ABOUT THIS COURSE.

Nothing you learned in the Speedcourse is replaced. Every move stays correct. What changes is depth: you now learn WHY the moves are chosen, what White's best tries are, and what to do when your opponent knows the theory too.

THE THREE THINGS THAT SEPARATE 1200 FROM 1600 IN THIS OPENING:

1. MOVE ORDER. In the Advance, the difference between releasing the tension with ...cxd4 and keeping it with ...Bg4 decides whether you get a comfortable game or a slightly passive one. This course teaches you when to do which.

2. THE ONE EXCEPTION TO THE BISHOP RULE. Everywhere in this repertoire you develop the c8-bishop before ...e6. There is exactly one place where the opposite is right, and knowing it is worth a lot of points. See Lesson 03.

3. PLANS INSTEAD OF MOVES. From here on, most of your games leave theory around move twelve. What decides them is whether you know the standard plan for the structure in front of you. Lesson 09 collects them.

THE FOUR STRUCTURES OF YOUR CARO REPERTOIRE.

Most of your games leave theory around move twelve. What decides them is whether you recognise which of these four you are in.

1. THE ADVANCE FRENCH STRUCTURE (pawns e5 vs e6/d5, our bishop OUTSIDE the chain).
Plan: pressure d4 with ...Nc6, ...Qb6, ...Nf5. Trade the light-squared bishops if you can. Break with ...f6 only when your pieces are ready.
Do not: play ...e6 before the bishop is out. That is the whole variation thrown away.

2. THE TARTAKOWER STRUCTURE (doubled f-pawns, open e-file).
Plan: ...Bd6, ...Re8, ...Nd7-f8, ...Be6, ...Qd7 and play against h3 or with ...f5.
Do not: allow mass exchanges into an endgame. Our structure is a middlegame asset and an endgame liability.

3. THE ISOLATED PAWN STRUCTURE (from the Panov).
Plan: survive the middlegame, trade pieces, then attack the pawn. Blockade the square in front of it.
Do not: weaken your king to avoid the initiative. Sit tight - it fades.

4. THE SYMMETRICAL STRUCTURE (from the Exchange).
Plan: create imbalance. ...Ne4, ...b5-b4, or the ...e5 break.
Do not: assume it is a draw. Symmetry is not equality.

At move twelve, before you calculate anything, ask yourself which of these four structures is on the board. Then play the plan. Most opponents at your level do not do this, and that is where your extra points come from.

WHY WE ARE FINE EVEN A PAWN DOWN - three concrete reasons, straight from the theory:
1. THE BISHOP PAIR. Swapping our knight for White's dark-squared bishop, as we just did, leaves White with knights against our remaining bishop in an open, French-like position - exactly where bishops earn their keep.
2. FORCING A WEAKNESS. If White insists on defending c5 with the pawn move b4 instead of just letting it go, his queenside pawns get permanently damaged and become a long-term target.
3. THE ...b6! PAWN SACRIFICE. In some versions we can even offer a second pawn with ...b6, ripping open the queenside files for our pieces - very similar to Benko Gambit pressure.
Whichever of the three shows up in your game, the underlying reason is the same: White spent moves grabbing and holding a pawn, so we are ahead in development and our pieces have easy squares. As Tartakower put it, the worst bishop is still better than the best knight.

THE CASE FOR: Johnsen and Hansen call this their favourite opening and give it their whole first section. Their argument is that you cannot get far here by memorising - you need understanding - which means your study time compounds instead of expiring when theory moves on.

THE CASE AGAINST: Peter Wells, in his book on the Caro-Kann, writes plainly that he lacks enthusiasm for 5...exf6. He is a strong grandmaster and his view deserves to be heard.

WHAT THE DISAGREEMENT IS ABOUT: we accept a slightly inferior pawn structure for easy development and a clear attacking plan. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much you value structure versus activity - and that is a genuine question of taste, not a settled fact.

2. Do not over-press. Many of our positions are equal, and equal positions punish ambition.

THE CASE FOR: Johnsen and Hansen call this their favourite opening and give it their whole first section. Their argument is that you cannot get far here by memorising - you need understanding - which means your study time compounds instead of expiring when theory moves on.
THE CASE AGAINST: Peter Wells, in his book on the Caro-Kann, writes plainly that he lacks enthusiasm for 5...exf6. He is a strong grandmaster and his view deserves to be heard.
WHAT THE DISAGREEMENT IS ABOUT: we accept a slightly inferior pawn structure for easy development and a clear attacking plan. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much you value structure versus activity - and that is a genuine question of taste, not a settled fact.
WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU IN PRACTICE:
1. Do not steer for endgames. Our structure is a middlegame asset and an endgame liability.
2. Do not over-press. Many of our positions are equal, and equal positions punish ambition.
3. Against a well-prepared opponent, expect a fight for a draw with chances - not an advantage out of the opening.

THE PATTERN TO MEMORISE: once our queen and bishop both aim at h3, a typical shot is ...Bxh3! gxh3 Qxh3, stripping White's king bare, with a rook on e8 or a knight swinging to g6-h4 or e4 joining in within a move or two. This exact sacrifice appears again and again in this variation - opponents who have not seen it before frequently just lose on the spot. Once White has castled kingside, ask yourself every move: is Bxh3 already working?
IF WHITE CASTLES QUEENSIDE INSTEAD: our bishops point at his king from exactly the same squares. Switch your queenside pawns into an attack with ...b5 and ...a5-a4, and welcome any trade of White's dark-squared bishop for our f8-knight - it removes one of his few defenders.
WHAT NOT TO DO:
1. Do not push ...f5 early. Our structure is only a weakness if we open the position before our pieces are ready.
2. Do not rush to swap everything down to a bare pawn or rook ending. Our doubled f-pawns and White's queenside majority genuinely favour White once almost everything is off the board, so with pieces still on, use your extra open file and activity to attack. Only head for an ending once you already have a concrete advantage, not out of habit.

The whole point of playing 7...Be7 instead of 7...Qe7. By leaving e7, our bishop reopens the entire e-file for our own rook, which now attacks the queen on e2 - while at the very same moment the bishop attacks the rook on e1 along the other diagonal. White's queen cannot defend e1 and escape the attack from our rook at once, so material falls. Remember the pattern: clearing your own piece off a key file can be as strong as any direct attacking move.

WHAT IT MEANS, and there are exactly two answers:
- In the MIDDLEGAME it gives White active pieces, open lines and attacking chances.
- In the ENDGAME it is a weak pawn that needs constant defence.

HOW TO THINK ABOUT THIS STRUCTURE, and this is the key lesson:
White has an isolated pawn on d4. That gives him ACTIVE PIECES and attacking chances in the middlegame. It gives him a WEAK PAWN in the endgame.

2. Head for the endgame, where the d-pawn becomes a target.

The queen sidesteps and keeps an eye on the queenside. Trying to hold the extra pawn with 8.Qxe4?? Nxe4 simply loses a piece.
Heading for c7, and keeping an eye on the b4- and c5-squares.
Ruling out ...Nb4 for good.
An active square for the queen, adding pressure down the a-file and the fifth rank.

A COMPLETELY DIFFERENT APPROACH. White is not fighting for the centre move by move - he is heading for a fixed set-up (knight on d2, fianchetto on g2, often Re1 and a kingside pawn storm with Nh4, f4 and g4) regardless of what we do. This can also arise from a 1.Nf3, 1.g3 or 1.d3 move-order.
The main move.

GRAB THE CENTRE IMMEDIATELY - the single most important idea in this whole lesson. Do not wait passively for White to finish his set-up; stake your claim in the middle right away, before he is ready to meet it.
The central grab you already know from the Speedcourse. At this level we go two moves deeper on both of White's serious tries.

THE CORE PRINCIPLE against the King's Indian Attack set-up, wherever you meet it in this repertoire: if White declines to contest the centre, take it yourself, immediately and without hesitation. White's whole KIA plan depends on a slow build-up with Ngf3, g3, Bg2 and O-O; a prompt ...e5 denies him the chance to do that on his own terms.
Covers e5, prepares quick development, and eyes h2 later - the same idea as our bishop on d6 in Lesson 05.
Developing actively and preparing quick kingside castling - there is no need for special measures against the King's Indian Attack once Black already controls the centre.
A useful waiting move. We stay flexible about where our queenside knight belongs until we see White's plan.
From here the knight can jump to c5, hitting d3, or regroup via f8 and g6.
Useful luft, and it also rules out any future Ng5 or Bg5 tricks.
Only now do we release the bishop, adding real pressure.

A COMPLETE, COMFORTABLE POSITION.
WHY THIS IS AN EVEN OR BETTER VERSION FOR BLACK: White's plan needs a lot of set-up moves (Nh4, f4, g4, f5) before it means anything. Meanwhile we already have more central space, an easy plan, and no weaknesses. If White ever allows it, ...d4 is a strong central break; otherwise we simply improve every piece and look for chances on the queenside with ...b5.
REMEMBER: this is one of the few set-ups in the whole course where White is not really "playing the Caro-Kann against us" - he is playing his own pet system. The antidote is always the same: seize the centre with ...e5 while you still can, and do not let him dictate the pace.
WHITE'S MORE TESTING TRY, not covered in the Speedcourse. White opens the centre at once, trying to prove our bishop is misplaced on d6.
Simple and natural - White is not interested in complications.
Gaining space and hitting our bishop.
The most natural square, preparing to win back the pawn on d4.
Black should be preferred here - we have the bishop pair, a completely healthy structure, and White's centre is not nearly as strong as it looks on the board.
THE TRAP YOU MUST KNOW, and it is a real one at this level - it has caught real players.
Threatening mate on h7.
The simple, calm defence: the bishop covers h7 and Black is simply winning the piece back with interest. Know this pattern cold, and you will never fear the sacrifice.
Stops our central break for now. Simplify instead.
White has lost the right to castle and must now spend a move defending e4. Black is at least equal, often better, in a simple structure with no theory at all.
Also delays our central break.
There is nothing to fear - the queen is oddly placed on e2, and we simply reach an open, balanced position where our development lead is worth at least as much as White's set-up.

THIS COURSE IS DIFFERENT FROM THE OTHER THREE.

The opening courses tell you WHICH MOVES to play. This one tells you WHAT TO DO once the opening is over - which is where almost every game is actually decided.

THE PRINCIPLE: openings do not produce positions, they produce STRUCTURES. The Colle produces only five. Learn the plan for each structure and you will never again reach move 15 without knowing what to do.

THE FIVE STRUCTURES:
1. THE GREEK GIFT - the h7 sacrifice. Not really a structure but a recurring pattern you must recognise instantly.
2. THE ROOK LIFT - your rook swings to h4 and joins the attack.
3. THE e5 WEDGE - pawn on e5, knight support, kingside pawn storm.
4. THE ISOLATED PAWN - you play against it, or with it.
5. BISHOP PAIR VERSUS SPACE - the slow anti-Colle games.

HOW TO STUDY THESE GAMES:
Do not memorise the moves. Play through each game once, then close the file and ask yourself: what was White's plan, and what was the move that made it work? If you can answer that, you have got what you need.

Every game here was actually played. The commentary explains the PLAN, not the variations.

WELCOME TO THE COLLE SYSTEM.

WHY THIS OPENING IS PERFECT FOR YOU RIGHT NOW:
You play almost the same seven moves in every single game. You do not need to memorise twenty different openings. You do not need to know what your opponent plays. You set up your pieces the same way, and then you attack.

Most players your level lose games in the opening because they do not know what to do. After this course, you will always know what to do.

THE SEVEN MOVES YOU MUST KNOW BY HEART:
d4, Nf3, e3, Bd3, Nbd2, O-O, and c3 (only when needed).
That is it. Learn these and you have an opening for life.

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS COURSE:
- Lesson 1: The setup and the plan
- Lesson 2: The e4 break (this is how you win)
- Lesson 3: The bishop sacrifice on h7 (the knockout punch)
- Lesson 4-6: What to do when Black plays something else
- Lesson 7: The three mistakes that cost you the game

TIME NEEDED: about two hours. Then start playing it immediately.

THIS IS THE BIG ONE. Twenty complete tournament games, chosen because every single one lands on a position from YOUR repertoire - the same c3 Colle-Koltanowski lines you already studied in Cursus 1-3. Nothing here is a random "Colle game found on the internet." Every game was checked move by move against the lines you were taught, and only kept if it matches.
WHY A WHOLE COURSE OF COMPLETE GAMES?
Opening theory tells you WHAT to play. Model games teach you HOW to play it - what the pieces are actually trying to do once the book moves run out, which plans work, which plans look good but do not, and what a real opponent does when things go wrong for him. You cannot get that from a variations tree. You can only get it from full games.
HOW THIS COURSE IS ORGANISED - the same opening tree logic as Cursus 4, but far bigger:
SECTION A - The main line and the Nc6 set-up (5 games)
SECTION B - The Nbd7 set-up and the Re1/Rxe4 recapture (6 games)
SECTION C - The Reversed Stonewall, against ...Be7 and ...b6 (4 games)
SECTION D - The Phoenix, 9.b4 (3 games)
SECTION E - Colle versus Queen's Indian, when the Stonewall is not available (2 games)
Every lesson starts on move 1, exactly like the other courses, so ChessTempo folds everything into one giant opening tree. You do not need to remember which lesson is which - just play through them in order.
HOW TO STUDY: play each game through once at normal speed without stopping. Then go back and read the comments at the marked moments - these are the moves where a plan succeeds, a plan fails, or a tactic decides the game. Ask yourself before reading each comment: what would I have played here, and why? That single habit is worth more than memorising any of these games move for move.
A NOTE ON THE SOURCES: these games and much of the analytical detail come from Colle's own tournament praxis and from Cyrus Lakdawala's "The Colle: Move by Move" (Everyman Chess, 2013), reworked here into our own words and tied directly to the repertoire decisions from Cursus 1-3. If a game or an idea grips you, the original books are worth owning - full annotated collections go far deeper than any single course can.

WELCOME TO THE MODEL GAMES ENCYCLOPEDIA FOR YOUR BLACK REPERTOIRE.

This course does for your Black repertoire what the Model Games Encyclopedia already did for your Colle-Koltanowski White repertoire: it takes every structure you have learned in the Speedcourse, Intermediate and Advanced courses and shows it played out by strong players, usually with Black in exactly your seat.

WHY THIS MATTERS: a repertoire course teaches you the moves. A model games course teaches you what those moves are FOR. Watching a 2600-rated grandmaster nurse the same ...b5/...a6 queenside majority you are learning, or defend the same isolated queen's pawn structure from the Exchange Slav side, does more for your understanding than another ten lines of pure theory.

HOW THIS COURSE IS ORGANISED: by repertoire branch, in the same order as your existing courses.
Semi-Slav side: Games 01-02 - the Meran; Game 03 - the Anti-Meran (6.Qc2); Games 04-05 - the Moscow declined and the Anti-Moscow Gambit accepted; Game 06 - the Exchange Slav.
Caro-Kann side: Game 07 - the Classical Tartakower/Korchnoi; Game 08 - the Advance (3...c5); Game 09 - the Panov (5...e6); Game 10 - the King's Indian Attack.

SOURCES FOR THIS COURSE: Cyrus Lakdawala and Keaton Kiewra, Opening Repertoire: ...c6 (Everyman 2017), for every game in this delivery, since its "Index of Complete Games" is built almost entirely from Alexey Dreev's and Igor Khenkin's own tournament praxis in exactly this repertoire.

A NOTE ON ACCURACY: the ...c6 sourcebook survives only as a heavily degraded OCR scan - the original figurine piece symbols are gone, replaced by near-random Latin characters, which is a worse starting point than the source books used for your White model games course. Every game in this course has therefore been cross-checked move by move with python-chess for legality, and where a middlegame or endgame passage could not be reconstructed with full confidence from the scan, the game is presented as a verified opening-to-middlegame excerpt with an honest note on how the rest unfolded, rather than a guessed-at move sequence. You will never be shown a move that has not been confirmed legal and consistent with the source. Two games (06, Exchange Slav; and the ...a6-first note in Game 03) diverge slightly from your repertoire's exact move order in the source material; both are flagged transparently at the point of difference rather than silently altered.

STILL TO COME: the Catalan set-up (5.g3), the London/Colle/Torre systems, the Reti and the English on the Semi-Slav side; the Two Knights and Fantasy Variation sidelines on the Caro-Kann side; and the Moscow & Anti-Moscow monograph has not yet been mined for additional games beyond Game 05. These are lower-frequency branches of your repertoire and are flagged here as the natural next expansion pass, exactly as Koltanowski's uncatalogued games were for the White course.

YOU ALREADY KNOW THE SETUP. This course is about the part that actually decides games: knowing WHICH plan fits WHICH structure, and when to switch.

THE FOUR STRUCTURES THIS OPENING PRODUCES:
1. ISOLATED QUEEN'S PAWN (IQP) - after e4 and the exchanges. You attack; you must not let the game reach a simple endgame.
2. HANGING PAWNS c4/d4 - more space, but two pawns to defend. Push d4-d5 at the right moment.
3. THE e5 WEDGE - after Ne5 and f4. You attack on the kingside with g4; Black counters on the queenside.
4. BISHOP PAIR VS SPACE - the anti-Colle lines with h3 and g4. Slow, positional, and your two bishops decide the endgame.

THE ONE DECISION THAT MATTERS MOST:
Does e4 work, or not?
- Black plays ...Nc6 and ...c5 → dxc5 first, then e4. (Lessons 01-06)
- Black plays ...Nbd7 → Re1 first, then e4, and take with the ROOK. (Lessons 07-08)
- Black plays ...b6 and ...Bb7, or a very solid ...Be7 → e4 is blunted. Switch to Ne5 and f4. (Lessons 09-10)

WHAT CHANGED SINCE THE SPEEDCOURSE:
Your opponents now defend. They will play ...h6 to stop the sacrifice, or trade pieces to kill your attack. This course teaches you what to do when the knockout punch is not available - which is most games from here on.

THE FORK IN THE ROAD. Everything up to here stays exactly as you already know it. Only move nine changes.

WEAPON 1: 9.e4 - the classical Koltanowski. Direct, attacking, and what you have played until now.
WEAPON 2: 9.b4 - the Phoenix. Positional, and objectively the harder nut for a prepared opponent.

WHY YOU NOW NEED A SECOND WEAPON:
Against accurate defence, 9.e4 gives White very little. Lessons 01 to 03 show you exactly where and how strong players neutralise it. That is not a reason to abandon 9.e4 - below 1800 it still scores heavily - but you should know its limits rather than discover them in a tournament.

WHAT 9.b4 ACTUALLY IS:
A Semi-Slav with colours reversed and a tempo extra. That framing, which comes from Lakdawala, is the most useful thing to know about it. If you have ever played or faced the Semi-Slav, you already understand the plans: expand on the queenside, break with c3-c4, and use the majority.

THE CATCH, and be honest about it: your extra tempo is Bd3, and that bishop can become a target for ...e5-e4 and ...Ng4-e5. The tempo is not free.

HOW TO CHOOSE AT THE BOARD:
- Opponent unknown or under 1800 → 9.e4. Play for the attack.
- Opponent clearly prepared, or plays 9...Qc7 and 10...h6 confidently → 9.b4. Take him out of book into a slow game.
- You need a win with less risk → 9.b4. The structures are unbalanced without being sharp.

THE DECISION POINT. Here is how to think about it.

PLAY 9.e4 WHEN:
- Your opponent is under roughly 1800, or unknown.
- He has already played a slightly passive move (...Be7, ...Re8 early, ...Nbd7 setups).
- You want a sharp game and the initiative.
- You need to win and are willing to take some risk.

PLAY 9.b4 WHEN:
- Your opponent looks prepared, or confidently answers 9.e4 Qc7 10.Qe2 with 10...h6.
- You want an unbalanced game with less concrete risk.
- You are the stronger player and want a long game with many chances to outplay him.
- You are facing someone who has clearly studied your games. This is your surprise weapon - use it sparingly and it stays one.

A WORD OF CAUTION ON REPERTOIRE BUILDING:
Do not try to play both in the same tournament game. Decide before you sit down. The worst outcome is knowing two systems shallowly instead of one deeply.

My recommendation for most students: master 9.e4 completely first. Add 9.b4 only once you are consistently reaching the middlegames from Lessons 01 to 03 and finding them unsatisfying. That is the signal you have outgrown the classical line - and not a day before.

SOURCES USED IN THIS COURSE:
- Richard Palliser, Starting Out: The Colle (Everyman 2007) for the classical lines and their critical tests.
- Cyrus Lakdawala, The Colle: Move by Move (Everyman 2013) for the 9.b4 Phoenix treatment and the reversed Semi-Slav framing.
- George Koltanowski, The Colle System, for the original plans and the advice to switch plans when the position asks for it.

THE GREEK GIFT. This is the sacrifice you came here for. Learn this pattern - it wins games at every level.

WHY IT WORKS HERE (check these three things every time):
1. Black's knight has left f6, so nothing guards h7.
2. Your knight can jump to g5 with check.

This exact sequence is Steinitz's treatment of Chigorin himself, from their 1889 World Championship match (10th game, Havana) - one of the very first Chigorin Defences ever played, and White won in style: pressure down the open g-file, a well-timed 0-0-0, and a mating attack that arrived before Black ever got his king to safety.

An independent approach that has been played by Lasker, Capablanca and Seirawan - and one your opponents will not know.

SECTION D, the Advanced-level weapon from Cursus 3: 9.b4, nicknamed the Phoenix. THE CORE IDEA, worth understanding before a single move is played: the position White reaches here is a real Semi-Slav structure (1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.e3 Nf6 5.Nc3 Nbd7 6.Bd3 dxc4 7.Bxc4 b5) with Black's side of the board - but with an extra developing move already banked, since the bishop is already sitting on d6 instead of needing a tempo to get there. Study a handful of genuine Semi-Slav games with either colour and this whole structure will feel instantly familiar.

THE FORK IN THE ROAD. Everything up to here stays exactly as you already know it. Only move nine changes.

WEAPON 1: 9.e4 - the classical Koltanowski. Direct, attacking, and what you have played until now.
WEAPON 2: 9.b4 - the Phoenix. Positional, and objectively the harder nut for a prepared opponent.

WHY YOU NOW NEED A SECOND WEAPON:
Against accurate defence, 9.e4 gives White very little. Lessons 01 to 03 show you exactly where and how strong players neutralise it. That is not a reason to abandon 9.e4 - below 1800 it still scores heavily - but you should know its limits rather than discover them in a tournament.

WHAT 9.b4 ACTUALLY IS:
A Semi-Slav with colours reversed and a tempo extra. That framing, which comes from Lakdawala, is the most useful thing to know about it. If you have ever played or faced the Semi-Slav, you already understand the plans: expand on the queenside, break with c3-c4, and use the majority.

THE CATCH, and be honest about it: your extra tempo is Bd3, and that bishop can become a target for ...e5-e4 and ...Ng4-e5. The tempo is not free.

HOW TO CHOOSE AT THE BOARD:
- Opponent unknown or under 1800 → 9.e4. Play for the attack.
- Opponent clearly prepared, or plays 9...Qc7 and 10...h6 confidently → 9.b4. Take him out of book into a slow game.
- You need a win with less risk → 9.b4. The structures are unbalanced without being sharp.

THE DECISION POINT. Here is how to think about it.

PLAY 9.e4 WHEN:
- Your opponent is under roughly 1800, or unknown.
- He has already played a slightly passive move (...Be7, ...Re8 early, ...Nbd7 setups).
- You want a sharp game and the initiative.
- You need to win and are willing to take some risk.

PLAY 9.b4 WHEN:
- Your opponent looks prepared, or confidently answers 9.e4 Qc7 10.Qe2 with 10...h6.
- You want an unbalanced game with less concrete risk.
- You are the stronger player and want a long game with many chances to outplay him.
- You are facing someone who has clearly studied your games. This is your surprise weapon - use it sparingly and it stays one.

A WORD OF CAUTION ON REPERTOIRE BUILDING:
Do not try to play both in the same tournament game. Decide before you sit down. The worst outcome is knowing two systems shallowly instead of one deeply.

My recommendation for most students: master 9.e4 completely first. Add 9.b4 only once you are consistently reaching the middlegames from Lessons 01 to 03 and finding them unsatisfying. That is the signal you have outgrown the classical line - and not a day before.

THIS COURSE IS DIFFERENT FROM THE OTHER THREE.

The opening courses tell you WHICH MOVES to play. This one tells you WHAT TO DO once the opening is over - which is where almost every game is actually decided.

THE PRINCIPLE: openings do not produce positions, they produce STRUCTURES. The Colle produces only five. Learn the plan for each structure and you will never again reach move 15 without knowing what to do.

THE FIVE STRUCTURES:
1. THE GREEK GIFT - the h7 sacrifice. Not really a structure but a recurring pattern you must recognise instantly.
2. THE ROOK LIFT - your rook swings to h4 and joins the attack.
3. THE e5 WEDGE - pawn on e5, knight support, kingside pawn storm.
4. THE ISOLATED PAWN - you play against it, or with it.
5. BISHOP PAIR VERSUS SPACE - the slow anti-Colle games.

HOW TO STUDY THESE GAMES:
Do not memorise the moves. Play through each game once, then close the file and ask yourself: what was White's plan, and what was the move that made it work? If you can answer that, you have got what you need.

Every game here was actually played. The commentary explains the PLAN, not the variations.

THIS IS THE BIG ONE. Twenty complete tournament games, chosen because every single one lands on a position from YOUR repertoire - the same c3 Colle-Koltanowski lines you already studied in Cursus 1-3. THE FIVE RECURRING DECISIONS OF YOUR BLACK REPERTOIRE.

Almost every game you play with 1...c6 comes down to one of these. Learn to recognise them and you will rarely be without a plan.

DECISION 1 - WHERE DOES THE LIGHT-SQUARED BISHOP GO?
Default: out to f5 or g4 BEFORE ...e6.
Exception A: the Semi-Slav proper, where we accept a shut-in bishop because ...dxc4 and ...b5 pay for it.
Exception B: the English move order with 4.Nc3 Nbd7, where ...Bf5 runs into cxd5 and Qb3.
Exception C: against 4.Ne2 in the Advance, where White's own knight clogs his position.
The rule is not "always ...Bf5". It is: only bury the bishop if you are being paid for it.

DECISION 2 - WHEN DO WE TAKE ON c4?
Only when the recapture suits us. Against 6.Qc2 the same capture is bad on move six and excellent on move eight, because by then the bishop must recapture instead of a pawn.

DECISION 3 - WHEN DO WE BREAK WITH ...c5?
Only once it is supported: ...a6, ...b4 or a rook on c8 first. An unprepared ...c5 is met by d4-d5 with tempo.

DECISION 4 - DO WE ACCEPT THE PAWN?
Advance 4.dxc5: develop first, take later.
Catalan 5.g3: take it, but give it back for development when the moment comes.
Moscow 6.Bh4: only if you have studied the gambit properly.

DECISION 5 - MIDDLEGAME OR ENDGAME?
Tartakower: keep queens on. Our structure is a middlegame asset.
Moscow: patient - the bishop pair does not expire.
Panov: trade pieces. The isolated pawn gets weaker with every exchange.

THE HABIT: at move fifteen, name the structure and name the decision in front of you. Then play.

SOURCES: Cyrus Lakdawala and Keaton Kiewra, Opening Repertoire: ...c6 (Everyman 2017); Sverre Johnsen and Torbjorn Ringdal Hansen, Win with the Caro-Kann; Milos Pavlovic, The Modernized Semi-Slav (Thinkers Publishing 2024). These are model plans written for this course; the full annotated games are in those books.

THE TRAPS YOU MUST AVOID:

1. ...dxc4 against 6.Qc2 before White commits the bishop. He recaptures with a pawn after b3 and the entire ...b5 plan disappears.
2. ...Bf5 in the English move order 1.c4 c6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 Nf6 4.Nc3 Nbd7, because 5.cxd5 cxd5 6.Qb3 hits b7 and d5 and the bishop must return to c8.
3. ...dxc4 against 5.Bg5 - that is the Botvinnik, and we avoid it with 5...h6 every single time.
4. ...c5 in the Meran before the rook and the b-pawn are ready. The break needs ...a6 or ...b4 first.

THE TRAPS YOU CAN SET:

1. The delayed capture. Against 6.Qc2, take on c4 only once the bishop must recapture. The same move is worthless on move six and excellent on move eight.
2. The ...b4 deflection. In the modern Meran, ...b4 before ...c5 drives the knight to a4 or e2, where it does far less.
3. The Exchange Slav ...Ne4 and ...f5. Most opponents assume symmetry means safety and never adjust.
4. The fork after 12.Nxe4 dxe4 in the Exchange - the pawn hits bishop and knight at once.

THE BRIDGE TO YOUR WHITE REPERTOIRE:
- The e5-outpost you build with White in the Colle is the outpost you deny with Black by playing ...Nd7 and ...f5.
- The Bxh7 sacrifice you hunt for with White is the one you defuse with ...h6 and ...Nf8.
- The isolated queen's pawn you attack in the Colle is the one you attack again in the Panov, from the same side of the board.

Teach the two colours together. A student who has seen a structure from both sides understands it roughly twice as fast as one who has only defended it.

Pavlovic compares the Meran to the Open Sicilian, and the comparison is exact: sharp, concrete, and unforgiving of general principles. This course gives you the modern main lines and, where a line is genuinely too heavy to learn from a course, says so instead of pretending.

WHAT YOU ADD HERE:

AN HONEST AUDIT OF YOUR 1.d4 REPERTOIRE.

WHERE WE ARE GENUINELY FINE:
- The Meran with 9.a3 and 11...Rc8. Modern, tested, and balanced.
- The Anti-Meran with 6.Qc2. The queen really does end up misplaced on c2.
- The Catalan set-up with 5.g3. Lakdawala is right that White is the one taking a risk.
- The Exchange Slav with 6...Ne4. Not better, but full of play.

WHERE WE ARE EQUAL AND SHOULD BE HAPPY WITH IT:
- The Moscow with 6.Bxf6 Qxf6. We have the bishop pair and no weaknesses. Do not over-press.

WHERE WE MAKE A CONCESSION:
- Against 6.Bh4 we either accept a gambit that demands real study, or we decline and give White a comfortable game. There is no third road. Choose deliberately, and do not pretend the declining line is objectively equal - it is sound, not equalising.

WHERE THE THEORY MOVES FASTEST:
The Meran and the Moscow Gambit. If you take those up, expect to refresh them every year or two. The Exchange Slav, the Catalan set-up and the London lines will still be valid in ten years.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR HOW YOU SPEND YOUR TIME:
Put your study hours into the lines that do not expire, and use a reliable declining line in the ones that do - unless the sharp line is genuinely your style. A repertoire you maintain badly is worse than a slightly quieter one you know well.

NOTHING YOU LEARNED IS REPLACED. Every move from the Speedcourse stays correct. What you add here is depth and, above all, timing.

A NOTE ON NAMES, because the books disagree and it confuses students:
- 5.Bg5 h6 6.Bxf6 is called the Moscow by most sources, and the Anti-Moscow by Lakdawala.
- 5.Bg5 h6 6.Bh4 is the Anti-Moscow to most sources, and the Moscow Gambit to Lakdawala.
Do not worry about the labels. Learn the positions.

THE THREE THINGS THAT MATTER AT THIS LEVEL:
1. WHEN to play ...dxc4. The same capture is bad on one move and excellent two moves later. Lessons 01 and 03 are entirely about this.
2. WHERE the light-squared bishop belongs. Sometimes f5, sometimes b7, and once neither. Lesson 08 has the exception.
3. WHAT to do once theory ends around move fourteen. Lesson 10 collects the plans.

THE FOUR STRUCTURES OF YOUR 1.d4 REPERTOIRE.

Most of your games leave theory around move fourteen. What decides them is whether you recognise the structure in front of you.

1. THE MERAN STRUCTURE (pawns a6-b5-c5 against White's centre).
Plan: ...Bb7, ...a6, then ...c5. After d4-d5 and the exchange on e6, use the f-file and think seriously about castling long.
Do not: hurry ...c5 before ...a6 - the break loses its force.

2. THE MOSCOW STRUCTURE (we own the bishop pair, no weaknesses).
Plan: ...g6 and ...Bg7, then ...e5 or ...c5 at the right moment.
Do not: rush. The bishop pair does not expire; improve a piece and wait.
