AN HONEST AUDIT OF YOUR 1.d4 REPERTOIRE.
WHERE WE ARE GENUINELY FINE:
- The Meran with 9.a3 and 11...Rc8. Modern, tested, and balanced.
- The Anti-Meran with 6.Qc2. The queen really does end up misplaced on c2.
- The Catalan set-up with 5.g3. Lakdawala is right that White is the one taking a risk, and even Kramnik as White could not prove anything against careful play.
- The Exchange Slav with 6...Ne4. Not better, but full of play, and genuinely better for Black in some of the sharper tries White can choose to allow.
WHERE WE ARE EQUAL AND SHOULD BE HAPPY WITH IT:
- The Moscow with 6.Bxf6 Qxf6. We have the bishop pair and no weaknesses. Do not over-press.
WHERE WE TAKE ON REAL COMPLEXITY BY CHOICE:
- Against 6.Bh4, we now recommend accepting the pawn with 6...dxc4 at this level, entering positions that Dreev himself, a lifelong specialist in exactly this variation, describes as among the most complicated in the whole opening and still not definitively evaluated. This is not a line you can safely improvise. If you do not have the study time for it right now, 6...Be7 remains completely sound and always available - there is no shame in choosing it deliberately, only in not knowing you have the choice.
WHERE THE THEORY MOVES FASTEST:
The Meran and the Anti-Moscow Gambit. If you take those up, expect to refresh them every year or two - Dreev himself notes that new games and improvements appear in the Anti-Moscow at essentially every major tournament. The Exchange Slav, the Catalan set-up and the London lines will still be valid in ten years.
WHAT THIS MEANS FOR HOW YOU SPEND YOUR TIME:
Put your study hours into the lines that do not expire, and use a reliable declining line in the ones that do - unless the sharp line is genuinely your style. A repertoire you maintain badly is worse than a slightly quieter one you know well.

THE MERAN. Now our plan is fixed and easy to remember:

THE ANTI-MERAN. A tricky waiting move, and it does four things at once:
1. It prepares b3, so that after a later ...dxc4 White can recapture with a PAWN instead of the bishop - denying us the whole ...b5 plan.
2. It keeps a sharp g4 advance in reserve (the so-called Shirov Attack). We are not going to provoke it.
3. The queen already eyes the b1-h7 diagonal, ready to support Bd3 or Ng5 ideas later.
4. If we do get our ...dxc4 and ...b5 in anyway, the queen aims straight at our backward c6-pawn and the hole on c5.

WHAT IF WHITE ACTUALLY PLAYS THE SHIROV ATTACK WITH g4!?, instead of waiting? We are not obliged to just sit and defend. Lakdawala's own recommendation against it is to counter-attack rather than hunker down: meet the kingside advance with our own central and queenside strike, using ...dxc4, ...e5 and a knight jump to d5, turning the attacker into the one who has to worry about his own king. That is a topic for the Advanced course once you actually face it - for now, simply know that "we are not going to provoke it" does not mean "we would be lost if it came".

THE MODERN SYSTEM, in Dreev's own words - this is how he characterises White's choice at this exact juncture. From here Black has two genuinely different roads, and this is the single most important branching point in the whole variation.
BRANCH A: 11...h5!? Theory here is still comparatively undeveloped, which is either an opportunity or a warning depending on how you like your chess. Dreev's own assessment is that the resulting positions differ completely from the alternative below, and that there remains real room to find new ideas rather than just reciting known theory.
BRANCH B: 11...Bg7, the move Dreev describes as becoming very popular in recent years, and the one we recommend studying first, since it is the more principled and more thoroughly tested of the two. But be warned before you commit to it: White's sharpest try here, 12.Nxf7!?, is the exact piece sacrifice Topalov played against Kramnik at Wijk aan Zee 2008 - one of the most famous games in this entire opening. Kramnik did not defend accurately and lost brilliantly; the defence has since been improved, and Dreev's own verdict is that Black now has more than enough resources, but the theory of that one move is still actively developing and no final word has been spoken. The calmer alternative, 12.Nxd7, is not calm at all in practice - it leads directly to 12...Qxd7 13.Bd6!, a genuine wedge in Black's position where only the precise 13...a6! holds the balance; more natural-looking tries such as 13...e5?! walk into forced, only-move sequences that can lose outright within a handful of moves.
THE HONEST CONCLUSION, and it applies to every single branch of this chapter: there is no safe, simplified single line to memorise here the way there is almost everywhere else in this repertoire. Dreev's own book runs to some two hundred pages on this variation alone, packed with only-moves, novelties and improvements from year to year. The correct way to take this line up is to work through his book chapter by chapter with a board and an engine, treat every sharp position as something to verify rather than trust from memory, and keep 6...Be7 in your back pocket for any game where you cannot afford a theoretical accident. When it is worth it: when you meet 6.Bh4 often, when you need real winning chances with Black, and when you actually have the study time to put in. Not otherwise.

Lakdawala half-jokingly calls this the most sedative line in the whole Slav complex. His advice, after years of experience with it, changed over time: he used to tell students to avoid the sharp reply below, but now recommends it without reservation, precisely because it turns a boring position into a real fight.

This move deliberately breaks a well-known opening rule - do not move the same piece twice without a reason - and Lakdawala openly admits it does exactly that. The point is that White cannot easily punish it: he too must spend more time, recapturing on e4 or defending c3, so the "wasted" tempo evens out. What we get instead of a drab, symmetrical Exchange Slav is a livelier, more Grunfeld-like fight, with genuine winning chances for both sides.

A HONEST SOURCING NOTE, useful at this level precisely because it is about timing: the source game for this whole plan (Giertz-Khenkin, Lucerne 1994) actually continues 7...Nxc3 8.bxc3, heading into a sharp, Grunfeld-like structure with doubled white pawns rather than the calmer route below. That line is well regarded and fully sound. This repertoire keeps the knight on e4 instead, because it gives us one single plan that stays identical from the Speedcourse all the way through the Advanced course - not because the alternative is worse.

WHY THIS MOVE MATTERS: the Exchange Slav has a reputation as a dull, drawish try, and objectively it is - White has committed his structure symmetrically and given up any hope of an opening advantage. The single most important decision Black has in the whole variation is refusing to let the position stay symmetrical and boring. 6...Ne4 does exactly that: it creates immediate imbalance and steers the game toward Grunfeld-like piece activity rather than a lifeless carbon-copy structure.

EDITORIAL NOTE: this particular source game continues with 7...Nxc3, trading down further. Your repertoire instead keeps the knight actively posted on e4 for as long as possible (the line continues 7.e3 e6 8.Bd3 Bd6 9.Bxd6 Qxd6 10.O-O O-O, reaching a position where Black's actively placed pieces and White's slightly compromised structure balance out favourably) - a small, deliberate difference in technique, not a correction of an error. Both approaches are entirely sound; this course teaches the knight-on-e4 version for consistency with the rest of your repertoire's general style of meeting symmetrical structures with maximum piece activity rather than further simplification.

THE ANTI-MERAN. A tricky waiting move, and it does four things at once:
1. It prepares b3, so that after a later ...dxc4 White can recapture with a PAWN instead of the bishop - denying us the whole ...b5 plan.
2. It keeps a sharp g4 advance in reserve (the so-called Shirov Attack). We are not going to provoke it.
3. The queen already eyes the b1-h7 diagonal, ready to support Bd3 or Ng5 ideas later.
4. If we do get our ...dxc4 and ...b5 in anyway, the queen aims straight at our backward c6-pawn and the hole on c5.
That sounds excellent for White on paper.

2. He keeps the g4 advance in reserve - the Shirov Attack.

That sounds excellent for White. But Lakdawala points out the flip side, and it is the key to the whole chapter.
WHAT IF WHITE ACTUALLY PLAYS THE SHIROV ATTACK WITH g4!?, instead of waiting? We are not obliged to just sit and defend. Lakdawala's own recommendation against it is to counter-attack rather than hunker down: meet the kingside advance with our own central and queenside strike, using ...dxc4, ...e5 and a knight jump to d5, turning the attacker into the one who has to worry about his own king. That is a topic for the Advanced course once you actually face it - for now, simply know that "we are not going to provoke it" does not mean "we would be lost if it came".

THE FULL PICTURE OF WHAT THIS MOVE DOES, worth knowing precisely at this level rather than just in outline:
1. It prepares b3, so a later ...dxc4 can be met by a PAWN recapture, denying the whole ...b5 plan.
2. It holds the sharp g4 Shirov Attack in reserve.
3. The queen already eyes the b1-h7 diagonal.
4. If Black does get ...dxc4 and ...b5 in anyway, the queen aims at the backward c6-pawn and the c5-hole.
IF WHITE ACTUALLY PLAYS THE SHIROV ATTACK with an early g4, Lakdawala's own recommendation is not to just defend passively - counter in the centre and on the queenside with ...dxc4, ...e5 and a knight jump to d5, so the attacker has to start worrying about his own king. That is real, concrete counterplay, not just "hope it doesn't happen" - know it exists before you meet it over the board.
THE WAITING MOVE. Compare this with your Advanced Lesson 03: White delays committing the bishop, keeping Black guessing between a Meran-style set-up and a queenside fianchetto for himself.

THIS COURSE IS DIFFERENT FROM THE OTHER THREE.

The opening courses tell you WHICH MOVES to play. This one tells you WHAT TO DO once the opening is over - which is where almost every game is actually decided.

THE PRINCIPLE: openings do not produce positions, they produce STRUCTURES. The Colle produces only five. Learn the plan for each structure and you will never again reach move 15 without knowing what to do.

THE FIVE STRUCTURES:
1. THE GREEK GIFT - the h7 sacrifice. Not really a structure but a recurring pattern you must recognise instantly.
2. THE ROOK LIFT - your rook swings to h4 and joins the attack.
3. THE e5 WEDGE - pawn on e5, knight support, kingside pawn storm.
4. THE ISOLATED PAWN - you play against it, or with it.
5. BISHOP PAIR VERSUS SPACE - the slow anti-Colle games.

HOW TO STUDY THESE GAMES:
Do not memorise the moves. Play through each game once, then close the file and ask yourself: what was White's plan, and what was the move that made it work? If you can answer that, you have got what you need.

THIS IS THE BIG ONE. Twenty complete tournament games, chosen because every single one lands on a position from YOUR repertoire - the same c3 Colle-Koltanowski lines you already studied in Cursus 1-3. Nothing here is a random "Colle game found on the internet." Every game was checked move by move against the lines you were taught, and only kept if it matches.
WHY A WHOLE COURSE OF COMPLETE GAMES?
Opening theory tells you WHAT to play. Model games teach you HOW to play it - what the pieces are actually trying to do once the book moves run out, which plans work, which plans look good but do not, and what a real opponent does when things go wrong for him. You cannot get that from a variations tree. You can only get it from full games.
HOW THIS COURSE IS ORGANISED - the same opening tree logic as Cursus 4, but far bigger:
SECTION A - The main line and the Nc6 set-up (5 games)
SECTION B - The Nbd7 set-up and the Re1/Rxe4 recapture (6 games)
SECTION C - The Reversed Stonewall, against ...Be7 and ...b6 (4 games)
SECTION D - The Phoenix, 9.b4 (3 games)
SECTION E - Colle versus Queen's Indian, when the Stonewall is not available (2 games)
Every lesson starts on move 1, exactly like the other courses, so ChessTempo folds everything into one giant opening tree. You do not need to remember which lesson is which - just play through them in order.
HOW TO STUDY: play each game through once at normal speed without stopping. Then go back and read the comments at the marked moments - these are the moves where a plan succeeds, a plan fails, or a tactic decides the game. Ask yourself before reading each comment: what would I have played here, and why? That single habit is worth more than memorising any of these games move for move.
A NOTE ON THE SOURCES: these games and much of the analytical detail come from Colle's own tournament praxis and from Cyrus Lakdawala's "The Colle: Move by Move" (Everyman Chess, 2013), reworked here into our own words and tied directly to the repertoire decisions from Cursus 1-3. If a game or an idea grips you, the original books are worth owning - full annotated collections go far deeper than any single course can.

WELCOME TO THE MODEL GAMES ENCYCLOPEDIA FOR YOUR BLACK REPERTOIRE.

This course does for your Black repertoire what the Model Games Encyclopedia already did for your Colle-Koltanowski White repertoire: it takes every structure you have learned in the Speedcourse, Intermediate and Advanced courses and shows it played out by strong players, usually with Black in exactly your seat.

WHY THIS MATTERS: a repertoire course teaches you the moves. A model games course teaches you what those moves are FOR. Watching a 2600-rated grandmaster nurse the same ...b5/...a6 queenside majority you are learning, or defend the same isolated queen's pawn structure from the Exchange Slav side, does more for your understanding than another ten lines of pure theory.

YOU ALREADY KNOW THE SETUP. This course is about the part that actually decides games: knowing WHICH plan fits WHICH structure, and when to switch.

THE FOUR STRUCTURES THIS OPENING PRODUCES:
1. ISOLATED QUEEN'S PAWN (IQP) - after e4 and the exchanges. You attack; you must not let the game reach a simple endgame.

THE FORK IN THE ROAD. Everything up to here stays exactly as you already know it. Only move nine changes.

WEAPON 1: 9.e4 - the classical Koltanowski. Direct, attacking, and what you have played until now.
WEAPON 2: 9.b4 - the Phoenix. Positional, and objectively the harder nut for a prepared opponent.

WHY YOU NOW NEED A SECOND WEAPON:
Against accurate defence, 9.e4 gives White very little. Lessons 01 to 03 show you exactly where and how strong players neutralise it. That is not a reason to abandon 9.e4 - below 1800 it still scores heavily - but you should know its limits rather than discover them in a tournament.

WHAT 9.b4 ACTUALLY IS:
A Semi-Slav with colours reversed and a tempo extra. That framing, which comes from Lakdawala, is the most useful thing to know about it. If you have ever played or faced the Semi-Slav, you already understand the plans: expand on the queenside, break with c3-c4, and use the majority.

THE CATCH, and be honest about it: your extra tempo is Bd3, and that bishop can become a target for ...e5-e4 and ...Ng4-e5. The tempo is not free.

HOW TO CHOOSE AT THE BOARD:
- Opponent unknown or under 1800 → 9.e4. Play for the attack.
- Opponent clearly prepared, or plays 9...Qc7 and 10...h6 confidently → 9.b4. Take him out of book into a slow game.
- You need a win with less risk → 9.b4. The structures are unbalanced without being sharp.

THE DECISION POINT. Here is how to think about it.

PLAY 9.e4 WHEN:
- Your opponent is under roughly 1800, or unknown.
- He has already played a slightly passive move (...Be7, ...Re8 early, ...Nbd7 setups).
- You want a sharp game and the initiative.
- You need to win and are willing to take some risk.

PLAY 9.b4 WHEN:
- Your opponent looks prepared, or confidently answers 9.e4 Qc7 10.Qe2 with 10...h6.
- You want an unbalanced game with less concrete risk.
- You are the stronger player and want a long game with many chances to outplay him.
- You are facing someone who has clearly studied your games. This is your surprise weapon - use it sparingly and it stays one.

A WORD OF CAUTION ON REPERTOIRE BUILDING:
Do not try to play both in the same tournament game. Decide before you sit down. The worst outcome is knowing two systems shallowly instead of one deeply.

My recommendation for most students: master 9.e4 completely first. Add 9.b4 only once you are consistently reaching the middlegames from Lessons 01 to 03 and finding them unsatisfying. That is the signal you have outgrown the classical line - and not a day before.

Compare this directly to the sacrifice lessons from Cursus 1-2: taking away one sacrifice does not win the game on its own, and it can even hand White a fresh target on h6 instead.

Releasing the central tension helps White, as usual - see the note to move 9 in game 1.
Eyeing f4 and forcing White's reply.
A passive regrouping. Black had to accept a sharper position with 14...f5, when White still keeps an edge but the game stays far more complicated.
Quietly preparing c3-c4-c5, since Black's last move did nothing to stop it.
A pawn sacrifice in appearance only - White wins it straight back with a large initiative.
White's queen and bishop pair now dominate the whole board while Black's king sits exposed on g8 with his queenside completely undeveloped.
Regaining the piece with a winning position - the point behind the pawn sacrifice on move 16.
White has real compensation beyond the extra piece: Black's king is stuck in the middle, his queenside pieces have not moved, and his rook and queen constantly get in each other's way.
A decisive attack - the knight heads for d6 or f6 next.
Even with queens off, White's initiative rolls on into the endgame.
Allowing the fork on purpose - it changes nothing.

SUMMARY: 10...h6 removes one sacrifice, not the whole attack. If Black spends a tempo defusing the Greek gift, look for the queenside break with b4 and c4 instead - the reversed Semi-Slav plan behind the Phoenix works here too.
L.Pecot - A.J.Tavares, correspondence 1998.
Move-order twist: ...Qc7 before ...Bd6. It makes no real difference - White treats it exactly the same way.
Black's most natural move. He defends and prepares to play ...e5 himself.

Black's most natural move. He defends c7 and prevents you from playing e5 with tempo, since e5 no longer hits a piece. Palliser calls this Black's main try - and it is the position you will meet most often against booked-up opponents.
Objectively Black's most testing try. Compare this to the simpler 9...dxe4 lines from Cursus 1-2, which hand White an edge more or less by force - see games 2 and 4 later in this section.
The Phoenix works just as well here, regardless of whether Black's bishop first stopped on e7 or went straight to d6.
An alternative move order to the direct 11.b5 - both are playable; this course covers the a3 approach.
Black's other main try against the Phoenix, distinct from the immediate 10...e5 seen in the last two games: rather than a pawn break, Black tries to win a tempo on the d3-bishop with a piece.
Not to c2, where the bishop would aim straight at Black's king - here the priority is simply to achieve c3-c4 as quickly as possible.
The fight for the c4-square continues - note that Black's knight manoeuvre cost real time without actually preventing this plan.
Now c3-c4 cannot be stopped, since the knight is driven away with tempo.
The point of the whole plan - remember the idea from game 16: this is simply a Semi-Slav a tempo up, and c3-c4 is exactly the break that structure calls for.
Black's queen already looks uncomfortable on c7.
A further weakening that does not solve anything.
Not falling for any tactics based on ...Qxd5 - the knight arrives with a strong attack on the queen.
Objectively 21.dxe6! was even stronger, but the move played still keeps a clear and lasting advantage.
White holds rolling kingside pawns and much better-placed pieces - a large, stable advantage.
Eyeing the d6-square.
A powerful further pawn thrust that both attacks and gains more space.
A striking combination that removes Black's best remaining piece.

SUMMARY: whether Black plays the direct 10...e5 or tries to save a tempo with ...Ng4-e5, the Phoenix idea works the same way - White simply plays for c3-c4 at the first opportunity, treating the whole position as a favourable, tempo-up Semi-Slav.
E.Gausel - Z.Gorecki, Oslo 2002.
The identical plan, now between two strong grandmasters, with Black's knight already on c6.

A key strategic decision for Black: trade on e5, or allow White the full Stonewall Dutch structure with 9.f4. Since an early ...c5xd4 tends to favour White here as everywhere else in this repertoire, and holding the tension only invites a stronger version of White's attack, trading on e5 is Black's most solid try - though even here White keeps a pleasant position.

THE WEDGE IS BUILT. Pawn on e5, supported by f4. This structure appears in every Colle where e4 does not work.

WHAT THE WEDGE GIVES YOU: space, a permanent outpost, and a clear attacking direction. What it costs you: the d5-square and a slightly loose king if you push too far.
Black's standard freeing try.
A near-forced structural decision, just as in a real French Defence - without it, White's space and attacking chances on the kingside simply grow unopposed.

ESSENTIAL. White has tried a host of alternatives here, but they are all inferior - when Black plays ...f5, you must always be ready to take en passant, or he gets a comfortable position and a long, dull game.
Trading now in order to free e4 for a future central break.
Preparing counterplay with ...Nc5 - probably Black's best practical try.
A thematic pawn sacrifice-in-spirit: Black hands over the d4-square in exchange for activating his own game via c5 and, more importantly, the g4-square for his knight.
The second key idea - Black opens the position for his own pieces before White can consolidate.
All three of Black's threats - ...Ne3, ...Nf2+ and ...Nxh2 - look dangerous at once, but White has a single move that covers every one of them.
Force the trade of queens - once the queens leave the board, Black's entire "attack" evaporates.
A powerful zwischenzug rather than the automatic recapture on f4.
The critical point of the whole ending.
Black had to accept the complications with 22...Kxh7 23.Rxe3, when White keeps only a small edge rather than a large one.
Getting too clever at exactly the wrong moment - the simple 23.Bxg6! kept a winning advantage.
Patient defence - the advanced d-pawn is not running away, so there is no need to grab it yet.
Both sides now trade inaccuracies in a complicated position - a reminder that even strong grandmasters do not play perfectly once a game turns sharp and unclear.
The move that saves the game for Black.

SUMMARY: even at grandmaster level, the Reversed Stonewall gives White a genuine, long-lasting initiative - Black needed nearly perfect play across the whole game just to hold the draw. Learn this structure well and you will find yourself with a real practical plus in a large share of your games, even against strong opposition.
E.Bareev - V.Tukmakov, Tilburg (rapid) 1994.
This move order rules out any Reversed Stonewall ideas for White (compare Section C) - the queen defends e5 in advance.

SECTION D, the Advanced-level weapon from Cursus 3: 9.b4, nicknamed the Phoenix. THE CORE IDEA, worth understanding before a single move is played: the position White reaches here is a real Semi-Slav structure (1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.e3 Nf6 5.Nc3 Nbd7 6.Bd3 dxc4 7.Bxc4 b5) with Black's side of the board - but with an extra developing move already banked, since the bishop is already sitting on d6 instead of needing a tempo to get there. Study a handful of genuine Semi-Slav games with either colour and this whole structure will feel instantly familiar.
THE COLLE BISHOP. Look at where it points: straight at h7, next to Black's king. Almost every win in this opening ends with a sacrifice on that square. Never trade this bishop cheaply.

NOW we play c3, because Black attacks d4 and we need to defend it.

GOLDEN RULE: play c3 only when Black plays ...c5. If you play c3 too early you waste a move.

NOW we play c3, because Black attacks d4 and we need to defend it.
GOLDEN RULE: play c3 only when Black plays ...c5. If you play c3 too early you waste a move.

Black's second main system. Compared with ...Nc6:
PLUS for Black: c5 is defended an extra time, so dxc5 achieves less.
MINUS for Black: the knight blocks his light-squared bishop, which struggles to find a home.

Black's other main setup: the knight goes to d7 instead of c6.

ONE THING CHANGES FOR YOU: do NOT play dxc5 here. Instead play Re1.

Black's other main setup: the knight goes to d7 instead of c6.

ONE THING CHANGES FOR YOU: do NOT play dxc5 here. Instead play Re1. Why? From d7 the knight already overprotects c5, so ...Nxc5 would come with tempo on your bishop and grab extra control of e4 - dxc5 simply helps Black instead of you. Re1 avoids that problem entirely.

Black's other main setup: the knight goes to d7 instead of c6.
ONE THING CHANGES FOR YOU: do NOT play dxc5 here. Instead play Re1. Why? From d7 the knight already overprotects c5, so ...Nxc5 would come with tempo on your bishop and grab extra control of e4 - dxc5 simply helps Black instead of you. Re1 avoids that problem entirely.

SECTION B: Black's knight goes to d7 instead of c6. The point is concrete - after a future d4xc5, the recapture ...Nxc5 would hit your bishop on d3 with tempo, so White's automatic Cursus 1 plan of 8.dxc5 no longer works cleanly. The answer, as you already know from Cursus 2, is to change plans completely: forget dxc5, and play Re1 followed by e3-e4 instead.

NO dxc5 HERE. Memorise the rule:
- knight on c6 → dxc5 then e4
- knight on d7 → Re1 then e4
Getting this the wrong way round is the single most common mistake in the whole opening.
Knight on d7, so the rook goes to e1. Standard.

THE ROOK MOVE. Remember this: knight on c6 means dxc5, knight on d7 means Re1.

The rook backs up the e-pawn and gets ready for something special.

THE ROOK MOVE. Remember this: knight on c6 means dxc5, knight on d7 means Re1.

The rook backs up the e-pawn and gets ready for something special. Do not be tempted by the natural-looking 8.Qe2 instead - Black then has time for 8...e5! with a fine game, since without pressure on d4 there is no rush.

THE ROOK MOVE. Remember this: knight on c6 means dxc5, knight on d7 means Re1.
The rook backs up the e-pawn and gets ready for something special. Do not be tempted by the natural-looking 8.Qe2 instead - Black then has time for 8...e5! with a fine game, since without pressure on d4 there is no rush.
The Cursus 2 signature move. The rook supports e3-e4 in advance, so that after the central exchanges White's rook - not just his queen and bishop - joins the attack.
Black grabs the centre before you are ready. Punish it by opening lines immediately.
Black grabs the centre before you are ready. Punish it by opening lines immediately - this loosening try is even worse than it looks.
Black strikes back in the centre himself rather than waiting passively.

The exact position from the previous game. Worth noting who Black is here: the same Marcel Duchamp famous for founding the Dadaist art movement, and a genuinely strong amateur player - this was not a weak opponent.
Still correct, and still necessary - this is White's only realistic way to fight for an edge.

And you are back in a familiar Colle structure.

WHY MOVE ORDERS MATTER AT YOUR LEVEL:
1. They let you steer opponents into positions you know.
2. They stop opponents from steering YOU into positions you do not.

THE THREE RULES THAT COVER ALMOST EVERYTHING:
- If Black's light-squared bishop is already outside the pawn chain (on g4 or f5), do not play Bd3. Play c4 or h3 instead.
- If Black has not played ...c5, do not play c3. Play e4 straight away.
- If Black has played ...b6 and ...Bb7, or ...g6 and ...Bg7, forget e4 and think about Ne5 and f4 - except against the fianchetto, where you play in the centre instead.

Learn those three and you will almost never be out of book, whatever your opponent tries.

And you are back in a familiar Colle structure.

2. They stop opponents from steering YOU into positions you do not.
THE THREE RULES THAT COVER ALMOST EVERYTHING:

- If Black has not played ...c5, do not play c3. Play e4 straight away.
- If Black has played ...b6 and ...Bb7, or ...g6 and ...Bg7, forget e4 and think about Ne5 and f4 - except against the fianchetto, where you play in the centre instead.
Learn those three and you will almost never be out of book, whatever your opponent tries.
All four central pawns are gone. Do not assume this means an automatic draw - White still leads in development, and that lead has to be proven, not assumed, by Black.
Offering the trade of queens rather than retreating - a small point but a real one, since it denies Black any use of his queen's activity.
The bishop lands on its best square, eyeing b7 and f7 simultaneously.
Rather than retreating meekly, White keeps his rook active on the e-file, ready to swing sideways.
As so often in this structure, f7 turns out to be Black's soft spot - notice this same theme recurring in the Colle-Duchamp and Kukov-Enchev games later in this section.
Removing Black's last active piece.
Forking the a8-rook.
The material harvest begins.

SUMMARY: this is the cleanest possible illustration of the Cursus 2 rule for facing ...Nbd7 - Re1 first, then e3-e4, and do not worry when the centre liquidates completely. White's small lead in development, on its own, was enough to win material by force within a dozen moves of the queens coming off.
E.Colle - G.A.Thomas, Paris 1929.

IMPORTANT NUANCE, worth flagging clearly: here White recaptures with the BISHOP, not the rook, even though this is the same Nbd7/Re1 family as the last three games. The difference is move order - Black has already played 8...e5 himself before the central exchanges, so by the time White recaptures on e4 there is no longer a clean e-file battery to exploit with Rxe4. Compare this carefully with game 8 (Goodman-Conde), where Black held back ...e5 and Rxe4 was correct. Learn to tell the two move orders apart rather than recapturing with the rook automatically.
A small difference from the Thomas game: here Black keeps queens on and challenges the bishop immediately.
Giving up the bishop pair to win a clean pawn by force.
The bishop must declare which side it belongs to - it cannot hold both b2 and the long diagonal.
Simplest - the passed pawn is worth more than trying to trap the bishop.
Cashing in the point: material is now clearly in White's favour.
A clean extra pawn with the safer king and the better structure - technically won, though Black puts up a long defence.
The decisive breakthrough.

SUMMARY: the same message as the previous game, from a slightly different route - erasing every central pawn does not hand Black a free draw. As long as White is even fractionally ahead in development, keep finding active moves and the advantage tends to grow rather than disappear.
E.Colle - M.Duchamp, Paris 1929.
Ruling out the Greek gift on h7 in one move, at the cost of a tempo and a fresh target on h6 - the same idea and the same trade-off you saw in game 3 (Pecot-Tavares).
Principle: do not be the side that releases the central pawn tension - let your opponent do it and gain a tempo when he does.
Black blinks first.
Keeping the tension principle alive with pieces, too - Qd3 is coming next.
A small inaccuracy - 16.Qxd4! was more testing, since it develops Black's rook for him only in order to invade the seventh rank immediately afterward.
The recurring theme of this whole section: f7 is Black's permanent soft spot whenever his king's knight has left f6 and his dark-squared bishop is gone.
White's remaining bishop now dominates the light squares, and f7 ties Black down for the rest of the game.
Forcing a favourable endgame - or, more directly, 26.Qe5! keeps queens on with an even stronger attack.
Ignoring the knight completely and going after Black's weak back rank instead - by far the most efficient plan.
Two clean pawns up with the better minor piece as well - essentially decided.

SUMMARY: know the difference between the two move orders. If Black plays ...e5 only after the central exchanges (games 6-8), recapture on e4 with the rook and aim for a direct attack. If Black plays ...e5 first, before ...dxe4, the e-file battery is gone and recapturing with the bishop, aiming for a long strategic squeeze instead, is simply correct.
V.Kukov - I.Enchev, Bulgarian Championship, Blagoevgrad 2009.
Black holds back the central break this time and just finishes development.

TAKE WITH THE ROOK. This is why Re1 was played.

If you recapture with the bishop you get a normal, slightly dull position. With the rook you get an attack.

THE ROOK RECAPTURE. This is the whole reason Re1 was played on move eight.

Ask yourself why it is better than 12.Bxe4. Answer: the bishop on e4 has no future - it stares at a pawn on b7. The rook has a future: h4.
TAKE WITH THE ROOK, not the bishop. This is the whole point of Re1.

TAKE WITH THE ROOK, not the bishop. This is the whole point of Re1: your rook lands on an active square where it eyes e6 and can swing sideways, and it keeps your bishop on the long b1-h7 diagonal for the coming attack.

TAKE WITH THE ROOK. This is why Re1 was played - it cannot be emphasised enough how important this recapture is. Taking with the bishop instead gives Black time to develop with ...Nf6 and ...Bd7, and far fewer attacking chances.
If you recapture with the bishop you get a normal, slightly dull position. With the rook you get an attack.

THE MOVE THAT DEFINES SECTION B. Because the rook, not the bishop, stood behind the e-pawn all along, White recaptures with the rook - and a rook on e4 has a completely different future to a bishop there. It can swing sideways along the fourth rank to attack the king directly.
Black tries to blockade d5 before the rook lift arrives.
The point of 12.Rxe4 - the rook heads straight for the kingside, leaving Black's king without a single natural defender.

A critical decision point for White here: whether to sacrifice the bishop on h6 immediately. As a rule, look first for ...f7-f5 as Black's most testing defensive resource in this whole structure - it costs Black real structural concessions (a hole on e5, a backward e-pawn) in exchange for king safety, which is usually a fair trade for him. Here White instead builds up first.
Improving further rather than committing to the sacrifice at once - a perfectly reasonable practical choice, though 14.Bxh6!? gxh6 15.Rxh6 was also directly promising.
This just hands White everything he was hoping for. Black had to try 14...f5 immediately.
Now the sacrifice is completely correct - Black's last defender of the dark squares around his own king is gone.
Threatening mate ideas around g7 and h7 simultaneously.
Adding yet another attacker down the newly opened lines - the point being g4-g5-g6 next, sealing the black king in completely.
Black finally sees the danger and returns the extra pawn to trade queens and survive into an endgame.
White's earlier attack has converted itself cleanly into a pawn up in a technically won rook ending.
Preventing the bishop from ever reaching its best square on c6.

SUMMARY: this is the reference game for facing ...Nbd7 - Re1, then e3-e4, and recapture with the ROOK on e4, never the bishop, whenever the position allows it. The point of Rxe4 over Bxe4 is entirely about what happens next: only the rook can swing to h4 (or g4, or f4) and join a direct kingside attack.
C.Goodman - J.Conde Poderoso, correspondence 1999.
A principled-looking central counter - meet a wing build-up with central play - but the timing is simply wrong here. Black's development is not far enough along to support it.

Correct in spirit, but this course includes it specifically because the game that follows shows how easy it is to misplay even a winning position - even for a strong, experienced Colle player. The cleaner path was 12.dxe5! Nxe5 13.Nxe5 Bxe5 14.Qh5, when White's bishop pair, development lead, and open lines add up to a completely dominant position with far less risk.
Another natural-looking move that lets the advantage slip. 13.Bh6! Re8 14.Ng5 kept up overwhelming pressure.
Black finds the only real defence, and the awkwardly placed rook on h4 suddenly has no good square.
A last, over-optimistic try. The calm 15.cxd4 would simply have kept the game roughly balanced.

A draw by perpetual check follows - a fair result after both sides missed their best tries. SUMMARY: two lessons in one game. First, the chess lesson - 11...e5 here is premature, since Black's pieces are not developed enough to support the central break, and 12.dxe5! simply refutes it. Second, and just as important: even a completely winning position needs to be converted accurately, move by move - a "won" position on the board is not the same thing as a won game until you actually find the moves. Honesty about your own mistakes, including in your own games, is part of getting better.
C.Lakdawala - K.Griffith, San Diego (rapid) 2012.
Black avoids the ...e5 liquidating break entirely and instead prepares a queenside fianchetto. The answer does not change: e3-e4 regardless.

A bishop recapture here, not a rook - with Black's centre pawn still on e6 rather than committed to e5, there is no e-file battery to build on, so the position resembles the Rubinstein French (1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nd2 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nbd7) with colours and a tempo in White's favour.
Preparing a queen-and-bishop battery aimed squarely at h7.
A necessary concession - without it, the coming Bh6/Qd3 ideas simply walk in.
Correctly avoiding the sharper 15...Bxf3!? lines, but this retreat is too slow. Black had to try to trade off the dangerous dark-squared bishop.
Open the game while ahead in development - always the reflex once the position allows it.
No draw - White declines the repetition and plays for more.
A serious miscalculation - Black hoped for counterplay against the rook and queen but missed a powerful zwischenzug.
The point - 24.Bxe4? Qxe5 would have let Black off completely, but this keeps everything under control.
A second zwischenzug - the knight on c5 is simply left hanging so that the attack can continue at full speed.
A fork that regains all the material with interest.
White now has two pieces and a strong attack for the exchange - a decisive material and positional edge.
The final breakthrough.

SUMMARY: another concrete demonstration that facing ...b6 without an early ...e5 does not change your plan - e3-e4 remains correct, and the resulting Rubinstein-French-style structure, a tempo up, is simply pleasant for White. Recognise the Rubinstein French comparison and you will feel instantly at home in this type of position.
C.Lakdawala - V.Akobian, SCCF Championship, Los Angeles 2001.
King is safe. Development is finished. Now the second half of the plan starts: the attack.
Both knights are out. Notice the knight goes to d2, not c3 - it must not block the c-pawn.

A move-order error, and a common one from players who normally play the Grunfeld or another fianchetto system with Black and are not familiar with Colle structures. The bishop belongs on b7 eventually, but not yet - Black has not finished developing his queenside knight, and ...Bd6 combined with an early ...b6 simply does not work together (this exact clash is why the repertoire treats the ...b6/...Be7 set-up completely differently - see Section C).
Open the position while ahead in development - the reflex you should have by now.
An attempt to complicate matters with a piece sacrifice, since Black's position is already unpleasant after any quiet continuation.
A zwischenzug: before recapturing on d4, White first kicks the f6-knight and wins a piece by force.

Black has scraped together three pawns for the piece, but this does not come close to compensation: he is miles behind in development, his dark squares are full of holes, and every white piece points at his king.
Heading for d4 and preparing Ba3, which will round up the wandering black queen.
Correct - both 15...Nbd7 and 15...Bb7 walk into immediate tactics.
Provoking further dark-square weaknesses around the black king.
Black defends tenaciously and reaches an endgame - but one still very much in White's favour.
Assess White's assets in the ending: a full development lead even this deep into the game, the bishop pair, permanently weak black dark squares, and clear infiltration squares on c6, c7 and b5.

SUMMARY: an out-of-book opponent who does not know Colle structures will often misplace a piece early - here, a bishop on d6 and a pawn on b6 that do not actually work together. When you spot it, the answer is always the same: open the position immediately with e3-e4 while you are still ahead in development.
C.Lakdawala - D.Lawrence, SCCF Championship, Los Angeles 2008.

SECTION C: Black develops solidly with ...Be7 instead of ...Bd6, and has not yet committed his queenside knight to c6. This is exactly the signal from Cursus 2 to abandon the normal c3/e4 plan and switch to the Reversed Stonewall instead.
Plan B, straight away. There is no point waiting - the moment ...Nc6 is not yet played to contest the e5-square, jump in.

If Black holds this move back with something like 7...Nfd7, White should simply continue in the same spirit with f2-f4 and, if the position calls for it, be ready to attack even with the king still in the centre - see the next game for exactly that idea.
The Stonewall pawn structure is complete: pawns on d4, e3 and f4 supporting a knight on e5.

As a rule in this whole repertoire, an early ...c5xd4 tends to help White far more often than not - it opens the long diagonal for White's queen bishop and the e-file for the major pieces, exactly as you learned in Cursus 1.
A further weakening. 10...f5 was more solid, blunting White's light-squared bishop even at some structural cost.
Ruling out both ...f6 and ...f5 in one move.
This only helps White's structure and attacking chances even more.
Forced, or White simply builds up a decisive attack unopposed.
Assess Black's position: a hole on e5, a backward e6-pawn, and serious dark-square weakness all across the kingside - a near-perfect French Defence structure for White to attack.
The knight returns to its favourite square, aiming straight at f7 and g6.
Necessary - none of the alternatives survive.
Preventing the freeing ...Nf7 and keeping the powerful bishop anchored on h6.
The point - the whole attack has been building toward this exact breakthrough.

SUMMARY: the Reversed Stonewall is entirely optional - you can always return to the normal plan with a well-timed d4xc5 if you prefer. But once you commit to f2-f4, remember the two automatic reflexes: punish an early ...c5xd4 hard, and treat any dark-square weakness around Black's king as an invitation for the dark-squared bishop and a knight route back through e5.
C.Lakdawala - P.Pena, San Diego (rapid) 2005.

NOW we play c3, because Black attacks d4 and we need to defend it.

GOLDEN RULE: play c3 only when Black plays ...c5. If you play c3 too early you waste a move.

NOW we play c3, because Black attacks d4 and we need to defend it.
GOLDEN RULE: play c3 only when Black plays ...c5. If you play c3 too early you waste a move.
The Queen's Indian fianchetto version of the same idea - Black has not committed a knight to c6 or d7, so the Stonewall plan is available exactly as before.
Straight to the plan, regardless of whether Black's bishop went to e7 or b7 first.
An idea borrowed from the French Defence - Black hopes to trade off White's powerful attacking bishop.

Declining. Even though the light-squared bishop looks cut off from the kingside now, White can work around it and, as this game shows, even attack with the king still uncastled if the position calls for it.

A committal decision - White's king has not castled, and here it may not castle at all. In a fully closed centre this is a legitimate and even a strong plan, since Black simply cannot open the position quickly enough to punish it. It should not be tried the moment there is any realistic central break available to the opponent.
Helping White yet again, as in the previous game.
A manoeuvre borrowed straight from the London System - the point is to force a further weakening of the dark squares around Black's king.
Black finally finds active counterplay.
Understandable, but this abandons the e5-blockade at exactly the wrong moment - Black had a real tactical chance here that goes unplayed.
Both sides survive their respective errors and the position resets.
A forced concession - White now takes total control of the dark squares.
Step one: the rook lifts, ready to swing across to f3 and control c3 at the same time.
Step two: the bishop re-routes to a3, where it dominates f8 and d6.
No one can dislodge this bishop.
Effectively sealing the kingside shut.

SUMMARY: this game is the proof that a well-prepared Reversed Stonewall attack does not need a safe king to succeed - if the centre is fully closed, g2-g4-g5 and h2-h4-h5 can be played even with the king still on e1 or f1. Do not try this the moment your own centre could still be opened by your opponent; here Black's own c5xd4 had already closed the position for good.
C.Lakdawala - P.Hummel, Los Angeles 1998.
The full Stonewall, this time against the ...b6/...Bb7 fianchetto rather than ...Be7 - confirmation that the plan travels equally well against either bishop development.
Black weighs up queenside castling given the obvious build-up on the other wing.
The single most important move to remember in the whole Stonewall structure: grab control of e4 as early as you possibly can, before Black's pieces get there first.
Preparing a future b2-b4 expansion.
Black opts for the sharper try, castling into the teeth of White's space advantage rather than short, where the kingside build-up would hit him even harder.
The correct moment for the central break - with the position now closed on the queenside, opening the centre only helps the side who is further ahead in development and space, which is White.
15...Bxd5, keeping the d5-square open for a piece rather than a pawn, held things together better.
Punishing the inaccuracy immediately.
Allowing the a-file to open is a serious concession here - keeping it closed with 18...b5 was called for.
Both c6 and d7 become tender squares.
Multi-purpose: covers f4, sets up a future battery there, and prepares Ne3 hitting both d5 and f5.
Principle: opposite-coloured bishops favour the attacker, and here that is White.
Black's last realistic try lay in 31...Rg5, though even then White keeps a large advantage.
The queen and knight together now dominate the position completely - Black's remaining dark squares are simply gone.

SUMMARY: whichever way Black fianchettoes - ...Be7 or the full ...b6/...Bb7 - and whichever way he eventually castles, the Reversed Stonewall plan stays the same: grab e4 with the queen first, then expand with a2-a4-a5 or f4-f5 depending on which side gives the faster attack.
C.Lakdawala - W.Longren, SCCF Championship, 1995.
Rather than ...Bd6, Black develops modestly to e7 first and waits.
With the knight already headed for c6, e5 is covered and the Stonewall plan is off the table for this game.
The identical structural problem as the previous game - Black's knight covers e5, so the Stonewall plan is not available here either.

THE CRITICAL MOMENT OF THE WHOLE GAME, and the entire reason this game is in the course. Recapturing with the knight drops White into a passive Open-Sicilian-type structure with no real activity to show for it. Compare this directly with the next game, where 9.cxd4! is shown to be correct - keeping central control rather than handing it away for a knight move that achieves nothing.
A powerful centralising move. Yes, the knight can be met by f2-f4 later on, gaining a further tempo - but Capablanca already has a much deeper point in mind.
Consistently improving every piece while White's structure only gets more committal.
Black now controls the long light-squared diagonal, the dark squares around d4, and has a clear plan, while White's attack has not actually started.
Every White piece drifts further from home while every Black piece finds a natural, useful post.

A deliberate positional decision: giving up the bishop pair and the dark squares in exchange for total domination of the light squares and specifically the blockade on d5 - years ahead of its time for 1929.
Challenging the head of White's pawn chain - unusual advice in general, but correct here, since it opens the f-file exactly where White is weakest.
Every one of White's remaining pawns and pieces now comes under fire at once.

SUMMARY: the single lesson to take from this loss - if Black opens the c-file with an early ...c5xd4 against the Queen's Indian set-up, recapture with the PAWN, not the knight. 9.Nxd4?! hands Black exactly what he wants: an open, comfortable game with no target to attack, while White's own attacking chances never materialise. See the next game for the correct treatment of the identical structure.
E.Colle - J.R.Capablanca, Karlsbad 1929.

THE CORRECT ANSWER, and the direct fix for White's mistake in the previous game. Recapturing with the pawn keeps the full centre intact and gives White a real space advantage to build on - exactly the difference between a passive position and an active one.
Trying to exploit the momentarily undefended d3-bishop and c2-square.
The knight reaches what looks like a dream outpost.
At first glance Black looks comfortable: the bishop pair, no more light-squared bishop staring at h7, and easy development ahead. Do not be fooled - White has one powerful resource still in reserve.

THE KEY MOVE OF THE WHOLE STRUCTURE. This single central thrust is worth more than Black's whole set of small structural gains, since it opens the position right when White is by far the better developed side.

The original, and still a common, inaccuracy here. Note the trap for the natural-looking alternative: castling immediately loses on the spot to 13...O-O?? 14.d6!, when Black cannot deal with the threats along the newly opened long diagonal and against e7.
Simple and correct - Black already has no fully satisfactory answer.
A double attack that more or less forces Black's reply.
Paralysing Black completely along the dark squares - the bishop pair Black won a few moves ago now counts for nothing.
Clearance - opening the position fully for the remaining pieces.
White's pieces flood into the position with decisive effect.
A double attack on the a6-bishop and the threat of Nd6+, winning material by force.
Attacking the a8-rook while simultaneously covering g2 - real economy of force.
Threatening Re4 followed by Qxf7+.
Removing Black's only genuinely useful piece.

SUMMARY, AND FOR THE WHOLE COURSE: the difference between these last two games is a single recapture - 9.Nxd4?! for Colle against Capablanca, 9.cxd4! here - yet it decided everything. That is really what this entire course has been about: not memorising forty-move games, but training the instinct for the two or three moves in each structure that actually matter. Go back through Sections A to D with that same question in mind - which move was the hinge the whole game turned on? - and you will get more out of a second pass through these twenty games than most players get from a hundred.

SECTION E, a short but important appendix. Your main plan against the Queen's Indian fianchetto is the Reversed Stonewall from Section C - but that plan depends on getting your knight to e5 before Black finishes developing. If Black castles and strikes with ...c5 quickly enough, backed up by ...Nc6 controlling e5, the Stonewall may simply not be available. These last two games show what happens then: one full-blooded warning, and one clean demonstration of how to actually handle it. This particular game is included deliberately as a loss - even the founder of our whole system got this one badly wrong, and the mistake is exactly the kind worth seeing once so you never make it yourself.

THIS COURSE IS DIFFERENT FROM THE OTHER THREE.

The opening courses tell you WHICH MOVES to play. This one tells you WHAT TO DO once the opening is over - which is where almost every game is actually decided.

THE PRINCIPLE: openings do not produce positions, they produce STRUCTURES. The Colle produces only five. Learn the plan for each structure and you will never again reach move 15 without knowing what to do.

THE FIVE STRUCTURES:
1. THE GREEK GIFT - the h7 sacrifice. Not really a structure but a recurring pattern you must recognise instantly.
2. THE ROOK LIFT - your rook swings to h4 and joins the attack.
3. THE e5 WEDGE - pawn on e5, knight support, kingside pawn storm.
4. THE ISOLATED PAWN - you play against it, or with it.
5. BISHOP PAIR VERSUS SPACE - the slow anti-Colle games.

HOW TO STUDY THESE GAMES:
Do not memorise the moves. Play through each game once, then close the file and ask yourself: what was White's plan, and what was the move that made it work? If you can answer that, you have got what you need.

Every game here was actually played. The commentary explains the PLAN, not the variations.

WELCOME TO THE COLLE SYSTEM.

WHY THIS OPENING IS PERFECT FOR YOU RIGHT NOW:
You play almost the same seven moves in every single game. You do not need to memorise twenty different openings. You do not need to know what your opponent plays. You set up your pieces the same way, and then you attack.

Most players your level lose games in the opening because they do not know what to do. After this course, you will always know what to do.

THE SEVEN MOVES YOU MUST KNOW BY HEART:
d4, Nf3, e3, Bd3, Nbd2, O-O, and c3 (only when needed).
That is it. Learn these and you have an opening for life.

- Lesson 3: The bishop sacrifice on h7 (the knockout punch)
- Lesson 4-6: What to do when Black plays something else
- Lesson 7: The three mistakes that cost you the game

TIME NEEDED: about two hours. Then start playing it immediately.

THIS IS THE BIG ONE. Twenty complete tournament games, chosen because every single one lands on a position from YOUR repertoire - the same c3 Colle-Koltanowski lines you already studied in Cursus 1-3. Nothing here is a random "Colle game found on the internet." Every game was checked move by move against the lines you were taught, and only kept if it matches.
WHY A WHOLE COURSE OF COMPLETE GAMES?
Opening theory tells you WHAT to play. Model games teach you HOW to play it - what the pieces are actually trying to do once the book moves run out, which plans work, which plans look good but do not, and what a real opponent does when things go wrong for him. You cannot get that from a variations tree. You can only get it from full games.
HOW THIS COURSE IS ORGANISED - the same opening tree logic as Cursus 4, but far bigger:
SECTION A - The main line and the Nc6 set-up (5 games)
SECTION B - The Nbd7 set-up and the Re1/Rxe4 recapture (6 games)
SECTION C - The Reversed Stonewall, against ...Be7 and ...b6 (4 games)
SECTION D - The Phoenix, 9.b4 (3 games)
SECTION E - Colle versus Queen's Indian, when the Stonewall is not available (2 games)
Every lesson starts on move 1, exactly like the other courses, so ChessTempo folds everything into one giant opening tree. You do not need to remember which lesson is which - just play through them in order.
HOW TO STUDY: play each game through once at normal speed without stopping. Then go back and read the comments at the marked moments - these are the moves where a plan succeeds, a plan fails, or a tactic decides the game. This course does for your Black repertoire what the Model Games Encyclopedia already did for your Colle-Koltanowski White repertoire: it takes every structure you have learned in the Speedcourse, Intermediate and Advanced courses and shows it played out by strong players, usually with Black in exactly your seat.

Pavlovic compares the Meran to the Open Sicilian, and the comparison is exact: sharp, concrete, and unforgiving of general principles. This course gives you the modern main lines and, where a line is genuinely too heavy to learn from a course, says so instead of pretending.

WHAT YOU ADD HERE:
1. The modern Meran with 9.a3 and 11.Qc2 - the current main battleground.
2. The critical Anti-Meran and Catalan set-ups.
3. The Moscow Gambit, which is the upgrade you were promised in the earlier courses.
4. An honest account of which of our positions are equal rather than better.

THE ONE HABIT THAT MATTERS MOST: in every line of this course, ask when to take on c4 and when to break with ...c5. Get those two decisions right and the rest follows.

AN HONEST AUDIT OF YOUR 1.d4 REPERTOIRE.

WHERE WE ARE GENUINELY FINE:
- The Meran with 9.a3 and 11...Rc8. Modern, tested, and balanced.
- The Anti-Meran with 6.Qc2. The queen really does end up misplaced on c2.
- The Catalan set-up with 5.g3. Lakdawala is right that White is the one taking a risk.
- The Exchange Slav with 6...Ne4. Not better, but full of play.

WHERE WE ARE EQUAL AND SHOULD BE HAPPY WITH IT:
- The Moscow with 6.Bxf6 Qxf6. We have the bishop pair and no weaknesses. Do not over-press.

WHERE WE MAKE A CONCESSION:
- Against 6.Bh4 we either accept a gambit that demands real study, or we decline and give White a comfortable game. There is no third road. Choose deliberately, and do not pretend the declining line is objectively equal - it is sound, not equalising.

WHERE THE THEORY MOVES FASTEST:
The Meran and the Moscow Gambit. If you take those up, expect to refresh them every year or two. The Exchange Slav, the Catalan set-up and the London lines will still be valid in ten years.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR HOW YOU SPEND YOUR TIME:
Put your study hours into the lines that do not expire, and use a reliable declining line in the ones that do - unless the sharp line is genuinely your style. A repertoire you maintain badly is worse than a slightly quieter one you know well.

NOTHING YOU LEARNED IS REPLACED. Every move from the Speedcourse stays correct. What you add here is depth and, above all, timing.

- 5.Bg5 h6 6.Bxf6 is called the Moscow by most sources, and the Anti-Moscow by Lakdawala.
- 5.Bg5 h6 6.Bh4 is the Anti-Moscow to most sources, and the Moscow Gambit to Lakdawala.
Do not worry about the labels. Learn the positions.

THE THREE THINGS THAT MATTER AT THIS LEVEL:
1. WHEN to play ...dxc4. The same capture is bad on one move and excellent two moves later. Lessons 01 and 03 are entirely about this.
2. WHERE the light-squared bishop belongs. Sometimes f5, sometimes b7, and once neither. Lesson 08 has the exception.
3. WHAT to do once theory ends around move fourteen. Lesson 10 collects the plans.

THE FOUR STRUCTURES OF YOUR 1.d4 REPERTOIRE.

Most of your games leave theory around move fourteen. What decides them is whether you recognise the structure in front of you.

1. THE MERAN STRUCTURE (pawns a6-b5-c5 against White's centre).
Plan: ...Bb7, ...a6, then ...c5. After d4-d5 and the exchange on e6, use the f-file and think seriously about castling long.
Do not: hurry ...c5 before ...a6 - the break loses its force.

2. THE MOSCOW STRUCTURE (we own the bishop pair, no weaknesses).
Plan: ...g6 and ...Bg7, then ...e5 or ...c5 at the right moment.
Do not: rush. The bishop pair does not expire; improve a piece and wait.

3. THE DOUBLED g-PAWN STRUCTURE (after Nxg6 hxg6).
Plan: use the open h-file, and remember that f5 and h5 are permanently denied to White.
Do not: think of the doubled pawns as a weakness. You accepted them on purpose.

4. THE SYMMETRICAL EXCHANGE STRUCTURE.
Plan: ...Ne4 and ...f5, or a minority attack with ...b5-b4.
Do not: assume a draw.

THE HABIT TO BUILD: at move fourteen, before calculating anything, name the structure. Then play the plan.

THE BRIDGE TO YOUR WHITE REPERTOIRE: three of these four structures appear in the Colle course from the other side. The e5-outpost you build with White is the outpost you must deny with Black. The Bxh7 sacrifice you look for with White is the one you defuse with ...h6 and ...Nf8. Studying both colours of the same structure is the fastest way to understand it.

The declining line in Lesson 06 and the London treatment in Lesson 09 are practical recommendations for this level rather than book lines.

THE SEMI-SLAV. Look at our pawns: c6, d5 and e6.

WHY THIS FORMATION IS SO GOOD:

THE MERAN. Now our plan is fixed and easy to remember:
1. Take on c4 with tempo.
2. Play ...b5 to gain queenside space.
3. Put the bishop on b7, where it finally gets the long diagonal.
4. Break with ...c5 to open the position for our pieces.

That is four moves and one idea. Learn it and you will never be lost in this opening.

THE ANTI-MERAN. A tricky waiting move, and it does four things at once:
1. It prepares b3, so that after a later ...dxc4 White can recapture with a PAWN instead of the bishop - denying us the whole ...b5 plan.
2. It keeps a sharp g4 advance in reserve (the so-called Shirov Attack). We are not going to provoke it.
3. The queen already eyes the b1-h7 diagonal, ready to support Bd3 or Ng5 ideas later.
4. If we do get our ...dxc4 and ...b5 in anyway, the queen aims straight at our backward c6-pawn and the hole on c5.

THE MOSCOW VARIATION proper. White gives up the bishop pair for extra space and a small lead in development. Grandmaster Alexey Dreev, who has played this exact structure as Black dozens of times, sums up the whole idea in one sentence: White is betting that he can put his space and development to use before our two bishops start to matter. If he plays passively, he loses that bet.

THE STRUCTURE: we own the bishop pair and have no structural weaknesses at all. White has slightly more space and easier short-term piece play.

THIS IS THE MOST UNDERRATED POSITION IN YOUR WHOLE REPERTOIRE, because it teaches patience - the hardest skill to sell to a club player.

THE TRAPS YOU MUST AVOID.

1. In the Advance, ...e6 before the bishop is out. This is not a small inaccuracy - it is the whole variation thrown away. You reach an Advance French a tempo down, and Lakdawala calls it a clear mistake.

2. In the Advance with 4.dxc5, spending two or three moves recovering the pawn immediately. Develop first. The pawn usually comes back on its own.

3. In the Tartakower, recapturing with the g-pawn. 5...gxf6 is a completely different variation with a different character and much more risk.

4. In the Panov, ...Nc6 instead of ...Nbd7 at the wrong moment, allowing d4-d5 with tempo.

THE TRAPS YOU CAN SET:

1. The delayed pin. In the Tartakower, play ...Re8 before ...Bg4 and let White commit to h3. Most opponents play it automatically and hand you a target for the rest of the game.

2. The delayed capture. Against 6.Qc2 setups and in the Advance with 4.c3, wait until White commits a knight before taking or releasing the tension. The same move is worth much more two moves later.

3. The queen retreat. Against system players, provoking a committal pawn move and then retreating the queen is a real gain, even though it looks like you wasted time. Students hate this - teach it explicitly.

THE HABIT THAT SEPARATES 1600 FROM 2000:
Before every capture and every developing move, ask one question: does this move commit me to something? If yes, can I wait one move and make my opponent commit first?

THE FOUR STRUCTURES OF YOUR CARO REPERTOIRE.

Most of your games leave theory around move twelve. What decides them is whether you recognise which of these four you are in.

1. THE ADVANCE FRENCH STRUCTURE (pawns e5 vs e6/d5, our bishop OUTSIDE the chain).
Plan: pressure d4 with ...Nc6, ...Qb6, ...Nf5. Trade the light-squared bishops if you can. Break with ...f6 only when your pieces are ready.
Do not: play ...e6 before the bishop is out. That is the whole variation thrown away.

2. THE TARTAKOWER STRUCTURE (doubled f-pawns, open e-file).
Plan: ...Bd6, ...Re8, ...Nd7-f8, ...Be6, ...Qd7 and play against h3 or with ...f5.
Do not: allow mass exchanges into an endgame. Our structure is a middlegame asset and an endgame liability.

3. THE ISOLATED PAWN STRUCTURE (from the Panov).
Plan: survive the middlegame, trade pieces, then attack the pawn. Blockade the square in front of it.
Do not: weaken your king to avoid the initiative. Sit tight - it fades.

4. THE SYMMETRICAL STRUCTURE (from the Exchange).
Plan: create imbalance. ...Ne4, ...b5-b4, or the ...e5 break.
Do not: assume it is a draw. Symmetry is not equality.

THE SINGLE MOST USEFUL HABIT YOU CAN BUILD:
At move twelve, before you calculate anything, ask yourself which of these four structures is on the board. Then play the plan. Most opponents at your level do not do this, and that is where your extra points come from.

A COMPLETELY DIFFERENT APPROACH. White is not fighting for the centre move by move - he is heading for a fixed set-up (knight on d2, fianchetto on g2, often Re1 and a kingside pawn storm with Nh4, f4 and g4) regardless of what we do. This can also arise from a 1.Nf3, 1.g3 or 1.d3 move-order.
The main move.

GRAB THE CENTRE IMMEDIATELY - the single most important idea in this whole lesson. Do not wait passively for White to finish his set-up; stake your claim in the middle right away, before he is ready to meet it.
The central grab you already know from the Speedcourse. At this level we go two moves deeper on both of White's serious tries.

THE CORE PRINCIPLE against the King's Indian Attack set-up, wherever you meet it in this repertoire: if White declines to contest the centre, take it yourself, immediately and without hesitation. White's whole KIA plan depends on a slow build-up with Ngf3, g3, Bg2 and O-O; a prompt ...e5 denies him the chance to do that on his own terms.
Covers e5, prepares quick development, and eyes h2 later - the same idea as our bishop on d6 in Lesson 05.
Developing actively and preparing quick kingside castling - there is no need for special measures against the King's Indian Attack once Black already controls the centre.
Preparing to meet a future ...dxe4 with tempo, and keeping an eye on the e-file.
White's most testing try, opening the position immediately rather than continuing the slow fianchetto build-up.

EXCERPT NOTE: this reaches a normal isolani middlegame, transposing in spirit to structures you already know well from the Panov and Semi-Slav branches of your repertoire - the same plans (pressure down the c- and e-files, trading down toward a favourable minor-piece ending) apply directly.

TAKEAWAY: the King's Indian Attack is not a system to fear. Meeting it with an early, well-timed ...e5 turns White's quiet set-up into an open isolani position where Black's activity and structural soundness generally outweigh White's slightly easier development.

I.Glek-A.Dreev, European Club Cup, Saint Vincent 2005.
